1 Corinthians 9:20-21: and to the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might win Jews; to those who are under the law, as under the law, that I might win those who are under the law; to those who are without law, as without law (not being without law toward God, but under law toward Christ), that I might win those who are without law; Psalm 141:2: Let my prayer be set before You as incense, The lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice.
What does he say “without law” means in 1 Corinthians 9:21?

He says “you’re not under the civil law, you’re under the shadow laws fulfilled in Christ,” and that those without law are “still under law to Christ.” He says Paul went among people without approving them but “accepting them and respecting them where they’re at to preach the gospel.”
What does he say “without law” means in 1 Corinthians 9:21?

law as without law.” And then he clarifies this, because there’s a lot of people say, “I’m not under law.” What law? The shadow law. You’re not under the civil law, you’re under the shadow laws fulfilled in Christ. You’re under, ain’t that right, your faith must be in Jesus’s death on the cross, the shadow law fulfilled. Amen. “Not being without law toward God, but under law toward Christ.” See, he plainly says those without law are still under law to Christ, cuz he fulfilled all the shadows, “that I might win those who are,” what? “Without law.” In other words, whatever choice people made, it didn’t bother him from going right in their midst and preaching the gospel and accepting them where they’re at, not approving them but accepting them and respecting them where they’re at to preach the gospel, that he might win them. And what in America we’re divided. Man, anybody doesn’t believe our way, we won’t go near them, they don’t go near us. You know why? Because we don’t have people that are really mature, really free in themselves, that can handle
What does he say “without law” means in 1 Corinthians 9:21?

1 Corinthians 9:20-21: and to the Jews I became as a Jew, that I might win Jews; to those who are under the law, as under the law, that I might win those who are under the law; to those who are without law, as without law (not being without law toward God, but under law toward Christ), that I might win those who are without law;
What does “to the weak I became as weak” mean?

He says Americans are divided because “we don’t have people that are really mature, really free in themselves, that can handle opposition.” He links 1 Corinthians 9:22 to the earlier teaching on meat sacrificed to idols and says extreme worry is a kind of weakness.
What does “to the weak I became as weak” mean?

opposition that is obviously against the Bible. You know, we want to judge them, we want to point our finger, and we want to separate from them, but Paul says, “Hey, I go right in the midst of them, I don’t care what stage they’re at, I’m going to go in and preach the gospel that I might win some.” Isn’t that a good attitude? Isn’t that a good focus? Verse 22 of chapter 9, “To the weak I became as weak.” Now, remember we learned last week that a person who was so extreme in idol worship that they would want to check out whether the meat was sacrificed to idols or not, did it have the kosher stamp of approval, and Paul says, you know, that’s extreme, that’s weak, just get the meat and don’t ask any questions, because meat’s nothing, ain’t that right? And if someone says, “You’re not sacrificed to idols,” then don’t use it, because it’s going to violate their conscience. And so when we get to extremes, we are what?
What does “to the weak I became as weak” mean?
1 Corinthians 9:22: to the weak I became as weak, that I might win the weak. I have become all things to all men, that I might by all means save some.
What does “all things to all men” not mean?

He says Paul went to people “in any condition they were in, that he might win some and preach the gospel,” but he did not partake of sexual immorality or get drunk with them: “common sense tells you that.” He reads 1 Corinthians 9:22 as winning people, not joining their sin.
What does “all things to all men” not mean?

Weak. Did that bother Paul? No, he went in and ministered to them anyway. He would go to the pagans’ houses, or even the believers’ houses where they were doing these festivals and sacrifices, and at their homes, and partaking, and to preach the gospel to them. Hallelujah. “I became all things to all men, that I might save some.” Now, does that mean he went to the prostitutes and partook of sexual immorality? Does that mean he went to the drunks and got drunk with them? No, come on, common sense tells you that. What he did, he just went in any condition they were in, that he might win some and preach the gospel to
What does “all things to all men” not mean?
1 Corinthians 9:22: to the weak I became as weak, that I might win the weak. I have become all things to all men, that I might by all means save some.
What is the goal in 1 Corinthians 9:23, and what does it mean to be a partaker?

He says the goal is to be “a partaker of the gospel prize,” not just a hearer or talker. He says “you don’t possess it till you got it,” and that Christians think they possess the gospel because they have heard it. He mentions that a Bible study on possessing the promises drew no interest.
What is the goal in 1 Corinthians 9:23, and what does it mean to be a partaker?

them. Now we come to verse 23 of 1 Corinthians 9. He’s going to talk about the goal. He’s going to give us the goal, and he’s going to give us what the goal is, and he’s going to tell us that we need to be a partaker of the goal, not just a hearer of the goal, not just a talker of the goal, but a what? Partaker. Say the word: partaker. I sent out a flyer back in November and December about a Bible study, “Possessing the Promises,” and no one was interested. See, Christians think because they’ve heard the gospel they possess the gospel, but you don’t possess it till you got it. See, you don’t have joy till you got joy, you don’t have peace till you got peace, you don’t have wisdom till you got wisdom, you didn’t hear a message about it, you got to possess it. And Paul is going to tell, you tell us the goal of this whole thing is to be a partaker of the gospel prize. Verse 23, “All this I do,” preaching without being paid, going to every stage of everyone in the country, whatever stage they’re at, “all this I do for the gospel’s sake.” You see, remember he said it’s just in me, I got to preach the gospel, ain’t that right? I’m not up there to, to be in front, “Look at me, I’m an apostle, look at me, I’m a worshipper, look at me, I have a ministry in God’s house.” I get sick and tired of people saying “my
What is the goal in 1 Corinthians 9:23, and what does it mean to be a partaker?
1 Corinthians 9:23: Now this I do for the gospel’s sake, that I may be partaker of it with you.
Why does he say Paul still says he must remain a partaker?

He says Paul’s “whole motive” was “the gospel, to win people to Christ,” and that even as an apostle who had seen Christ and done miracles, he said “I do these things so I can keep being a partaker of the gospel.” He says Paul uses natural illustrations, which confuse many readers until the Spirit reveals truth “line upon line.”
Why does he say Paul still says he must remain a partaker?

ministry.” You give up your ministry, you might get to be one in attitude, I’m talking about, are you there? He said my whole motive, my whole source of action is the gospel, to win people to Christ, and not just win them to Christ, he wants to do something with them after he wins them to Christ, “that I might be a partaker of the gospel with you.” Now he’s specifically talking in the first person, he’s an apostle, but he does all these things that as an apostle he is still a what? Partaker, a participant, a reaper of the benefits. He’s saying I want to be a partaker with you, I’m the one to preach to you, but I still have to live a life that keeps me a partaker. Now that was a good statement, did you hear that statement? He is using himself, and those he’s seen Christ and he’s done miracles, he still, he still says, “I do these things so I can keep being a partaker of the gospel.” And then he goes on in verse 24, “Those who run in a race all run.” Now, he’s using a natural illustration, this is his, this is his method of doing things, he uses natural and scriptural illustrations, he’s really good, but in doing it, it confuses a lot of people when they read his epistles. Would you raise a hand and say, “Yeah, that’s me”? You see, and we got to remember it’s the Spirit that reveals things to us, and so you can’t understand Paul until, this, you, you really get a hunger and a compelling for truth, then the Spirit starts, little by little, line upon line, precept upon precept, revealing truths to
Why does he say Paul still says he must remain a partaker?

1 Corinthians 9:23: Now this I do for the gospel’s sake, that I may be partaker of it with you. Isaiah 28:10: For precept must be upon precept, precept upon precept, Line upon line, line upon line, Here a little, there a little.”
What does the race in 1 Corinthians 9:24 teach?

He reads 1 Corinthians 9:24, “those who run in a race all run,” and that only one receives the prize. He says “you got to get across the line.” He says being in the race is not enough: “the reward goes to the one that crosses the line.” He says Paul gives four qualifications for the prize.
What does the race in 1 Corinthians 9:24 teach?

you. “So those who run in a race all run, but how many received the prize?” One. When I ran a 100-yard dash back in my fast days, coming in second place didn’t do anything, you might as well come in last, the only guy that was declared the winner was the guy who went across the line first. Isn’t that right? So he, he’s using a natural illustration. “Run in such a way that you may,” what? “Obtain the prize.” Obtain the prize of the gospel. See, you got to run, you got to get across the line, you got to finish the race. It’s not anything if you’re just in the race, the reward goes to the one that crosses the line. Amen. Better is the end of, of a thing than the beginning. “Oh, I’m in the race,” big deal. You got to get across the line, you got to get the prize, you got to be a partaker. Four qualifications to getting the prize. Okay, four qualifications he’s going to give. I tell you, this guy’s good, I’m glad I’m his microphone. “Grace and faith is all you
What does the race in 1 Corinthians 9:24 teach?

1 Corinthians 9:24: Do you not know that those who run in a race all run, but one receives the prize? Run in such a way that you may obtain it. Ecclesiastes 7:8: The end of a thing is better than its beginning; The patient in spirit is better than the proud in spirit.
What does he say being self-controlled in all things means?

He reads 1 Corinthians 9:25 and says the first qualification is being “temperate,” meaning self-controlled, which covers tongue, body, temper, drugs, sex life and anger. He says “self-control is a spiritual thing,” that Paul too is “still vulnerable to losing the prize,” and mentions that he himself was once a drug addict.
What does he say being self-controlled in all things means?

need.” We’ll see, we’ll see. Grace, faith, water baptism. “Everyone who competes for the,” what prize? What prize? The gospel’s prize, the gospel’s reward, “is first of all temperate.” Self-controlled. Whoa. Self-controlled. Yeah, it’s your job to control your tongue, it’s your job to control your body. Self-control is a spiritual thing, you don’t have to [unclear] and feel the vibes and shake, you have self-control, God will give you, you got to use self-control. You got to zip that lip, you got to put water and quench that fiery temper of yours, you got to muzzle your mouth, you, it, you got to refrain from hitting someone because they hit you or they said something. You got to use what? Self-control. And he says I got to, to do this so that I gain the prize with you. I am still vulnerable to losing the prize. I might have signs and wonders in my life, I might have patience and, and all these signs of an apostle and my, and my care for the gospel, but I must maintain it so I win it with you. And self-controlled in how many things? Oh, well, I got drugs under control. Well, big deal, get your sex life under control, get your anger under control. I mean, I deal with sinners, and yeah, you get them off drugs and they think that’s it. No, no, no, there’s a lot of things in your life that have to be delivered from, it’s not just drugs. I was once a drug addict, big deal, you’re having sex with everybody around you. You got to be what? Self-controlled in all things. All right, now, “they do it to obtain a perishable crown, but we for an imperishable one,” an eternal one. All right, verse 26, “Therefore,” for this reason, “I run this way,” this is how I run the race, I’m not only self-controlled but I run with confidence,
What does he say being self-controlled in all things means?
1 Corinthians 9:25: And everyone who competes for the prize is temperate in all things. Now they do it to obtain a perishable crown, but we for an imperishable crown.
What does running with confidence and boxing mean in 1 Corinthians 9:26?

He says Paul runs “with confidence, not with uncertainty,” and says “Christians are so indecisive.” He reads Philippians 4:13 and says we should stop saying “I’m just no good.” He explains “I box” as fighting to “put my flesh under control” and knocking out “my adversaries,” not shadowboxing.
What does running with confidence and boxing mean in 1 Corinthians 9:26?

not with uncertainty. I run this race with confidence. Amen. I mean, I’m out to get this, I’m on this track to win the race, I’m not out to just, you know, move around the track, I’m going to, I’m getting across that line, I’m going to do it with confidence, not uncertainty, not doubt, not indecision. Christians are so indecisive, hesitation. “Well, am I saved or am I not saved? I don’t know if I’m sa—“ He said you’re saved, get, get moving, get running the race. Amen. He said, “I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me.” “Well, I’m just the flea on the dog, you know, I’m just no good.” Oh, yes, we’re all no good, back up and run the race. Amen. And that’s what David said when he got down, “I’m just a flea on the dog, I’m just no good.” No, we all know we’re no good when you stand by Christ. Good Lord, who can line up to him? But we are in the race to be like him. “I fight, I box.” The word is “box.” He’s using the, the [unclear] games again, they had games there every two years and competition, and he’s talking about the boxing. “I box, I fight, not as one who beats the air.” I don’t go in the ring and just shadowbox and there’s no opponent there, there’s nothing to conquer. He said I box to beat the enemy, to put my flesh under control, to overcome these things, I’m, I’m fighting to knock out my
What does running with confidence and boxing mean in 1 Corinthians 9:26?

1 Corinthians 9:26-27: Therefore I run thus: not with uncertainty. Thus I fight: not as one who beats the air. But I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, lest, when I have preached to others, I myself should become disqualified. Philippians 4:13: I can do all things through Christ who strengthens me.
What does he say about leaving the fighting to ministers and disciplining the body?

He says some want ministers “to do our fighting for us,” sending money so someone else will pray, when “you got to fight.” He says Paul disciplines his body and brings it “into subjection,” and that we choose our habits: “you weren’t born that way, you chose that way.” He mentions a recent celebrity death as an example, by name in the transcript only.
What does he say about leaving the fighting to ministers and disciplining the body?

adversaries. Allelujah. Now, we want the ministers to do our fighting for us. Now, instead of us going to the prayer, we just send in an offering to [unclear] Roberts or somebody to go to the prayer tower and do our praying for us. And, you know, this is true in America, you know, instead of going to college and learning a degree or, or a technical school and learning a job skill or on-the-job training to learn a good job skill, oh, we just send our money to Benny [unclear] so that God will just rain money from heaven on us. Hallelujah. No, you got to fight. He’s got to fight to win the prize, even though he’s got the prize right now, and he’s telling you you got to fight the same way I do, you got to run this race the same way I do. Isn’t this good? Now, see, he gives us these qualifications. He said, “I discipline my body and bring it into subjection,” or bring my body into slavery. I don’t do what my body wants to do, my body does what I wanted to do. “Well, I just, you know, I was just born this way, that I just got to have alcohol, or I got to have drugs,” like they said of, uh, Whitney Houston over the weekend. You weren’t born that way, you chose that way. You got to bring your body into discipline, restrain it, make it a slave of you. When that body doesn’t want to get out of bed and pray, you say, “Body, get out of bed. Arms, lift yourself up. Mouth, move.” And you know what? They obey.
What does he say about leaving the fighting to ministers and disciplining the body?

1 Corinthians 9:26-27: Therefore I run thus: not with uncertainty. Thus I fight: not as one who beats the air. But I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, lest, when I have preached to others, I myself should become disqualified.
Why does he say Paul could be disqualified?

He reads 1 Corinthians 9:27, “lest when I have preached the gospel to others, I myself become disqualified,” and says “there goes once saved always saved right out the door.” He says Judas “at one time was saved” and preached and healed but was “in the end… disqualified.” This is his view.
Why does he say Paul could be disqualified?

You, you know, your body doesn’t make you watch TV four hours a night. You can get up and turn it off and listen to good Christian worship or read the Bible or have a Bible, you know, you have mastery over your body. Hallelujah. And he says this: “lest when I have preached the gospel to others, I myself become disqualified.” He’s an apostle, he was raised from the dead, he has done miracles, he has led many to Christ, and he can be disqualified. Wow. There goes once saved always saved right out the door. Yeah, don’t you believe that big lie. Judas at one time was saved, but he didn’t wind up being saved, did he? Judas once preached the gospel, cast out demons, and healed the sick, big deal, in the end he was what? Disqualified. And Paul knew this. He failed the test, he failed the qualifications, he didn’t keep the qualifications. He said it’s possible for me, who has exercised these qualifications, to violate them and become
Why does he say Paul could be disqualified?

1 Corinthians 9:26-27: Therefore I run thus: not with uncertainty. Thus I fight: not as one who beats the air. But I discipline my body and bring it into subjection, lest, when I have preached to others, I myself should become disqualified.
What does he say “disqualified” means, and does God empower us to reach the goal?

He says “disqualified” does not mean being benched but “getting kicked off the team.” He says that if Jesus gave us these goals, he empowers us to attain them, as with Abraham’s faith that God “had the power to perform what he promised,” but there are four requirements on our part.
What does he say “disqualified” means, and does God empower us to reach the goal?

disqualified. Wow. One preacher said it meant he was going to get benched. No, he’s getting kicked off the team, he’s getting kicked out of the gym, he’s getting kicked off the campus, he’s disqualified. He’s not even a benchwarmer. Wow. All of a sudden the things of God are serious, aren’t they? Now, if Jesus gave us these goals, does he empower us to attain to them? Yes. And see, that’s the faith Abraham had that was counted to him for righteousness in Galatians, that he had the faith, he believed that God had the power to perform what he promised. Now, if God can get us saved, can he keep us sav— and get us to the goal? Does he have the power? Yes. But is there requirements on my part? Yeah. Here’s four of them.
What does he say “disqualified” means, and does God empower us to reach the goal?

Romans 4:20-21: He did not waver at the promise of God through unbelief, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God, and being fully convinced that what He had promised He was also able to perform.
Who does he say the real leader of the church is?
He says “the real authority, the real boss, is Jesus Christ.”
Does he say ministers should force people to pay?
No. He says “you don’t force people to pay anything, they’ve got to do it from the drawing of Christ.”
What is another word he gives for “servant” in 1 Corinthians 9:19?
What does he mean by shadow laws?
He says “the sacrifice of the lamb was a shadow, an example of Christ coming to die for us,” and that the incense “was the example of prayer.”
Does he say the Old Testament civil laws changed?
No. He says “there are civil laws in the Old Testament which did not change, and then there’s shadow laws.”
Does “all things to all men” mean joining in sin?
No. He says Paul did not get drunk with drunks, and “common sense tells you that.”
What does he say a partaker is?
He says it is not “just a hearer of the goal, not just a talker of the goal” but a “partaker,” and a partaker is “a participant, a reaper of the benefits.”
How many receive the prize in a race, according to 1 Corinthians 9:24?
He says “one,” and “the only guy that was declared the winner was the guy who went across the line first.”
What is the first qualification for the prize?
He says it is being “temperate,” which he explains means “self-controlled.”
What does he mean by saying “I’m just a flea on the dog”?
He is describing a common thing people say about themselves, and says “we all know we’re no good when you stand by Christ,” but “we are in the race to be like him.”
Does he say we are born with habits we cannot control?
No. He says “you weren’t born that way, you chose that way,” and that you can “bring your body into discipline.”
Does he say once saved always saved is true?
No. He says “don’t you believe that big lie,” and that someone who was saved can end up “disqualified.”

items.d: In this message Pastor David G. Kincer shows from 1 Corinthians 10 that believers can displease God and be corrected, as Israel was even though they were under the cloud, through the sea and fed by the…
p: In this message Pastor David G. Kincer shows from 1 Corinthians 10 that believers can displease God and be corrected, as Israel was even though they were under the cloud, through the sea and fed by the spiritual rock. He teaches that the rock was Christ, explains water baptism and the rivers of living water, and warns the church not to lust, practice idolatry or sexual immorality.
Can believers displease God and be punished for it?

He says believers can displease God and be “disciplined for it,” and that a better word is “correction.” He lists ways God allowed Satan to correct His sinning people, including plagues, wars, famine, wild animals, family rebellion, harmful spirits and captivity, and says Christians don’t want to hear this “but it’s still Bible.”
Can believers displease God and be punished for it?

He’s going to show us that believers can displease God and be punished for it. A better word is correction. Say the word: correction. Correction. Be disciplined for it. And we find all throughout the Bible that God allowed Satan to correct God’s people that sinned through plagues, wars, acts of God, famine, wild animals, uh, family issues. David’s son died, uh, his sons rebelled, David had to deal with his own sons, uh, he caused rebellion in the home, uh, through, through Satan, uh, evil spirits, harmful spirits to individuals, and captivity. All these things can happen to, for God’s people to be corrected. But Christians don’t want to hear this, but it’s still Bible, and Paul’s going to approach this subject this morning. And, uh, a quick, short reminder: remember, one quarter of the 16th chapter is about division, which America is full of. All of us think we got the answer, and we don’t like the other guy that has a different answer. Uh, 3/16 of his seminar is about sexual immorality, and it’s bad in America and it’s bad in the church in our day. Then he talked about idolatry, and so he took up one half of this seminar on three subjects. Then he talked about himself being an apostle and clarifying what an apostle was, and then he gave us this tremendous example of how he pursued the gospel prize using four necessities to reach it, so that he, the apostle, called to the third heaven, saw Jesus personally, would not get disqualified while he was winning others.
What did Israel experience under the cloud and through the sea? (1 Corinthians 10:1)

He says Paul turns to the Corinthian believers and reminds them that all the fathers were under the cloud and passed through the sea. He cites Exodus 13:21 and 14:27, where God’s presence led them in a cloud and a pillar of fire and the Egyptian army was destroyed, and says today Satan is “destroyed through the death of the cross.”
What did Israel experience under the cloud and through the sea? (1 Corinthians 10:1)

And with that great statement, then he turns and he points to the Corinthian believers, and he says, “Moreover, brethren, I do not want you to be unaware that all of our fathers were under the cloud and all passed through the sea.” He directing everything at them. Now in Exodus 13:21, “The Lord went before them by day in a pillar of a cloud to lead the way.” See, they were all under the cloud. The cloud spread over them, and then there was a pillar of a cloud down leading them, and so God’s presence was there in the form of a cloud. They actually saw God in the form of a cloud and a pillar of fire, and He was leading the way. All right, in Exodus 14:27, “The Lord overthrew the Egyptians in the midst of the sea. There remained not one.” See, they all experienced the power of the enemy being destroyed. Paul knows what he’s doing here. Are you with me so far? Then we read in Revelation 7:17 that the New Testament church, “the Lamb shall feed them and lead them into living fountains of water.” See, they were headed for Canaan land, the Promised Land, but God’s leading us to living waters. Hallelujah. I get so excited about this, and you guys look at me like, “What?” Now, not only that, but in Hebrews 2:14, “through death Jesus destroyed him that had the power of death, that is the Devil.” So see, in the sea they had the enemy of the Egyptian army, the enemy that was wanting to destroy them, destroyed. But today we have who? Satan destroyed through the death of the cross. The power of the cross, the cross is powerful. See, Satan’s destroyed. Remember, he’s rendered powerless. He don’t have power over us anymore.
What did Israel experience under the cloud and through the sea? (1 Corinthians 10:1)

1 Corinthians 10:1: Moreover, brethren, I do not want you to be unaware that all our fathers were under the cloud, all passed through the sea, Exodus 13:21: And the LORD went before them by day in a pillar of cloud to lead the way, and by night in a pillar of fire to give them light, so as to go by day and night. Exodus 14:27-28: And Moses stretched out his hand over the sea; and when the morning appeared, the sea returned to its full depth, while the Egyptians were fleeing into it. So the LORD overthrew the Egyptians in the midst of the sea. Then the waters returned and covered the chariots, the horsemen, and all the army of Pharaoh that came into the sea after them. Not so much as one of them remained. Revelation 7:17: for the Lamb who is in the midst of the throne will shepherd them and lead them to living fountains of waters. And God will wipe away every tear from their eyes.” Hebrews 2:14: Inasmuch then as the children have partaken of flesh and blood, He Himself likewise shared in the same, that through death He might destroy him who had the power of death, that is, the devil,
What does “baptized unto Moses” and “spiritual food” mean? (1 Corinthians 10:2-3)

He says Paul is explaining that just as Israel experienced these things, we experience them. He quotes 1 Corinthians 10:2 and John 6:48, “I am the bread of life,” and says Israel had spiritual food “but they all died,” while those who eat Jesus’ food “will never die.”
What does “baptized unto Moses” and “spiritual food” mean? (1 Corinthians 10:2-3)

And so Paul is explaining just like they experienced these things, we experience these things. And then he says in verse 2, 1 Corinthians 10:2, “All were baptized unto Moses in the cloud and in the sea. All ate the same spiritual food.” Okay, every one of them. And in John 6:48, “I am the bread of life. Your fathers ate manna in the wilderness.” He said, yes, they had spiritual food, but they all died. You say, “But I’m the bread of life, you eat My food and you will never die.” Isn’t that beautiful?
What does “baptized unto Moses” and “spiritual food” mean? (1 Corinthians 10:2-3)

1 Corinthians 10:2-3: all were baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea, all ate the same spiritual food, John 6:48-50: I am the bread of life. Your fathers ate the manna in the wilderness, and are dead. This is the bread which comes down from heaven, that one may eat of it and not die.

He says we identify with the death, burial and resurrection of Christ, and “something is actually done in water baptism that a lot of people don’t understand.” He says we go into the grave with Christ and come out “a new creature,” and cites Romans 6 that the body of sin might be destroyed so that we would no longer serve sin.

And in Romans 6:4 and 6 he says, “We are buried with Jesus by baptism unto death.” This is why water baptism is important. You see, we identify with the death, burial and resurrection of Christ, and something is actually done in water baptism that a lot of people don’t understand, but they need to understand it. It’s not just a little sermon or ceremony, I’m sorry, that we do in the church. He says all of us are buried with Him. When we get water baptized, we go into the grave with Christ, and as Christ was raised up out of that grave by the glory of the Father, so we should walk in newness of life. You see, He came out of the grave, but we come out of the water a new creature. And now he doesn’t stop there. He goes on and says this: “Knowing that our old man of sin is crucified with Him,” in water baptism, “that the body of sin might be” what? Destroyed. See, God destroyed the Egyptian army over in Israel, but it was an illustration that He was going to destroy the sinful nature in the new covenant, “that the body of sin might be destroyed, that from this time forth he would not serve sin.” Isn’t that powerful? See, that’s the power of water baptism, and most people, even when they got baptized, they just did it as a thing, but this is the power of baptism. Paul knew all this, and he’s setting the Corinthians up.

Romans 6:4-6: Therefore we were buried with Him through baptism into death, that just as Christ was raised from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life. For if we have been united together in the likeness of His death, certainly we also shall be in the likeness of His resurrection, knowing this, that our old man was crucified with Him, that the body of sin might be done away with, that we should no longer be slaves of sin.
What does Paul mean that a spiritual rock followed Israel? (1 Corinthians 10:4)

He says Israel “drank of that spiritual rock that followed them” and Paul tells us “that rock was Christ.” He says he doesn’t remember reading that, which is why we need teachers: “you can’t receive things that you haven’t understood yet.” He then reads Exodus 17:6, where Moses struck the rock and water came out, and says a stone cannot produce water by itself, so this is a supernatural thing.
What does Paul mean that a spiritual rock followed Israel? (1 Corinthians 10:4)

Okay, he says they all drink, in verse 3, “the same spiritual drink, and they drank of that spiritual rock that followed them.” A rock followed Israel. Wow. Now that should get your attention. I don’t remember reading no rock following anybody. Well, Paul’s going to show us. All right, Paul’s a really sharp boy, he really is. Okay, and he tells us who the rock was. That rock was Christ. Christ was following them in the wilderness. I don’t remember reading that. That’s why we need to come to church. That’s why we need teachers. See, you can’t receive things that you haven’t understood yet and believe for. Okay, now we’re going to take a closer look at Israel’s rock. How many want to see that? Yeah, okay. We have a map up here. Right down here is a little circle, Mount Sinai, and up here is another circle, uh, Kadesh Barnea is right above it. This is what it says in Exodus 17, verse 6: “You shall smite the rock, and there shall come water out of it that the people may drink.” And Moses went and smote the rock in sight of the elders and the people. And literally, I was going to bring a stone in, I forgot to bring a stone in, but anyway, uh, just pretend there’s a stone here, that I’m a muscle man and I can carry a 500-lb stone here, you know. Now, can a stone bring forth water? Is there anything in a stone that has anything to do with water? Nothing. You can heat it, you can freeze it, you can do anything to it, it isn’t going to produce water. So this is a miraculous thing, a supernatural thing. You young believers and teenagers, you’re serving a supernatural God here. This is not a religion. God is a reality, and He’s supernatural.
What does Paul mean that a spiritual rock followed Israel? (1 Corinthians 10:4)

1 Corinthians 10:3-4: all ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink. For they drank of that spiritual Rock that followed them, and that Rock was Christ. Exodus 17:6: Behold, I will stand before you there on the rock in Horeb; and you shall strike the rock, and water will come out of it, that the people may drink.” And Moses did so in the sight of the elders of Israel.
Why did God test Israel with no water at Sinai?

He says two and a half months after leaving Egypt God purposely brought them to a place with no water, and they failed the test and rebelled, saying they could be back in Egypt eating the leeks and onions. God then told Moses to strike the rock, and the water flowed in a stream through the camp for the people and the livestock.
Why did God test Israel with no water at Sinai?

All right, and so it happened. But let me tell you something, this was at Sinai, two and a half months after they came out of Egypt. How many months? Two and a half. And God tested them. He purposely brought them to a place where there was no water, and they failed the test. They rebelled. “You brought us out here to die in the wilderness. Man, we could be back in Egypt eating the leeks and the onions and all the cucumbers and all that stuff.” Yeah, you were slaves back there, and you were complaining there. Ain’t that right? So they failed the test and they rebelled, and then God told Moses, “Smite the rock,” and here come the water. And the Bible says the water came out in a stream, flowed all through the camp, and the livestock and the people ate of fresh water.
Why did God make Israel wander 40 years, and was everyone punished?

He says after the spies gave a bad report and the people would not go in, God punished them for disobeying and made them wander in the wilderness. Everybody who disbelieved died there, “except Joshua and Caleb, who had a different spirit,” and he says “not everybody’s punished and corrected when God does His correction.”
Why did God make Israel wander 40 years, and was everyone punished?

Wow. Ain’t that beautiful? But you got to remember this: after they left Mount Sinai, they traveled through this wilderness, they went to Kadesh Barnea, that second circle up there, and they sent out spies into the land. The spies came back with a bad report, they wouldn’t go in, so God punished them for disobeying Him and made them wander in the wilderness for 40 years, including the years that they came out, 40 total, to correct them. And everybody that disbelieved God died in the wilderness except Joshua and Caleb, who had a different spirit. See, in other words, not everybody’s punished and corrected when God does His correction. Hallelujah, thank God. Now, but what you got to understand, young believers, is this.
Why did God make Israel wander 40 years, and was everyone punished?

Numbers 14:29-30: The carcasses of you who have complained against Me shall fall in this wilderness, all of you who were numbered, according to your entire number, from twenty years old and above. Except for Caleb the son of Jephunneh and Joshua the son of Nun, you shall by no means enter the land which I swore I would make you dwell in.
How does the smitten rock point to Jesus on the cross? (Mark 14:27)

He cites Mark 14:27, “I will smite the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered,” and says the smiting of the rock, which Paul said was Jesus, is what Jesus used to say He was going to die on the cross. He says Jesus fulfilled that by being smitten, and He died only one time.
How does the smitten rock point to Jesus on the cross? (Mark 14:27)

Uh, Mark 14:27, Jesus said, “All of you shall be offended because of Me this night, for it is written, ‘I will smite the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered.’ And after that I’m risen, I will go to you into Galilee.” See, that smiting of the rock, who Paul said was Jesus, Jesus used it to say He was going to die on the cross. See, He was going to be smitten. See, and He used the Scripture that’s in the prophets of the Old Testament. Are you with me? So when Jesus died on the cross, He fulfilled that. He was smitten, and He only died how many times? One time.
How does the smitten rock point to Jesus on the cross? (Mark 14:27)

Mark 14:27: Then Jesus said to them, “All of you will be made to stumble because of Me this night, for it is written: ‘I will strike the Shepherd, And the sheep will be scattered.’ Zechariah 13:7: “Awake, O sword, against My Shepherd, Against the Man who is My Companion,” Says the LORD of hosts. “Strike the Shepherd, And the sheep will be scattered; Then I will turn My hand against the little ones.
Why did God tell Moses to speak to the rock 38 years later? (Numbers 20)

He says in the 38th year at Kadesh Barnea there was no water again, God tested them again, and they failed with murmuring and complaining, which he compares to the American church. God told Moses to speak to the rock, and he says it was not a new rock: Paul says “that rock had been following him,” and Paul knew because “he was a student of the scriptures.”
Why did God tell Moses to speak to the rock 38 years later? (Numbers 20)

Okay, now Numbers 20:8: 38 years later, 38 years later. They wandered in this wilderness right here for 38 years, but in the 38th year they came to Kadesh Barnea. And we read that there’s no water. The verse before this, there’s no water. God tested them again and they failed the test. They’re murmuring, complaining, rebellion. “You [unclear] out here, we’re going to die out here, little ones going to die.” Oh man, complain. Yeah, isn’t that American church? Aren’t we just the biggest complainers you ever heard? And we wonder why the unbelievers don’t want Christ. See, we got to pass these tests. And so God told Moses, “Go speak to the rock.” What rock? Is there a new rock? No. Paul says that rock had been following him. How did Paul know that rock followed them? How did he know that? Because he was a student of the Scriptures. Watch this. He said, “You speak to the rock to bring forth his water,” and that word “his” there in the King James really just means “it.” “And you shall bring forth to them water out of the rock to give the congregation drink.” Now, how did Paul know it was the same rock? Deuteronomy 8:15: “Who led you through the great and terrible wilderness.” How many years were they in the wilderness? 40 years. “A place where there were fiery serpents, scorpions, and drought, famine, dry places, no water.” And then he plainly says “where there was no” what? They were 38 years wandering in wilderness where there was not a drop of water. So how did they live for 38 years? The rock that followed them.
Why did God tell Moses to speak to the rock 38 years later? (Numbers 20)

Numbers 20:8: “Take the rod; you and your brother Aaron gather the congregation together. Speak to the rock before their eyes, and it will yield its water; thus you shall bring water for them out of the rock, and give drink to the congregation and their animals.” Deuteronomy 8:15: who led you through that great and terrible wilderness, in which were fiery serpents and scorpions and thirsty land where there was no water; who brought water for you out of the flinty rock;
Who was the rock, and what does that mean for us today? (John 7:38)

He says Paul knew the example: the rock was Jesus Christ, “the cornerstone” and “the rock of salvation,” who was with them in the wilderness before He became flesh. He cites John 7:38, “out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water,” and says since Jesus lives in us, “the rock is where? In us.”
Who was the rock, and what does that mean for us today? (John 7:38)

I tell you, this guy Paul is sharp. And who’s the rock that was with them a whole time? Jesus. See, Paul knew the illustration, Paul knew the example. That rock was Jesus Christ. He’s the cornerstone, He’s the rock of salvation, He’s the rock from which we’re [unclear]. He is the rock. Hallelujah. So Jesus was there with them in the wilderness before He ever became flesh and dwelt amongst us. And He was the rock, a flinty rock. It says that the water flowed out into a stream, giving water to who? 2 and a half million people. Hallelujah. Is that good? Yeah, that’s hot stuff. I like this Paul guy. Now, what does that mean for us today? John 7:38: “He that believes on Me, as the Scripture has said, out of his belly shall flow rivers of living water.” You see, Jesus lives in us, so the rock is where? In us. And He says out of our bellies shall flow rivers of living water. “But this spoke He of the” what? “Spirit, which was to come.” On the day of Pentecost, the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. Americans argue about it all the time. I just can’t believe that you can argue about something so plain in the Bible and something so wonderful.
Who was the rock, and what does that mean for us today? (John 7:38)

John 7:38-39: He who believes in Me, as the Scripture has said, out of his heart will flow rivers of living water.” But this He spoke concerning the Spirit, whom those believing in Him would receive; for the Holy Spirit was not yet given, because Jesus was not yet glorified.
Is the Holy Spirit a well of living water inside believers? (John 4:14)

He says the Holy Ghost “had been given, but it hadn’t been given to everyone,” and now it is, and he asks why people argue about something so wonderful. He cites John 4:14 and says it is “an artesian well” that “keeps quenching your thirst” and “keeps empowering you all the time.”
Is the Holy Spirit a well of living water inside believers? (John 4:14)

Jesus, the rock, lives in us, and He wants to pour the waters out of us so we drink and those around us, what? Drink. Are you there? Now, He said, “But the Holy Ghost was not yet given because He was not yet glorified,” or He hadn’t died on the cross yet. And in other words, it had been given, but it hadn’t been given to everyone. Uh, Joel said the Spirit will be poured out on all flesh. It hadn’t been done that way yet, but now it’s done, and why do we want to argue about something that’s so wonderful? It just blows my mind away, because some people make a wreck of it does not mean it’s not a truth. Could that be an amen? This is a powerful truth. In John 4:14, “Whosoever drinks of the water that I will give him shall never thirst, but the water that I shall give him shall be in him,” be in, in him, and what does it do? “A well of water springing up into” what? “Everlasting life.” It’s an artesian well. It just keeps quenching your thirst, it just keeps empowering you all the time. You don’t have to wait to go to the church in [unclear] and shake. It’s there in the morning when you get up, it’s there at night when you go to bed, and it’s there between, always rising in you.
Is the Holy Spirit a well of living water inside believers? (John 4:14)

Joel 2:28: “And it shall come to pass afterward That I will pour out My Spirit on all flesh; Your sons and your daughters shall prophesy, Your old men shall dream dreams, Your young men shall see visions. John 4:14: but whoever drinks of the water that I shall give him will never thirst. But the water that I shall give him will become in him a fountain of water springing up into everlasting life.”
Does God approve of everything His people do? (1 Corinthians 10:5)

He says verse 5, “with most of them God was not well pleased,” means God disapproved of their lifestyle, attitudes and decisions even though He was there and did great things for them. He says, “Just because you got God in your church, even miracles, and God is saving souls, does not mean God is pleased with everybody.”
Does God approve of everything His people do? (1 Corinthians 10:5)

Hallelujah. This is a powerful God we have, church. Powerful. And this Paul knows what he’s talking about. Now he’s setting these guys up. He said this is what God did for Israel, and they all knew that. Now, then in verse 5 he says this: “But with most of them God was not well pleased.” He disapproved of their lifestyle, He disapproved of their attitudes, He disapproved of their decisions. Yes, He was there, and He did great things for them, but that doesn’t mean He approved of what they did. Does he have the Corinthians now? Yeah. Just because you got God in your church, even miracles, and God is saving souls, does not mean God is pleased with everybody and what’s going on. Do we get that, church? Powerful, very powerful. This really helped me out as a young Christian. I can remember when God revealed it to me. It was powerful in my life. He gave me the substance to ignore sin and stick in the church and hang in there.
Does God approve of everything His people do? (1 Corinthians 10:5)
1 Corinthians 10:5: But with most of them God was not well pleased, for their bodies were scattered in the wilderness.
What are the “examples” Paul gives believers, and what is lusting after harmful things? (1 Corinthians 10:6)

He says these things became examples “to the intent, to the purpose,” that believers should not “lust after harmful things as they lusted,” and that it applies to all believers, not just apostles. He asks whether the American church is “filled with carried-out lust.”
What are the “examples” Paul gives believers, and what is lusting after harmful things? (1 Corinthians 10:6)

Now, “these things,” for “their bodies were scattered in the wilderness.” Verse 6: “Now these things became” what? “Examples,” a model, “to the intent that we,” us apostles and you church members, Paul says, “us” apostles. He, I’m not an apostle. “Us.” I’m Paul’s microphone, I’m just saying what he said. See, as powerful as us apostles are, these are our examples, and not just us apostles, all of you believers. It’s an example to the intent, to the purpose, that we should not, what? Lust after harmful things as they lusted. Is the American church filled with carried-out lust? Yeah.
What are the “examples” Paul gives believers, and what is lusting after harmful things? (1 Corinthians 10:6)
1 Corinthians 10:6: Now these things became our examples, to the intent that we should not lust after evil things as they also lusted.
Why does Paul warn the Corinthians not to become idolaters? (1 Corinthians 10:7)

He lists problems among believers, such as drunkenness, sexual immorality, division and greed, and says Paul shows God dealt with Israel so that now “cross or no cross, he’s going to correct you.” He cites “do not become idolaters,” the people who sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play, and ties the golden calf party to debauchery and a “festival mentality.”
Why does Paul warn the Corinthians not to become idolaters? (1 Corinthians 10:7)

Are believers getting drunk? Sexual immorality. Homosexuality. Incest. Yes. Are they divided? Are they greedy? Yeah. He’s got them. He showed them God dealt with Israel, now he’s going to show them: cross or no cross, he’s going to correct you. Watch, verse 7, 1 Corinthians 10: “Do not become idolaters, as were some of them.” How many of them? Some, not everybody did it. “As it is written, the people sat down to eat and drink and rose up to play.” Man, they had a big party going on, the beer, the wine, and the music playing, and they had their idol there, that golden calf, and that’s what goes along with all that debauchery: the music and the sexual immorality and, you know, the festival mentality, the big party mentality.
Why does Paul warn the Corinthians not to become idolaters? (1 Corinthians 10:7)

1 Corinthians 10:7: And do not become idolaters as were some of them. As it is written, “The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.” Exodus 32:6: Then they rose early on the next day, offered burnt offerings, and brought peace offerings; and the people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play.
Is there a punishment for sexual immorality, and is “once saved always saved” true?

He says Paul warns, “Nor let us commit sexual immorality, as some of them did, and God slew 23,000 in one day,” showing there is a punishment if you don’t get it corrected. He says many preachers do American Christians a “disfavor” by teaching that through grace and faith you can do anything and are saved no matter what, and that “our God who loves us will correct us.”
Is there a punishment for sexual immorality, and is “once saved always saved” true?

Is America in a party mentality? Absolutely. And that’s why he talked about idolatry before sexual immorality, talked about before: “Nor let us commit sexual immorality, as some of them did, and God slew 23,000 in one day.” And he already showed them they were committing sexual immorality earlier. Now he’s showing them there’s a punishment for it if you don’t get it corrected. And this is the disfavor many preachers are doing to American Christians today: through grace and faith you can do anything you want, God loves you, you’re going to heaven, once saved always saved. Listen, folks, we got a God that’s not worthless. He has power, and like a parent loves their children, will discipline them, our God who loves us will correct us. Amen. He doesn’t want us destroying our life in these things. He—
Is there a punishment for sexual immorality, and is “once saved always saved” true?
1 Corinthians 10:8: Nor let us commit sexual immorality, as some of them did, and in one day twenty-three thousand fell;
What does he recap that Paul covered earlier in the letter?

He says about a quarter of the letter was about division, 3/16 about sexual immorality, then idolatry, so one half was on three subjects. Then Paul talked about being an apostle and gave the example of how he pursued the gospel prize using four necessities so that he would not get disqualified.
How does he describe God’s presence with Israel in Exodus 13:21?
He says the cloud spread over them and a pillar of a cloud led them, so God’s presence was there in the form of a cloud and a pillar of fire, and “He was leading the way.”
What does he say the destruction of the Egyptian army illustrates?

He says in the sea Israel had the enemy that wanted to destroy them destroyed, but today Satan is destroyed through the death of the cross. He says Satan is “rendered powerless” and doesn’t have power over us anymore.
What does he say baptism does to the old man of sin?

He says “our old man of sin is crucified with Him” in water baptism, “that the body of sin might be destroyed.” He says God destroying the Egyptian army was an illustration that He was going to destroy the sinful nature in the new covenant.
Why does he say the water from the rock was supernatural?

He says there is nothing in a stone that has anything to do with water: you can heat it or freeze it and it isn’t going to produce water. He tells younger believers, “you’re serving a supernatural God here. This is not a religion. God is a reality.”
How does he say Paul knew it was the same rock?

He cites Deuteronomy 8:15 about the great and terrible wilderness with no water and says they wandered 38 years where there was not a drop of water. He asks, “how did they live for 38 years? The rock that followed them.”
Was Jesus with Israel in the wilderness before He became flesh?

He says Paul knew that rock was Jesus Christ, and so “Jesus was there with them in the wilderness before He ever became flesh and dwelt amongst us.” He says the water from the flinty rock served 2 and a half million people.
Do you have to wait until church to have the well of water in you?
He says it keeps quenching your thirst and empowering you all the time. He says “it’s there at night when you go to bed” and it is there in the morning when you get up, always rising in you.
How does he say this teaching helped him as a young Christian?
He says it “really helped me out as a young Christian,” and that God revealed it to him powerfully. He says “He gave me the substance to ignore sin and stick in the church and hang in there.”
Are the examples in 1 Corinthians 10 only for apostles?
He says Paul says “us apostles,” but it is “not just us apostles, all of you believers.” He says it is an example to the intent, to the purpose, that we should not lust after harmful things.
What does he say Israel’s party looked like in the wilderness?

He says they had “a big party going on, the beer, the wine, and the music playing,” and their idol, the golden calf, and that goes along with debauchery, sexual immorality and “the big party mentality.”
What does he mean when he says we have a God that is “not worthless”?

He says “we got a God that’s not worthless. He has power, and like a parent loves their children, will discipline them,” so our God who loves us will correct us. He says God doesn’t want us destroying our life in these things.

items.d: In this message Pastor David G. Kincer continues through 1 Corinthians 10, teaching that “tempt” means to test, that God corrects His people, and that 1 Corinthians 10:13 is about tests that prove and improve…
p: In this message Pastor David G. Kincer continues through 1 Corinthians 10, teaching that “tempt” means to test, that God corrects His people, and that 1 Corinthians 10:13 is about tests that prove and improve us, illustrated with tires tested for more miles. He then turns to Hebrews 11 to say that faith does not mean nothing bad happens, pointing to David, Joseph and those the world was not worthy of.
What does it mean to tempt (test) God? (1 Corinthians 10:9)

He says “tempt means to test,” and that Israel tested God by asking whether He could give them meat as well as water and manna. He says God can do anything, but “does he always say yes to your prayers? No.”
What does it mean to tempt (test) God? (1 Corinthians 10:9)

Verse 9: “Nor let us tempt God,” test Christ, “as some of them also tempted and were destroyed by serpents.” See, he again uses Christ. You notice, recognizing that Rock that was there giving them that water. “Tempt” means to test. And what they did is they said, “Well, God gave us this water and He gave us manna, but can He give us meat? Can He spread a table of meat in the wilderness?” Well, they had sheep and oxen, they had all kinds of animals around there, but the thing is, can God do this? If God is really that big. And so what do you do? That’s a testing God. Of course He can. God can do what? Anything. But does He want to do it? Not always. Does He always say yes to your prayers? No. When your prayers are dumb, He’s going to say no.
What does it mean to tempt (test) God? (1 Corinthians 10:9)
1 Corinthians 10:9: nor let us tempt Christ, as some of them also tempted, and were destroyed by serpents;
Why does God sometimes say no to prayer, and what does the Bible say about complaining? (1 Corinthians 10:10)

He says “God is a good parent” who knows when to say no, sometimes because the timing is not right, like a child who asks for a bicycle he cannot yet ride. Reading verse 10, “nor complain,” he says the American church is good at complaining, “we complain when it’s cold, we complain it’s hot.”
Why does God sometimes say no to prayer, and what does the Bible say about complaining? (1 Corinthians 10:10)

I don’t care what these faith people preach. God is a good parent. He knows when to say no, not even because your prayer is dumb, but the timing is not right. Do you give your kid a bicycle till it’s the right time for them to have the ability to ride it? No. Even though they want one, two years old: “I want a bike, 24-inch bike, man, I want.” They can’t do anything with it now. The kid isn’t doing anything wrong, but he’s asking for something that he can’t utilize. There’s a time for everything. Amen. Now, “and were destroyed by serpents.” Verse 10: “Nor complain.” Here’s the American church, man. We’re good at this. We complain when it’s cold, we complain it’s hot, we complain when there’s no traffic on the freeway, “Where’s everybody at?” We complain when everybody’s on the freeway, “My God, look at this traffic!” I mean, we just, we get up in the morning complaining.
Why does God sometimes say no to prayer, and what does the Bible say about complaining? (1 Corinthians 10:10)
1 Corinthians 10:10: nor complain, as some of them also complained, and were destroyed by the destroyer.
Who is “the destroyer,” and are we in the end of the ages? (1 Corinthians 10:10-11)

He says the destroyer is Satan, whom God created “to do God’s dirty work,” and that when God needs to correct, “God cannot do evil, so He’s got this guy to do His correction.” He says these things happened as examples written for our admonition, and that we are in the end of the ages, which he says started when Christ rose from the grave.
Who is “the destroyer,” and are we in the end of the ages? (1 Corinthians 10:10-11)

“And were destroyed by the destroyer.” Who’s the destroyer? Satan. See, he was created by God to do God’s dirty work. You can call him a fallen angel if you want to, but God created him to be who he was. There was no plan B. And he’s out to destroy you. And when God needs to correct, see, God cannot do evil, so He’s got this guy to do His correction. He loves it, he feasts off of it. “Now all these things happened to them as examples,” as a model, “and they were written for” what? “Our admonition, upon whom the ends of the ages have come.” Are we in the end of the ages? Yes. We don’t know how close we are to the end, but we know we’re in the end because the Bible tells us that the end of the days started when Christ rose from the grave. That’s when the end time started, and it’s been over 2,000 years so far, and honestly we don’t know how much further it’s going on. Everybody’s missed it so far, and they’ll keep missing it.
Who is “the destroyer,” and are we in the end of the ages? (1 Corinthians 10:10-11)

1 Corinthians 10:10-11: nor complain, as some of them also complained, and were destroyed by the destroyer. Now all these things happened to them as examples, and they were written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the ages have come.
Can a believer fall back into sin or lose salvation? (1 Corinthians 10:12)

He reads “let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he” fall, and says Paul was warning the Corinthians to learn from Israel and correct their problems. He says falling includes “falling back into sin and even losing your salvation,” but that God will correct you first, because “He’s a great Father.”
Can a believer fall back into sin or lose salvation? (1 Corinthians 10:12)

But the Bible, Paul says, God put this in the Bible so you would learn, so you would be warned, so you could be encouraged, so you would know. And then he says, “Therefore let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he” what? Fall. He said, you Corinthians, you think your condition and how you believe is okay, you better take heed and learn from Israel and correct your problems, because if not, you’re going to fall. And here he’s talking about falling back into sin and even losing your salvation, but you can fall also into the correction. Now, how many of you know God’s going to correct before He allows these things of losing your salvation to happen? Yeah, He’s going to correct you, He’s going to come after you. He’s a great Father.
Can a believer fall back into sin or lose salvation? (1 Corinthians 10:12)
1 Corinthians 10:12: Therefore let him who thinks he stands take heed lest he fall.
What does 1 Corinthians 10:13 mean by “temptation”? (the tire illustration)

He says the word “temptation” means “an experiment to prove, a test to prove,” and compares it to tires tested for 10,000, 20,000 or 60,000 miles. He says God tests us “to show where we’re at” so we go to the next level, and that “I don’t know what Bible you’ve been reading” if you say nothing bad happens to Christians who have faith.
What does 1 Corinthians 10:13 mean by “temptation”? (the tire illustration)

But then this great verse in verse 13. This is the verse I use all the time when I’m witnessing, uh, to establish people that say, “I can’t live for God.” This is a verse I use, 1 Corinthians 10:13: “No temptation has overtaken you except such as common to man.” Now, the word “temptation” means an experiment to prove, a test to prove. And you know, when they sell you a tire for your car, you can buy a tire that will last 10,000 miles and, you know, no road hazard protection, that’s all the tire is good for. Then they got a tire that’s 20,000 miles. Then they got a tire that’s 30,000 miles and road hazard: this tire is really built tough, it’s hard for anything to get through it, we will fix it if a road hazard happens. Then they got them 40,000 and 60,000 miles. Why? And what they do is they take them in the factory and they bend and flex it and beat them and drop them from an airplane and everything else, and get them on the raceway, and they drive them high speed, low speed, stop and starts and all that, to know and see, they proved that this tire will go 50,000 miles. Now, in our baby stage we’re good for 10,000 miles. That’s about one inch, say. And God comes to test us, what? To show where we’re at, so we learn from it and go to the next level. And boy, we think, “Man, hallelujah, man, I got it.” And then here comes another test. Now, is He trying to destroy you, trying to beat you up, trying to discourage you? No, He’s trying to prove to you where you’re at and change you so you go up to the next level. That’s what he’s talking about. And these people say, “Well, you know, nothing bad happens to Christians.” I don’t know what Bible you’ve been reading. “Oh, if you got faith, nothing will happen.” I don’t know what Bible you’ve been reading. Paul had a lot more faith than anybody I know of, and he got stoned, he got shipwrecked, he got rejected by the brethren, he got beaten and imprisoned. I don’t know what Bible you’re reading, faith people.
What does 1 Corinthians 10:13 mean by “temptation”? (the tire illustration)

1 Corinthians 10:13: No temptation has overtaken you except such as is common to man; but God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but with the temptation will also make the way of escape, that you may be able to bear it.
Will God let you be tested beyond what you can handle?

He says God is “reliable, you can count on God, who will not allow you to be tested beyond what you are able.” He says the test shows where you are lacking so you can improve and “bump up to the next level.”
Will God let you be tested beyond what you can handle?

Joseph got rejected by his brothers, put in prison. I can go on and on. Come on, get the blinders off of your eyes and see the truth. Could that be an amen? But he’s trying to tell us when these things come, look what he says. God is what? Faithful. He’s reliable, you can count on God, “who will not allow you to be tested beyond what you are able,” or what you have the power to handle. So see, the test is to show you where you’re lacking, so that you can what? Improve the lack and bump up to the next level. Now you’re not a 10,000 Christian anymore, you’re a 20,000 Christian. That’s two inches. We’re headed for 12 inches, we want to be the full foot. “But with the testing make a way of” what?
Will God let you be tested beyond what you can handle?

1 Corinthians 10:13: No temptation has overtaken you except such as is common to man; but God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but with the temptation will also make the way of escape, that you may be able to bear it.
What is the “way of escape,” and why didn’t “hamburgers from heaven” teaching work for him?

He says the way of escape is “not an escape where you don’t go through the test, but you can handle the test.” He says the faith-and-grace teaching he first received, that you don’t have to work and God just supplies, “wasn’t working,” so he went to “the real teachers” and learned these things by the Holy Spirit.
What is the “way of escape,” and why didn’t “hamburgers from heaven” teaching work for him?

“Escape,” a way out, “that you might be able to” what? Bear it. Endure it. Not an escape where you don’t go through the test, but you can handle the test, improve your life through the test, and bump up your life and get ready for the next test. Now, Paul’s good, church. I’m telling you, he knows what he’s talking about. This really helped my life as a young Christian, because I was getting teaching that was totally opposite of Paul’s teaching. Everybody back there was faith and grace people, and my goodness, you know, just because you’re a Christian you’re supposed to be fed manna from heaven, you know, hamburgers from heaven, I call it. You don’t have to work or do anything, just pray and live for God, and God will supply your need. You know, people bring food and put it on your doorstep and everything, you know. Hallelujah, you’re the golden spoon child. That’s the way it was in my day, and it wasn’t working, and I had to go find out, because the God I met was a real God, and what these people were teaching me wasn’t working, and so I went to the real teachers, and I learned these things by the Holy Spirit revealing them to me, and I became a very strong young Christian. See, we can endure it. Now listen, remember when Paul taught on sexual immorality? Okay, he said to avoid sexual immorality: premarital sex, homosexuality, prostitution, adultery, all those, incest, all those sexual vices. He said to avoid them, use self-control. See, God gives us tools to use. He says not only that, but he says God will give you a gift, a supernatural ability to handle yourself, ain’t that right? Remember that? Remember what we taught? These are important things. And then he not only says that, but there’s a third tool he gives: you power over your desires, a strong mind over your desires, a strong emotion over your desires.
What is the “way of escape,” and why didn’t “hamburgers from heaven” teaching work for him?

1 Corinthians 10:13: No temptation has overtaken you except such as is common to man; but God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but with the temptation will also make the way of escape, that you may be able to bear it.
What tools does Paul give against sexual immorality, idolatry and bad companions?

He says God gives “three tremendous tools to avoid sexual immorality”: self-control, a supernatural ability, and power over your desires, and that the answer to burning passion is marriage. He says for idolatry we can worship Jesus, and for bad companions the antidote is “good companions.”
What tools does Paul give against sexual immorality, idolatry and bad companions?

He gives you three tremendous tools to avoid sexual immorality, and then he says the antidote of it all, so you don’t live your life burning with sexual passion, is get married and have all the sex you want. So see, we have the ability to go through life until we get married. See, that is what Paul is backing up. Are you with me? Idolatry, you know, you want to worship something, you want to worship yourself or some other god or whatever. He gives us Jesus is it. We can worship Him. Amen. Uh, bad companions. Young believers have a hard time staying away from bad companions, and the Bible says bad companions corrupt good behavior, good manners. You can’t run around with bad people and not get influenced by them if you’re going to be intimate with them. So he says you got to use self-control, you got to use these things. Yeah, you can be around them for a mission field, but not to run with them, partake, or you’re going to wind up partaking of their sins. And what’s the antidote for evil companions? Good companions. Find some good people to run around with. See, Paul gives us answers for these things. Church, hallelujah, I love this guy, and I could go on and on about anything there. In closing, I’m going to destroy the faith camp right now.
What tools does Paul give against sexual immorality, idolatry and bad companions?
1 Corinthians 15:33: Do not be deceived: “Evil company corrupts good habits.”
Does having faith mean nothing bad will happen to Christians? (Hebrews 11:33-35)

He says Hebrews 11 starts with faith and lists those who subdued kingdoms, stopped lions’ mouths and received their dead raised, and “this is where the faith camp stops.” He says “it doesn’t stop there,” because the same chapter goes on to “and others.”
Does having faith mean nothing bad will happen to Christians? (Hebrews 11:33-35)

All right, the extreme faith camp, the [unclear], the [unclear], the [unclear] Roberts, all these people that tell you that you can name it and claim it, that because you’re believing it you’re going to get it, nothing bad happens to Christians. Paul’s going to expose all this, you know, the Bible exposes all this, and we need to know this stuff. Could that be an amen? Now, Hebrews chapter 11 is talking about faith, very beginning of the chapter he’s talking about faith. Then he comes down here and he says, “who through faith subdued kingdoms, worked righteousness, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, out of weakness were made strong, waxed valiant in fight, turned to flight the armies of the aliens. Women received their dead raised to life again.” Wow. And this is where the faith camp stops. Yeah, the widow woman got her son right back from the dead. Oh, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego come out of the fiery furnace. Yeah, Daniel came out of the lions’ den. Hallelujah, man, that’s us.
Does having faith mean nothing bad will happen to Christians? (Hebrews 11:33-35)

Hebrews 11:33-35: who through faith subdued kingdoms, worked righteousness, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, out of weakness were made strong, became valiant in battle, turned to flight the armies of the aliens. Women received their dead raised to life again. Others were tortured, not accepting deliverance, that they might obtain a better resurrection.
What happened to the “others” in Hebrews 11, like David and Joseph?

He says David had to hide in caves and run in the desert for 13 years before he got results, and Joseph was rejected by his brothers, sold into slavery, falsely accused and put in prison before the promise came. He says going through things “does not mean God is not going to fulfill His purpose in you.”
What happened to the “others” in Hebrews 11, like David and Joseph?

But it doesn’t stop there. It says “and others.” And what others? Some of these, David won great battles, but he had to hide in caves and run in the desert for 13 years before he got results. He had the hiding in caves and run in the desert for his life for 13 years. Joseph, before he ever became the deliverer of Egypt, was rejected by his brothers, thrown into a pit, sold into slavery, and then falsely accused by Potiphar’s wife and thrown into prison before he ever became the one that fulfilled God and received the promise. And you need to know this, young Christians, you need to know this, old Christians, that just because you’re going through things does not mean God is not going to fulfill His purpose in you. He is just testing you right now and developing you. That’s what Paul’s saying. Are you there? He’s shaping you for the end result, building you up. He says, “Others were tortured, not accepting deliverance, that they might obtain a better resurrection. Others had trial of cruel mocking, scourgings, and imprisonment.” No results in these people. “They were stoned, they were sawn asunder, tempted, slain with the sword. They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, being destitute, afflicted, tormented, of whom the world was not worthy.” Now, that sound like losers?
What happened to the “others” in Hebrews 11, like David and Joseph?

Hebrews 11:35-38: Women received their dead raised to life again. Others were tortured, not accepting deliverance, that they might obtain a better resurrection. Still others had trial of mockings and scourgings, yes, and of chains and imprisonment. They were stoned, they were sawn in two, were tempted, were slain with the sword. They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, being destitute, afflicted, tormented— of whom the world was not worthy. They wandered in deserts and mountains, in dens and caves of the earth.
What does it mean that “the world was not worthy” of them? (Hebrews 11:36-38)

He says those people went without clothing and food, lived in deserts and caves, and were beaten, stoned and imprisoned, “and he says the world wasn’t worthy of them.” He says when you are going through trials and hanging in there, “the world is not worthy that’s mistreating” and “you buck up, you’re doing something good.”
What does it mean that “the world was not worthy” of them? (Hebrews 11:36-38)

People, the Scripture says the world wasn’t worthy of these people. They went without clothing, they went without food, they couldn’t own a home because they weren’t allowed to, they had to live in the desert, live in a tent, live in a cave, they were beaten, they were stoned, they were imprisoned, they were mistreated, and he says the world wasn’t worthy of them. Wow. And when you’re going through these trials and these testings and you’re hanging in there, you need to know this: the world is not worthy that’s mistreating. You buck up, you’re doing something good. Hallelujah. Hallelujah. He says “they wandered in the desert, the mountains, and the dens and caves of the earth.” Good prophets did. Elijah had to flee for his life, folks.
What does it mean that “the world was not worthy” of them? (Hebrews 11:36-38)

Hebrews 11:35-38: Women received their dead raised to life again. Others were tortured, not accepting deliverance, that they might obtain a better resurrection. Still others had trial of mockings and scourgings, yes, and of chains and imprisonment. They were stoned, they were sawn in two, were tempted, were slain with the sword. They wandered about in sheepskins and goatskins, being destitute, afflicted, tormented— of whom the world was not worthy. They wandered in deserts and mountains, in dens and caves of the earth.
Does God’s presence in a church mean He approves of our lifestyle?

He says all the apostles were persecuted and “we think we’re some kind of golden spoon people in America because we believe in God.” He says “God isn’t pleased with our lifestyle” even when His presence is in our midst and people are healed and saved; “that does not mean God approves of our lifestyle.”
Does God’s presence in a church mean He approves of our lifestyle?

Jesus was persecuted. Where are these people getting off of this nonsense from? All the apostles were persecuted, weren’t they? All of them died a horrible death except John, and we think we’re some kind of golden spoon people in America because we believe in God? Oh, we got to go through the testing, just like Israel did. We got to hang in there and pass the test, amen. God isn’t pleased with our lifestyle, He isn’t pleased with the way we talk, even though God’s presence is in our midst and somebody might get physically healed and souls are getting saved. That does not mean God approves of our lifestyle. Look at this last statement.
What is the “good report” in Hebrews 11, and what is a 60,000-mile Christian?

He says all of them, whether they got results or not, “obtained a good report.” He says God is making a “60,000-mile Christian” out of David and Joseph, one that can handle road hazards and last through the wilderness, and that any church that wants to be something in God has to get through testings and trials.
What is the “good report” in Hebrews 11, and what is a 60,000-mile Christian?

Last statement, Hebrews chapter 11, last verse: “these all,” how many? Oh, the people that got results and the people that seemingly didn’t get results, they were mistreated, they all what? Had a good report. “Obtained a good report.” That person, that David, when he was living in caves and out on the desert, God says he’s got a good report, he’s doing My will, he’s getting the testing, bent and flexed and pressed, dropped from a plane. I’m making something, I’m making a 60,000-mile Christian out of him. Joseph, when he was rejected by his brothers, sold into slavery, falsely accused in court, put in prison for a false accusation, God’s just testing him, working him over so he comes out a 60,000-mile Christian that can handle road hazards without getting a flat, that can last through the wilderness and last through anything. Man, he’s got tread that lasts to the end. Amen. And then he got elevated to second in the kingdom. And any church that wants to be something in God, we got to get through the testings and trials and buck up and change our lifestyle. Amen. But while we’re getting there, do we have a good report? Yes. Why? Because we believe God is making something beautiful, something great out of our life. We’re believing that God will finish the good work that He what? Began in us. Now, we showed you Israel came out of Egypt for the promised land, but we are led by Jesus to living waters, Himself, His presence, His Word. His Word is life, He is life.
What is the “good report” in Hebrews 11, and what is a 60,000-mile Christian?

Hebrews 11:39: And all these, having obtained a good testimony through faith, did not receive the promise, Philippians 1:6: being confident of this very thing, that He who has begun a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ;
What does he say is the purpose of church?
