Why does he begin with a story about a baby being born?
He describes the worry of the nine months and says “I was just glad they came out okay after all that.” He uses it to say a baby either is born and lives or dies, and the same is true spiritually.
How does he say a person is “conceived” spiritually?
He says some people, when they hear God’s word, “it triggers a conception, and they begin to grow,” and the church continues that growth until they decide to accept Christ.
Does he say God wants anyone to go to hell?
No. He says “God doesn’t want any babies dying,” and that it happens “when we don’t accept him and let him birth us.”
Why does he say Jesus is the only one who can pay for sin?
He says “the payment for your sin is death. Jesus Christ is the only one that has the power to pay for your sin,” and that he is “the only one that went down into hell, and hell couldn’t stand him.”
What does he mean by “the milk of the word”?
He says it is “the basic understanding”: you “read the Gospels and find out about the death, burial, and resurrection of Christ,” which is “getting saved, faith, believing in God.”
What does he say about going to church every week?
He says “It was a habit to be in the house of God on Sundays,” and asks, “what about Jesus’s custom?” He says “we need to be here at church.”
What does he say about babies and praise in the Psalms?
He quotes “out of the mouths of babies” God has ordained praise to still the enemy, and says “This word means more than that.” He concludes that when we come to church “there’s no sitting down.”
How did praising God help him as a new believer?
He says “As a new believer, I was always praising God,” that he sang with all his heart whoever was next to him, and “that helped me in my life.”
What does he say about being embarrassed when we praise God?
He says “it may be embarrassing,” but “That’s the great thing about kids,” who don’t care. For a teenager or adult with cares, “you just got to get rid of it.”
What does he say the “yoke of bondage” is?
He says Galatians 5:1 is “the New Testament talking about, don’t be entangled with the yoke of bondage again, the yoke of sin,” and that “Sin is going to put you through the ringer.”
What does he say children learn from their parents?
He says “they’re going to copy the things that I do, no matter if they want to or not,” and later have to decide whether to reject what they saw.
What does he say about losing friends when you follow Christ?
He says “it’s very difficult when friends don’t decide to follow Christ,” and that they may ask you “to leave, or they’re not going to associate with you anymore.”
What does he say happened at the Red Sea?
He says “God destroyed the armies of Pharaoh,” who followed the Israelites after “He parted the Red Sea, the Israelites walked through it.”
What does he say Luke 10:19 shows about power?
He quotes “Behold, I give you power to tread upon scorpions and serpents,” and says “He has the power to deliver us from sin.”
What does he say about Saul sacrificing before Samuel arrived?
He says Saul “took things into his own hands” and went “outside of the pattern,” and that “We got to keep following the pattern.”

items.d: In this message Pastor David G. Kincer continues his series on the stages of Christian growth with the father stage of 1 John 2:13-14: fathers know Him who was from the beginning. He lays out John 1 and…
p: In this message Pastor David G. Kincer continues his series on the stages of Christian growth with the father stage of 1 John 2:13-14: fathers know Him who was from the beginning. He lays out John 1 and Genesis 1 as proof that Jesus is God, then compares the characteristics of a natural father and a spiritual father: not provoking children, training and cherishing them, birthing others through the Word, being an example, and disciplining as God does in Hebrews 12. He closes with the meat of the Word, righteousness, and what it means to practice it.
Who are the “fathers” in 1 John 2:13-14, and what does it mean that they know Him from the beginning?

He says the Bible repeats itself in 1 John 2:13-14 because “when the Bible repeats itself, it means it’s important.” He says fathers “not only understand with the mind, but they have a personal relationship and they keep His commandments,” and that they understand Jesus “existed at the beginning” and “was God from the very beginning of the world.”
Who are the “fathers” in 1 John 2:13-14, and what does it mean that they know Him from the beginning?

In 1 John 2:13 and 14 he says the same thing. He repeats himself, and when the Bible repeats itself, it means it’s important. “I write unto you, fathers, because you have known Him from the beginning.” Now we know from past sessions that the word “know” means to understand, okay, to be aware of, to recognize something. We recognize God, we get knowledge of God, but we also know from the Bible that knowing God is an intimate relationship. It’s used as an intimate, personal relationship. And we also know that by this do you know Him: if you keep His commandments. So the fathers know Him. They not only understand with the mind, but they have a personal relationship and they keep His commandments. That is from the beginning. Now here Paul, John is saying that Jesus was at the beginning. Okay, He wasn’t just, when He came, was born of a virgin, but He existed at the beginning, and fathers understand that. They have a personal encounter with that, and they obey that Jesus that was at the beginning. So fathers know Jesus was God. See, the father stage clearly understands that Jesus was God from the very beginning of the world. All right, John chapter 1, verse 1 through 14. We find in John 1:1 through 14 that “in the beginning was the Word.” Now John is going to lay this out very clearly: “In the beginning was the Word, the Word was with God.”
Who are the “fathers” in 1 John 2:13-14, and what does it mean that they know Him from the beginning?

1 John 2:13-14: I write to you, fathers, Because you have known Him who is from the beginning. I write to you, young men, Because you have overcome the wicked one. I write to you, little children, Because you have known the Father. I have written to you, fathers, Because you have known Him who is from the beginning. I have written to you, young men, Because you are strong, and the word of God abides in you, And you have overcome the wicked one.
What does John 1:1-14 teach about Jesus as the Word, Creator and Light?

He says John 1 shows “the Word was with God” and “the Word was God,” that “Jesus created the world,” and “if the Word is Jesus Christ, then Jesus is the Word, Jesus is God.” He offers a “spiritual brain teaser” about light on the first day before the sun, pointing to verses where God and Jesus are light: “Jesus was at the beginning with God, and Jesus was what? Light.”
What does John 1:1-14 teach about Jesus as the Word, Creator and Light?

You see, at the beginning of time in Genesis, the Word was with God, but also “the Word was God.” Now this is very important. Now this chapter threw me for quite a few years till I grew in the Word, but it’s very clear. “The same was in the beginning with God.” So God was with God. You got it? The same, the Word was with God, the Word was God, the same, the Word, the God was in the beginning with God. So God was with who? God. He said, well, you have to be a father to understand that. See, you got to get past the little baby doctrines and get into the richness of the Bible. All right, now let’s keep going. “All things were made by Him,” the Word, God, “and without Him was not anything made.” He goes on to say the world was made by Him. So John here emphasizes that Jesus created the world, created everything, and without Him nothing was made that was made, and the Word was God. Number five: “In Him was life, and the life was the light of men.” In Him was life, and that life was the light of men. Now I’m going to throw a few teasers at you, for those of you who are Bible students. The atheists, the humanists, the liberals, our opponents, all say that the Bible contradicts itself, and one of the places they say that it contradicts itself is God said, “Let there be light” on the first day, and there was light, but the sun and the moon was not created till the fourth day. So let me just throw out a little spiritual brain teaser to you. In Jesus was life, and that life was the light of men. Matthew 17:2: Jesus was transfigured before them, and “His face did shine as the sun, and His raiment white as the light.” 1 Timothy 6:16: the Lord Jesus Christ “dwelling in the light which no man can approach unto.” 1 John 1:5: “God is light, and in Him is no darkness at all.” Psalm 104:2: God “covers Himself with light as with a garment, and stretches out the heavens like a curtain.” Revelation 21:23: the city, the heavenly Jerusalem, the bride, “has no need of the sun, neither of the moon, to shine in it, for the glory of God lights it, and the Lamb is the light thereof.” Paul, on the road to Damascus, when he encountered Jesus, he encountered a great light. So when God said, “Let there be light,” and the sun was not created till the day before, we have a scriptural reference for light, because Jesus was at the beginning with God, and Jesus was what? Light. Just something for you to think on. See, human intellect cannot understand these things. All right, now we’ll get back to the kindergarten stage and continue. “The Word was made flesh and dwelt amongst us, and we beheld His glory, as of the only begotten Son of God, full of grace and truth.” And John the Baptist bore witness of Him. So clearly it is talking about the Word, who is Jesus Christ. So if the Word is Jesus Christ, then Jesus is the Word, Jesus is God, and fathers understand that. They’re not confused at all. Hallelujah. Now, Jesus from the beginning: is it true that back in Genesis I can find Jesus? All right, in Genesis chapter 1 you’re going to find the God four involved in creation. How many? Four. What are you used to? Three. But see, John very clearly brings out that the Word is also God. Have I got your minds thinking?
What does John 1:1-14 teach about Jesus as the Word, Creator and Light?

John 1:1-14: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God. All things were made through Him, and without Him nothing was made that was made. In Him was life, and the life was the light of men. And the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it. There was a man sent from God, whose name was John. This man came for a witness, to bear witness of the Light, that all through him might believe. He was not that Light, but was sent to bear witness of that Light. That was the true Light which gives light to every man coming into the world. He was in the world, and the world was made through Him, and the world did not know Him. He came to His own, and His own did not receive Him. But as many as received Him, to them He gave the right to become children of God, to those who believe in His name: who were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God. And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we beheld His glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth. Matthew 17:2: and He was transfigured before them. His face shone like the sun, and His clothes became as white as the light. 1 Timothy 6:16: who alone has immortality, dwelling in unapproachable light, whom no man has seen or can see, to whom be honor and everlasting power. Amen. 1 John 1:5: This is the message which we have heard from Him and declare to you, that God is light and in Him is no darkness at all. Psalm 104:2: Who cover Yourself with light as with a garment, Who stretch out the heavens like a curtain. Revelation 21:23: The city had no need of the sun or of the moon to shine in it, for the glory of God illuminated it. The Lamb is its light.
Do we find God, the Spirit and the Word in Genesis 1, and was Jesus always God’s plan?

He says Genesis 1 shows God, “the Spirit of God,” and the Word (“God said”) involved in creation, and that God spoke “let us” in the plural. He says God “never had a plan B”: “He had one plan the whole time, and that was Jesus Christ, reconciling people back to God,” and describes “one God doing things with four different explanations.”
Do we find God, the Spirit and the Word in Genesis 1, and was Jesus always God’s plan?

Now, is it true? And you know me, I always go back to see if what God says is true back there. So let’s go to Genesis chapter 1, and we find the first thing involved is God. “In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.” We got it colored in blue so that you know everything is related to Him. Verse 2, we have the Spirit, the second part, the second one involved in the creation: “The Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters.” Okay, and see, God continues His truth all throughout the Bible, and so it’s important that we understand it was set at the beginning. All right, so we have God and the Spirit, and then we have the Word. Verse 3: “God said.” God spoke, and this is the power of God. It’s in His spoken Word. God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light. See, when God said, Jesus said, who is God, “For God so loved the world that He gave His only begotten Son, that whosoever believes on Him shall not perish but have everlasting life.” Just like when He said, “Let there be light,” and there was light. When God speaks something, He backs it up, and if you believe, you will not perish. See, just like He said, “I will pour out My Spirit on all flesh.” We know what His spoken word is. He accomplishes it, and you can have the infilling, the baptism of the Holy Spirit, because God backs up His spoken Word. Hallelujah. Now we know it is the printed Word, but it was only printed because He what? Spoke it. Yes, it’s that spoken Word, and you can have confidence that that Word is God. See, that Bible is Jesus. Hebrews 6:1: faith toward God, repentance from dead works, baptism of the Holy Ghost, baptism in water, baptism in the body, laying on of hands, resurrection, eternal judgment. He says you haven’t even passed kindergarten yet. You haven’t even passed the newborn stage yet. You haven’t got repentance down, you haven’t got faith down, you haven’t got water baptism down, you haven’t been filled with the Holy Ghost and power, you haven’t been placed into the body as God wants you to be. You’re scared to death for someone to lay hands on you and bless you and impart to you, and you’re hung up on the second coming, the resurrection of the dead, and eternal judgment. That’s all you think about. That’s all baby food. That’s all baby doctrine. “You have come to need milk and not strong meat.” So milk is the what? First principles of God, the baby doctrine. Strong meat, solid food. “All who partake only of milk is unskillful in the word of righteousness.” When all you can handle is baby food and you haven’t even passed the baby food yet, you haven’t got a passing grade in kindergarten, you’re unskillful in the word of righteousness. You don’t even like to hear messages on righteousness, to be honest with you. You want to hear that once saved always saved. You want to hear that no matter what you do, God loves you and you’re going to go to heaven. That’s what you want to hear, because what? You’re a baby. “All who partake only of milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, for he is a baby.” Just letting you think on it. This is the writer of Hebrews talking, it’s not me, don’t blame me. This is what the apostles taught, and no one has a right to teach anything but what the Bible tells us to teach. “No one but strong meat,” which is, say it, the word of righteousness. “The strong meat, solid food, belongs to those who are full age,” adults, mature, that is the young men and the father stage, “those who by reason of use,” by practice, practice.
What is the “meat” of the Word, and why are many still on milk? (Hebrews 5:12-13; 6:1-2)

Hebrews 5:12-13: For though by this time you ought to be teachers, you need someone to teach you again the first principles of the oracles of God; and you have come to need milk and not solid food. For everyone who partakes only of milk is unskilled in the word of righteousness, for he is a babe. Hebrews 6:1-2: Therefore, leaving the discussion of the elementary principles of Christ, let us go on to perfection, not laying again the foundation of repentance from dead works and of faith toward God, of the doctrine of baptisms, of laying on of hands, of resurrection of the dead, and of eternal judgment.
How do you become mature: practice, exercised senses, and judging good and evil? (Hebrews 5:14)

He says “we put time into natural things, we need to put time into spiritual things,” like young men who go to the gym but won’t “exercise that spiritual man.” Reading Hebrews 5:14, he says the apostle is telling us to judge: senses “exercised, trained, to discern, to judge both good and evil.”
How do you become mature: practice, exercised senses, and judging good and evil? (Hebrews 5:14)

You know, these young men have no problem going to the gym and putting in time to be buffed so the girls will go, “Woo, look at his body,” but you can’t get him to open the Bible and exercise that spiritual man. And I know there’s couch potato men in this hour and day. They do nothing but play electronic games and watch football and basketball and so forth, and they’re not buffed at all, they’re wimps, they’re just a bunch of wimps walking around. But they put practice into being a wimp, is my point. They exercise being a wimp, and you say, “Let me see your muscle,” and nothing pops up, drops down. See, we put time into natural things, we need to put time into spiritual things, we need to practice them. “And have their senses,” their judgment. Everybody’s saying don’t judge, and here the apostle is telling us to what? Judge. “Have their senses,” their judgment, their understanding, “exercised,” trained, “to discern,” to judge, “both good and evil.” Now, are we to judge? Yes. Are we to judge what’s good and what’s evil? Yes. Jesus said it, the apostles are saying it. Forget Oprah Winfrey and all these people that say the Bible says don’t judge, they don’t even understand the Bible.
How do you become mature: practice, exercised senses, and judging good and evil? (Hebrews 5:14)
Hebrews 5:14: But solid food belongs to those who are of full age, that is, those who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern both good and evil.
How do you know you are righteous, and what does “faith in your faith” mean? (1 John 3:7)

He reads 1 John 3:7, “He who practices righteousness is righteous,” and says “you cannot have faith in your faith”: you can’t just believe you are saved or have the baptism of the Holy Ghost “without the evidence of it.” He says we are righteous because we “practice what is right,” with embryos and newborns expected to still have unrighteousness, children who “keep the Word of God,” and young men and fathers who “live righteously.”
How do you know you are righteous, and what does “faith in your faith” mean? (1 John 3:7)

1 John 3:7: “Little children, let no one deceive you. He who practices righteousness is righteous.” I told you before, and I’ve told you many times, you cannot have faith in your faith. You cannot just have faith that you have the baptism of the Holy Ghost without the evidence of it. You can’t just believe you’re saved because you believe you’re saved and you don’t have the evidence of it. That’s faith in your faith. You can’t just believe you’re going to heaven when you die and don’t have the evidence of it, the proof of it. That’s faith in your faith, and the Bible doesn’t tell us to have faith in our faith. Are you with me? We are righteous because we what? Practice what is right. Now, some of us are at different levels. That’s the growth thing. When you’re a new embryo we expect you to have unrighteousness in your life. When you’re a newborn baby we expect you to have some unrighteous areas in your life, because you’re a newborn baby, there’s no problem with that, you’re growing. Children, they keep the Word of God. All right, now we’re starting to get righteousness. Young men, they overcome the wicked one, the evil. They are living righteously, and the fathers live righteously. The results are the evidence.
How do you know you are righteous, and what does “faith in your faith” mean? (1 John 3:7)
1 John 3:7: Little children, let no one deceive you. He who practices righteousness is righteous, just as He is righteous.
What does he say the word “know” means in the Bible?
He says “know” means to understand, to be aware of, to recognize something, but “knowing God is an intimate relationship,” and that you know Him if you keep His commandments.
Why does he say John 1 is hard to understand?
He says “this chapter threw me for quite a few years till I grew in the Word,” and that “you got to get past the little baby doctrines and get into the richness of the Bible.”
Who does he say created the world?
He says John “emphasizes that Jesus created the world, created everything, and without Him nothing was made that was made.”
What does he mean by “four” involved in creation?

He says in Genesis 1 “you’re going to find the God four involved in creation. How many? Four. What are you used to? Three,” and later describes “one God doing things with four different explanations: God, the Holy Ghost, the Word, and Jesus.” This is his teaching, shown here as he said it.
Did God have a “plan B” after Adam and Eve sinned?

No. He says “He never had a plan B. He had one plan the whole time, and that was Jesus Christ, reconciling people back to God, back to what is right, and filling heaven with people that would repent and turn.”
Why does he say many young people lack motivation?
He says it is “because there’s a lack of fatherhood in the home,” and that “fathers are there to motivate you” and to make you into an adult “that can sustain themselves.”
What does he say most ministers are teaching?

He says “most ministers are just teaching baby doctrines all the time” and “a lot of ministers are teaching embryo stuff,” and that listeners are also at fault for “listening to the radio where all you hear is embryo preaching.”
Does he say evil spirits came from God?

He asks who the Father of spirits is (God) and whether the evil spirits came from God, answering “yeah, they did” since “without Him was not anything made,” and says “they rebelled and became evil spirits.”
What does he say about fathers who correct children for their own convenience?

He says a real father “doesn’t correct for their own convenience,” but “to train them up in the way they should go,” and calls it “the difference between disciplining for convenience and disciplining for future development.”
What does he say are the “first principles” of Hebrews 6:1?

He lists faith toward God, repentance from dead works, baptism of the Holy Ghost, baptism in water, baptism in the body, laying on of hands, resurrection, and eternal judgment, and calls them baby doctrine.
What does he say people who are still babies want to hear?

He says, “You want to hear that once saved always saved. You want to hear that no matter what you do God loves you and you’re going to go to heaven. That’s what you want to hear, because what? You’re a baby.”
Does he say Christians should judge?
He says “everybody’s saying don’t judge, and here the apostle is telling us to what? Judge,” meaning to discern “what’s good and what’s evil,” and says “Jesus said it, the apostles are saying it.”
What does he mean by “faith in your faith”?

He says you can’t just believe you’re saved or going to heaven “and don’t have the evidence of it, the proof of it. That’s faith in your faith,” and that “the Bible doesn’t tell us to have faith in our faith.”

items.d: In “Fitting the Mark,” Pastor David G. Kincer asks how anyone can meet the Bible’s requirement of righteousness, and answers with Abraham: a man full of fear and failures who was counted righteous because he…
p: In “Fitting the Mark,” Pastor David G. Kincer asks how anyone can meet the Bible’s requirement of righteousness, and answers with Abraham: a man full of fear and failures who was counted righteous because he believed God could do what he promised. He then applies this to seeing past our failures, to the church, and to taking the word of God to people.
How can a human fit the “mark of righteousness” when no one is righteous? (Genesis 12:2-3)

He says the Bible “requires righteousness to inherit his promises,” yet “there’s none righteous, no, not one.” To find out how, he looks at Abraham, who was promised “a great nation,” a great name and protection, and that through his seed “all the families of the earth” would be blessed.
How can a human fit the “mark of righteousness” when no one is righteous? (Genesis 12:2-3)

From creation to the book of Revelation, the Bible requires righteousness to inherit his promises, his benefits of life eternal, health, the necessity of necessities of life, the fruit of the Spirit like joy, peace, longsuffering and so forth, and all the rest. Remember when they came out of Egypt, God promised the blessings in the city, the blessings in the field, the blessings on the offspring, your children’s children. They said none would be barren among you. “I will bless you with food, I’ll bless you with houses, and I’ll bless you by having none of these diseases of Egypt to come upon you, if you obey my word and do right,” fitting into that mark of righteousness. But how can a human fit into that righteous goal and that righteous requirement when the Bible says there’s none righteous, no, not one, and all of sin to come short of the glory of God? To find out how we can, let’s take a look at a man that obtained the goal, and that is Abraham. God came to Abraham in Genesis 12:2 and said, “I’m going to make you a great nation. I am going to bless you. I’m going to make your name great. I’m going to make you a blessing to other people. I’ll bless those that bless you and curse those who curse you.” I’m going to protect you from those that hate you and despise you and want to misuse you. “I’m going to protect you, and you shall all the families of the earth be blessed.” In other words, Jesus Christ is going to come through your seed, and Jesus did, he fulfilled that by coming and turning people from sin to righteousness. In Genesis 13:16 he said, “I will make your seed as the dust of the earth.”
How can a human fit the “mark of righteousness” when no one is righteous? (Genesis 12:2-3)

Genesis 12:2-3: I will make you a great nation; I will bless you And make your name great; And you shall be a blessing. I will bless those who bless you, And I will curse him who curses you; And in you all the families of the earth shall be blessed.” Romans 3:10: As it is written: “There is none righteous, no, not one; Romans 3:23: for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God,
What did God promise Abraham and Sarah, and how impossible did it sound? (Genesis 13:16; 18)

He says God promised Abraham a seed “as the dust of the earth,” and that Sarah, “barren” and ninety, would have a son: “I’m going to change her, renew her, restore her.” He says it also included “tribulation four hundred years,” which “we don’t like to hear.”
What did God promise Abraham and Sarah, and how impossible did it sound? (Genesis 13:16; 18)

I’m going to multiply you unbelievably many times. Genesis 18:30: “Sarah your wife will have a son,” though she’s barren, though she’s past it, she’s ninety years old and she can’t have kids anymore and she’s hobbling around and she’s wrinkled and gray. “I’m going to change her, renew her, restore her, and she’s going to have a son in her old age, and you at a hundred years old and her at ninety.” And he says your seed’s going to have tribulation four hundred years. We don’t like to hear that part of “you’re going to have some troubles.”
What did God promise Abraham and Sarah, and how impossible did it sound? (Genesis 13:16; 18)

Genesis 13:16: And I will make your descendants as the dust of the earth; so that if a man could number the dust of the earth, then your descendants also could be numbered. Genesis 18:10-14: And He said, “I will certainly return to you according to the time of life, and behold, Sarah your wife shall have a son.” (Sarah was listening in the tent door which was behind him.) Now Abraham and Sarah were old, well advanced in age; and Sarah had passed the age of childbearing. Therefore Sarah laughed within herself, saying, “After I have grown old, shall I have pleasure, my lord being old also?” And the LORD said to Abraham, “Why did Sarah laugh, saying, ‘Shall I surely bear a child, since I am old?’ Is anything too hard for the LORD? At the appointed time I will return to you, according to the time of life, and Sarah shall have a son.” Genesis 15:13: Then He said to Abram: “Know certainly that your descendants will be strangers in a land that is not theirs, and will serve them, and they will afflict them four hundred years.
What failures did Abraham have, and was he still counted righteous?

He lists Abraham’s failures: lying about Sarah “out of fear for his own life,” running from the land during famine, and having a child by Sarah’s maid, which led to “a broken home.” He says Abraham even “laughed at God,” “and yet Abraham received every one of these promises because he believed God, and it was counted to him for righteousness.”
What failures did Abraham have, and was he still counted righteous?

Now this, you got to remember, sound impossible to Abraham. Here God’s talking to one man, an old man who’s married to an old woman who has wanted a child for decades and not got one. Abraham sees himself as old, ready to be put on the shelf, ready for retirement. His wife is old besides. He sees his failures in some areas to do right. He had lied twice about Sarah being his sister, not his wife, out of fear for his own life. He put Sarah on the line twice. He ran from the land that God told him to live in because of famine, because of economic hardships. He ran. Abraham had a lot of fear. He had a child by Sarah’s maid, which caused a rift in the family, till it wound up Ishmael, the son born to the maid Hagar, mocked and bullied Isaac, who was born later, so that Hagar and Ishmael left the family to make it on their own. So he had a child that ran away from home. He had a broken home. You think you’re the only one that has broken homes today? Jesus Christ himself was raised with a stepdad, and then no stepdad at all, just the dad died. The provider of the home was dead. Abraham laughed at God when God said Sarah would have a child at ninety years old. He laughed. Yeah. Sure. Yeah, I hear Christians all the time laughing, “Oh yeah, sure, yeah, sure,” at things of God. See, these were impossibilities to Abraham to [unclear] on his own, and yet Abraham received every one of these promises because he believed God, and it was counted to him for righteousness. In spite of his failures, in spite of his mistakes, in spite of laughing at God when God said, “I’m going to do the impossible with you,” yet Abraham fit into this mark. He obtained righteousness. It was counted unto him the righteousness because he what? Believed God.
What failures did Abraham have, and was he still counted righteous?

Genesis 12:10-13: Now there was a famine in the land, and Abram went down to Egypt to dwell there, for the famine was severe in the land. And it came to pass, when he was close to entering Egypt, that he said to Sarai his wife, “Indeed I know that you are a woman of beautiful countenance. Therefore it will happen, when the Egyptians see you, that they will say, ‘This is his wife’; and they will kill me, but they will let you live. Please say you are my sister, that it may be well with me for your sake, and that I may live because of you.” Genesis 15:6: And he believed in the LORD, and He accounted it to him for righteousness.
What kind of faith did Abraham have, as opposed to today’s “positive thinking” faith? (Romans 4:18)

He says today there is “the prosperity faith,” “the positive thinking faith,” “the purpose-driven faith” and a faith where we “really look at our own faith.” He then asks, “What kind of faith did he have?” and reads Romans 4:18 on Abraham believing “contrary to hope.”
What kind of faith did Abraham have, as opposed to today’s “positive thinking” faith? (Romans 4:18)

Now, isn’t that powerful? Now, what kind of faith did Abraham have? You know, today we have the prosperity faith, we have the positive thinking faith, we have the possibility thinking faith, we have the purpose-driven faith, all these P’s. You got your [unclear] faith, you got the grunt and grit and say, “I got faith.” We, we, we really look at our own faith. “Oh, do you believe? I got the faith, I got the faith, I’m a man of faith, I’m a woman of faith.” But Abraham, what kind of faith did he have? Okay, Romans 14:18, talking about Abraham, who “contrary to hope”... You know, how is he going to be a big nation when there’s only two of them? How are they going to have a child when they’re old and she’s barren? See, how can these things be, when they laughed at God and mocked God and was afraid and disobeyed God?
What kind of faith did Abraham have, as opposed to today’s “positive thinking” faith? (Romans 4:18)
Romans 4:18: who, contrary to hope, in hope believed, so that he became the father of many nations, according to what was spoken, “So shall your descendants be.”
What does “contrary to hope” mean, and what did being “fully convinced” look like? (Romans 4:19-21)

He says “contrary to hope” means “expectation,” and that Abraham “expected God to fulfill what he said he would do.” He says his faith was not his own power but “Abraham’s faith in God’s faithfulness,” “being fully convinced that God … was able to perform.”
What does “contrary to hope” mean, and what did being “fully convinced” look like? (Romans 4:19-21)

“Contrary to hope” means expectation. “Contrary to hope, in hope Abraham believed, so that he became the father of many nations.” He expected God to fulfill what he said he would do. “Not being weak in faith, he did not consider his own body already dead at a hundred years old and the deadness of Sarah’s womb.” Not being weak in what? Faith. What kind of faith did this guy have? “He did not waver at the promise of God through unbelief, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory, giving honor to God.” How many would you like to be strengthened in faith? Yeah. Did Abraham need strengthened in faith? Yeah. He laughed at God. His faith was really lacking. He mocked God. Romans 4:21: “Being fully convinced that God had” what? “God had promised, God was able to perform.” That was his faith that was put onto his account as righteousness: that God had the power to perform what he promised. Not Abraham had the power. It wasn’t Abraham’s faith, it was Abraham’s faith in God’s faithfulness, and it was what counted into him to righteousness. And we can today fit into that mark by believing like Abraham believed.
What does “contrary to hope” mean, and what did being “fully convinced” look like? (Romans 4:19-21)

Romans 4:19-21: And not being weak in faith, he did not consider his own body, already dead (since he was about a hundred years old), and the deadness of Sarah’s womb. He did not waver at the promise of God through unbelief, but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God, and being fully convinced that what He had promised He was also able to perform. Romans 4:21: and being fully convinced that what He had promised He was also able to perform.
Could Abraham receive God’s promises with a broken family and few believers around?

He says Abraham’s father was dead, his household was broken, and only three believers were in Canaan: “things don’t have to be perfect for you for God to bless your life.” He says that despite his failures Abraham “repented” and believed that God “had the power to do what God said he would do.”
Could Abraham receive God’s promises with a broken family and few believers around?

Now remember, Abraham’s father was dead. You know, your dad might have ran off somewhere, died, or your mom early, you know, things can happen in life. It did not stop Abraham from obtaining the promises, because of the faith that he had in God to perform. Things don’t have to be perfect for you for God to bless your life. Now that’s a good amen. He and his family, which were three people, him, Sarah and Lot, were the only believers in Canaan land. They were the only ones that worshiped God and did not worship idols. They were the only ones that believed to live right, stay married, marry one woman, stay married and so forth. Now, Abraham messed up with the maid, but he didn’t do that again. When they had church, there was only three there. Everybody else laughed at him, mocked at him. See, things weren’t great for Abraham here. Then Lot, his nephew, got mad, and they had a quarrel and Lot left. Now there’s two. And as I said before, he conceived a child out of God’s will, he was afraid for his life and left the land to live in a pagan land, twice put Sarah’s life on the line, and Sarah did it. She went into Pharaoh’s household and went along with the program, laughed at and questioned God. And yet, in spite of this, Abraham repented of his failures and saw past the impossibilities of the promises, because he believed God had the power to do what God said he would do. That was his faith. His faith was not in his faith. Sarah’s faith was not in Abraham’s faith or her faith.
Could Abraham receive God’s promises with a broken family and few believers around?

Genesis 12:14-15: So it was, when Abram came into Egypt, that the Egyptians saw the woman, that she was very beautiful. The princes of Pharaoh also saw her and commended her to Pharaoh. And the woman was taken to Pharaoh’s house.
What did Abraham begin to see above his failures? (Hebrews 11:10)

He says Abraham “began to see above himself, above his failures,” saw a city “whose builder and maker was God,” and knew that “if God said it, then it’s going to happen.” He says the faith that makes you righteous is faith “in God to perform what he promised.”
What did Abraham begin to see above his failures? (Hebrews 11:10)

Their faith was in God to perform what he promised, and that’s the faith that makes you righteous. Now, church, that’s good stuff. Abraham, you remember in the Bible, saw a city without foundations, or a city with foundations, made without human hands, whose builder and maker was God. He began to see above himself, above his failures, and he began to see what God was talking about. He saw a great nation, he saw a great name, he saw that he was going to be blessed by God. He knew it was going to come. If God said it, then it’s going to happen. He saw that Sarah could have a child in her old age though she was barren. Remember, the Bible says Christ is our treasure in earthly vessels. You say, we, and the Bible says, “Christ be formed in you.” Folks, we can have Christ formed in us. This is our treasure in earthly human vessels, that Christ can be formed in, birthed in us, be born again of the Spirit of God.
What did Abraham begin to see above his failures? (Hebrews 11:10)
Hebrews 11:10: for he waited for the city which has foundations, whose builder and maker is God.
How can Christ be formed in us, and can we see a “glorious church”? (2 Corinthians 4:7; Galatians 4:19)

He says our faith “should be in my God, that he has the power to back up what he said,” not in being “good enough.” He asks whether we see a “failed church with a bunch of sin,” or see “past” that to a “glorious church” that God is building.
How can Christ be formed in us, and can we see a “glorious church”? (2 Corinthians 4:7; Galatians 4:19)

These things look impossible, but if God said he can do it, then our faith should be in the fact that, not in my “good enough,” not in my righteousness, not in my faith, but my faith should be in my God, that he has the power to back up what he said, and by God, he’ll do it in my life, and that makes us righteous and fits in to the mark. Can we see today past our failures and impossibilities and see a glorious church without spot or wrinkle or any such thing that Jesus is coming for? Or all we see is a failed church with a bunch of sin going on? Or do we see past and see how God sees, that he is out to make and build a glorious church? Abraham saw the great nation, the great name, the blessing, the protection and this child being born. He saw past his failures, and I submit to you, by the kind of faith Abraham had, we can see past our failures and others’ failures and get our eyes focused on what God told us to get focused on, and then we’ll begin to obtain them. Could that be an amen?
How can Christ be formed in us, and can we see a “glorious church”? (2 Corinthians 4:7; Galatians 4:19)

2 Corinthians 4:7: But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellence of the power may be of God and not of us. Galatians 4:19: My little children, for whom I labor in birth again until Christ is formed in you, Ephesians 5:27: that He might present her to Himself a glorious church, not having spot or wrinkle or any such thing, but that she should be holy and without blemish.
Does God have people in our city and state? (Acts 18:10)

He says God told Paul “I have much people in this city,” and asks whether we can see past our own needs that “God has people in California, in spite of the way California is going.” He says some people “don’t become religious, they change,” because “they get that faith of Abraham.”
Does God have people in our city and state? (Acts 18:10)

Acts 18:10: “I am with you,” God said to Paul. “No man shall hurt you, for I have much people in this city.” Can we see that? Can we see beyond, away from our own needs and our own little schedule in life and see that God has people in [unclear], but we have to take the word to them? Can we see that God has people in California, in spite of the way California is going? Can we see beyond what California is doing and heading, and we see that God has some people, if we get the word to them, he will raise them up and change them? Some people, what, change? They don’t become religious, they change. Why? Because they get that faith of Abraham, that God can do what he said he would do. “He who has begun a good work in you will complete it,” finish it, “until the day of Jesus Christ.”
Does God have people in our city and state? (Acts 18:10)
Acts 18:10: for I am with you, and no one will attack you to hurt you; for I have many people in this city.”
Is getting saved just the start? (Philippians 1:6)

He says “when we got saved and accepted Christ, that’s just the start,” and that “God wants to complete his work in you.” He says we must get “your position of righteousness up to a condition of righteousness,” and that God has “a multitude of people in America that he will bring out if we get the word out.”
Is getting saved just the start? (Philippians 1:6)

Can we see that when we got saved and accepted Christ, that’s just the start? There’s much more after salvation than just getting saved and go into heaven. God wants to complete his work in you. Amen, and form Christ in you and actually get your position of righteousness up to a condition of righteousness, where you live rightly and talk rightly. Could that be an amen? See, can we see that? Can we see, [unclear], that God can reach many in [unclear], in California, and America, the nation? Yes. America, America is a mess and it’s going downhill, but can we see with God’s eyes that God has a multitude of people in America that he will bring out if we get the word out? And the nations of the earth, you know, we go to, I’ve been to the mission field, I’ve been to the nations, and I am saddened by the fact we go over there and we paint houses for them and walls for them and repair things for them.
Is getting saved just the start? (Philippians 1:6)
Philippians 1:6: being confident of this very thing, that He who has begun a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ;
What does he say about mission trips that paint buildings instead of preaching?

He says on the mission field “we paint houses for them” though “they’re very capable of painting and repairing,” and “very capable of preaching.” He says “what we got to take to the nations of the world is the word of God,” and that “Paul didn’t go and paint buildings. He went and preached the word.”
What does he say about mission trips that paint buildings instead of preaching?

Folks, they’re very capable of painting and repairing, and to be honest with you, they’re very capable of preaching. But what we got to take to the nations of the world is the word of God. When you start painting, you think that’s a mission field? You go over there and you do something that they can do. Paul didn’t go and paint buildings. He went and preached the word, isn’t that right? I mean, you’re reading the same Bible I am. And I saw people over there shouldn’t have been over there. One guy met in the airport that I knew was abusing his wife, he was a tyrant in the home, and he told me I was coming back and he was leaving, and he told me he was going to the mission field. I thought, my God, you are a mission [unclear]. You know, we get hyped up on this. “I’m going to a third world country.” You better get your own act together. Could that be an amen? And we need to take this word.
What does he say the nations need, and what is the “finished work”? (Matthew 9:27)

He says “the third world nations is sick and tired of these kind of missionaries” who take donated items, and “what they need is the word of God.” He says God promised to complete his work, and that believing God has power to do it “is my righteousness.” The recording ends as he begins a Bible story of two blind men following Jesus.
What does he say the nations need, and what is the “finished work”? (Matthew 9:27)

If we can’t get the word in our own life and live it in our own life and teach it, our, what good are we going to do the third world nations? And honestly, the third world nations is sick and tired of these kind of missionaries. Oh, they’ll take your money, and they’ll take your chairs that you donate, your Bibles you donate, and they’ll sell them. But what they need is the word of God. Adults, are you out there? I’m telling you some facts. God promised to complete his good work. Okay, God, you said you’re going to do the job, I’m believing you have power to do it. That is my righteousness, and that’s what’s going to lead me to what? The finished work. Matthew 9:27: let’s give some stories in the Bible where this faith worked. Two blind men followed Jesus Christ.
What does he say the nations need, and what is the “finished work”? (Matthew 9:27)
Matthew 9:27: When Jesus departed from there, two blind men followed Him, crying out and saying, “Son of David, have mercy on us!”
What does he say the Bible requires to inherit God’s promises?
He says “from creation to the book of Revelation, the Bible requires righteousness to inherit his promises,” including life eternal and health.
He says God promised to “make you a great nation,” “bless you,” make Abraham’s name great, and “protect you from those that hate you,” so that through his seed “Jesus Christ is going to come.”
How old does he say Sarah was when God promised her a son?
He says she was “ninety years old,” “barren,” “hobbling around and she’s wrinkled and gray,” and Abraham was “a hundred years old.”
What mistakes does he say Abraham made?
He says Abraham “had lied twice about Sarah being his sister,” “ran from the land that God told him to live in because of famine,” and “had a child by Sarah’s maid.”
Does he say Abraham laughed at God?
Yes. He says “Abraham laughed at God when God said Sarah would have a child at ninety years old,” yet “it was counted to him for righteousness.”
What kinds of faith does he say we have today?
He lists “the prosperity faith,” “the positive thinking faith,” “the possibility thinking faith,” and “the purpose-driven faith, all these P’s.”
What does he say “contrary to hope” means?
He says “contrary to hope means expectation,” and “in hope Abraham believed, so that he became the father of many nations.”
Whose faith does he say was counted as righteousness?
He says “it wasn’t Abraham’s faith, it was Abraham’s faith in God’s faithfulness,” that “God had the power to perform what he promised.”
Does he say things must be perfect for God to bless you?
No. He says “things don’t have to be perfect for you for God to bless your life,” and that Abraham’s father “was dead” and it “did not stop Abraham from obtaining the promises.”
How many believers does he say were with Abraham in Canaan?
He says it was “three people,” “him, Sarah and Lot,” the “only ones that worshiped God and did not worship idols,” and “when they had church, there was only three there.”
What does he mean that “his faith was not in his faith”?
He says “their faith was in God to perform what he promised, and that’s the faith that makes you righteous,” not faith in themselves.
What does he ask about seeing a “glorious church”?
He asks, “Can we see today past our failures and impossibilities and see a glorious church without spot or wrinkle” and not only “a failed church with a bunch of sin going on?”
What does God say to Paul in Acts 18:10 as he tells it?
He says God told Paul, “I am with you,” and “No man shall hurt you, for I have much people in this city.”
What does he say about people who go on the mission field?
He says “Paul didn’t go and paint buildings. He went and preached the word,” and that people going abroad should “get your own act together” first.
What does he say third-world nations need?
He says they are “sick and tired of these kind of missionaries” who bring items that get sold, and “what they need is the word of God.”

items.d: In “Five Fulfilled Predictions,” Pastor David G. Kincer walks through the five promises of comfort in Isaiah 40 (comfort, warfare ended, iniquity pardoned, double for her sins, and the glory of the Lord…
p: In “Five Fulfilled Predictions,” Pastor David G. Kincer walks through the five promises of comfort in Isaiah 40 (comfort, warfare ended, iniquity pardoned, double for her sins, and the glory of the Lord revealed) and shows how he says each was fulfilled in John the Baptist and Jesus Christ. He then teaches on grace and truth, the shortness of life, being born again by the Word and the Spirit, and the five rewards of Isaiah 40:10-11 that God gives his church.
What are the five prophecies of comfort in Isaiah 40:1-2?

He lists five predictions: comfort for God’s people, “her warfare is ended,” “her iniquity is pardoned,” double received “for all her sins,” and the glory of the Lord revealed so that “all flesh shall see it together.” He says he will show them “actually fulfilled in detail 700 years later.”
What are the five prophecies of comfort in Isaiah 40:1-2?

We’re going to see here in Isaiah 40, and we’re going to see them actually fulfilled in detail 700 years later, 700 years later, five prophetic predictions. Number one, in Isaiah 40:1: “Comfort ye, comfort ye my people. Speak comfort to Jerusalem, cry out comfort to her.” Okay, cheer up, encourage her, relieve her, bring comfort. Number two: “Her warfare is ended.” Her struggle, her conflicts, her fighting is ended; it’s accomplished, it’s done. Number three: “Her iniquity is pardoned.” Wow, powerful. “For she has received from the Lord’s hand double for all her sins.” Double. All this struggling, all this conflict, God doubled it, and it is ended.
What are the five prophecies of comfort in Isaiah 40:1-2?

Isaiah 40:1-2: “Comfort, yes, comfort My people!” Says your God. “Speak comfort to Jerusalem, and cry out to her, That her warfare is ended, That her iniquity is pardoned; For she has received from the LORD’s hand Double for all her sins.”
Why does God use opposing nations to correct His people, and what does he say about the church today?

He says God “uses nations as tools to correct his people,” but the nations “overdo it,” and God says “don’t mess with my people.” He says the natural house was destroyed and God switches to “spiritual Jerusalem,” his church, and tells believers not to “get down in the dumps” because people dislike them, since “God is not finished with us.”
Why does God use opposing nations to correct His people, and what does he say about the church today?

Now, we know that natural Israel’s sins, the doubling of their sins, was fulfilled in Daniel 9:12. It says, “He has confirmed his words which he spoke against us and against our judges who judged us by bringing upon us a great disaster; for under the whole heaven such has never been done as what has been done to Jerusalem.” Okay, but you don’t find comfort in Daniel, you don’t find the war ended, you don’t find the pardon, but you find the doubling of the punishment for natural Israel. Then we go over to Zechariah 1:5. See, God uses nations as tools to correct his people, but the nations, our opponents, they overdo it. And God brings this out in Zechariah: “I am zealous for Jerusalem and Zion. I’m exceedingly angry with the nations. I was a little angry at my people, and the nations helped, but with evil intent.” And in one other place it says they wanted Judah to cease as a nation. That’s how angry and hateful the nations that God used to correct his people come against his people. And we have the same thing today. You know, God, like children, he chastens us, he corrects us, and sometimes he uses our opponents to do that, and they do it with such hatred and with such evil intent, and they pick at us and everything else. And God says, “Hey, don’t mess with my people. I’m doing this. Don’t you add to it.” “Therefore,” says the Lord, “I’m returning to Jerusalem with mercy, and my house shall be built in it.” Now, there’s a switch here. Okay, the house, the natural house, was destroyed. He’s switching to spiritual Jerusalem, the bride coming down in Revelation out of heaven, God’s church, God’s people. He’s going to build his church. Hallelujah. In Jeremiah 29 verse 12 it talks about the great speckled bird: “My heritage is to me like a speckled bird; the birds all around her are against her.” “Many rulers have destroyed my vineyard.” And that’s what we have in America today. We, the church, the Christians, are attacked so much. We’re the only ones that are not tolerated. We’re the only ones that you can’t speak against, right now. You speak against blacks, you speak against homosexuals, you speak against Jews or whatever, they’re going to come after you; Muslims. But you speak against Christianity, and no, no one cares. They tear us apart, they rip us apart, and Jeremiah prophesied it years ago, and God and Zechariah pointed out more than one time, this is just one verse. So, church, don’t get down in the dumps because people disagree with you, dislike you and find fault with you. Amen. God is not finished with us. He will finish the good work that he begun in us.
Why does God use opposing nations to correct His people, and what does he say about the church today?

Daniel 9:12: And He has confirmed His words, which He spoke against us and against our judges who judged us, by bringing upon us a great disaster; for under the whole heaven such has never been done as what has been done to Jerusalem. Zechariah 1:14-16: So the angel who spoke with me said to me, “Proclaim, saying, ‘Thus says the LORD of hosts: “I am zealous for Jerusalem And for Zion with great zeal. I am exceedingly angry with the nations at ease; For I was a little angry, And they helped—but with evil intent.” ‘Therefore thus says the LORD: “I am returning to Jerusalem with mercy; My house shall be built in it,” says the LORD of hosts, “And a surveyor’s line shall be stretched out over Jerusalem.” ’ Jeremiah 12:9: My heritage is to Me like a speckled vulture; The vultures all around are against her. Come, assemble all the beasts of the field, Bring them to devour! Philippians 1:6: being confident of this very thing, that He who has begun a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ;
When were these five prophecies fulfilled, and who was the voice in the wilderness?

He says they are fulfilled when “the voice of one crying in the wilderness” comes, and that John the Baptist said “I am the voice.” He says Luke gives the date and the rulers of the time so that no one can say “these things never happened,” and he places it at 29 AD.
When were these five prophecies fulfilled, and who was the voice in the wilderness?

Now, when will these prophecies be fulfilled? Jeremiah addresses this issue: “The voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord.” Isaiah 40:3. And then he talks about making the road straight, the valleys coming up, the mountains going down, removing all obstacles. God is going to remove all obstacles that’s in our way. That’s when these five prophecies are going to be fulfilled, when that voice comes crying in the wilderness. And then he gives this fifth prophetic promise: “The glory of the Lord shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together.” So see, when the voice in the wilderness comes saying these words about the valleys being straight and the roads being straight and the glory of the Lord revealed and human beings seeing the glory, not just hearing about it but seeing the glory, that’s when these prophecies are going to come to pass. And so we see in 29 AD, when John preached baptism and repentance, these things are fulfilled. John said, John the Baptist said in John 1:23, “I am the voice of one crying in the wilderness: Prepare the way of the Lord,” as the prophet Isaiah said. See, John said, “I’m the voice.” Okay? And Isaiah said, when you hear the voice in the wilderness. John didn’t go to the cities; he went out into the desert, and people went out to the desert to hear him. In our generation, all the evangelists and everybody goes to the cities, ‘cause they can get a big crowd and make money. They don’t visit the small towns and all that. But John the Baptist went out there to the Mojave Desert and started preaching, and people came out to hear him, because he had a message from God, a living word. Then in Luke 3:1 he gives us the details, and God, knowing that our enemies would try to distort the Bible and say these things never happened and all this, here in Luke he gives us the details of the time. “In the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar”: Tiberius started ruling in 14 AD; 14 plus 15 equals 29, 29 AD. All right, “Pilate was governor of Judea.” History shows that he was governor of Judea. “Herod of Galilee,” “Philip his brother” was the ruler in another area, and [unclear] ruled with his mother until 29 AD; she died, and he ruled by himself in a region up by Lebanon, north, in Israel, north of the Sea of Galilee. And “Annas and Caiaphas were the high priests”; Caiaphas was high priest from 8 AD to 36 AD. So all of these people were there, they’re in natural history, they’re recorded in all kinds of historical documents, and the very date when this happened is given to us: 29 AD.
When were these five prophecies fulfilled, and who was the voice in the wilderness?

Isaiah 40:3-5: The voice of one crying in the wilderness: “Prepare the way of the LORD; Make straight in the desert A highway for our God. Every valley shall be exalted And every mountain and hill brought low; The crooked places shall be made straight And the rough places smooth; The glory of the LORD shall be revealed, And all flesh shall see it together; For the mouth of the LORD has spoken.” John 1:23: He said: “I am ‘The voice of one crying in the wilderness: “Make straight the way of the LORD,” ’ as the prophet Isaiah said.” Luke 3:1-2: Now in the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, Pontius Pilate being governor of Judea, Herod being tetrarch of Galilee, his brother Philip tetrarch of Iturea and the region of Trachonitis, and Lysanias tetrarch of Abilene, while Annas and Caiaphas were high priests, the word of God came to John the son of Zacharias in the wilderness.
What was the first fulfillment: how did John bring comfort?

He says John came “preaching a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins,” and that the blood of lambs and goats could not take away sin, so John’s message was that God would pardon those who repent and are baptized. He says that message “comforted the people,” and that John added that “all flesh shall see the salvation of God.”
What was the first fulfillment: how did John bring comfort?

So he came into the wilderness speaking this word. He went preaching a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins, as written in the book of Isaiah the prophet, saying; and we’ll finish that verse. So this is the first fulfillment: “Comfort ye, comfort ye my people.” These people have been offering sacrifices and burning incense and everything else, and the Bible says that it is impossible for the blood of lambs and goats to cleanse away sin. Only the blood of Christ. Only them looking forward to the Lamb of God, the real Lamb, when they sacrificed those lambs, would cleanse them. And so John came along with a message that, “Hey, God’s going to pardon you, God’s going to forgive you if you just repent and get water baptized,” the washing of the water, a washing away of sin. And that was the message that comforted the people. Now, continuing, “the voice of one crying in the wilderness.” John said that’s what he was speaking: “Prepare you the way of the Lord.” Then he quotes Isaiah 40. He quotes it, but he adds an explanation of something to it at the end. It says, “All flesh shall see it together,” in Isaiah, but John said, “All flesh shall see the salvation of God.” Oh! So the glory, when they say it, it is the glory, and it is the glory of salvation. Do you see that? So John amplifies it; he brings more clear explanation. The glory of the Lord revealed is going to be the salvation of God.
What was the first fulfillment: how did John bring comfort?

Luke 3:3: And he went into all the region around the Jordan, preaching a baptism of repentance for the remission of sins, Hebrews 10:4: For it is not possible that the blood of bulls and goats could take away sins. Luke 3:6: And all flesh shall see the salvation of God.’ ”
How was “her warfare is ended” fulfilled? (John 19:28, Hebrews 2:14)

He says Jesus on the cross “knew all things were accomplished,” so “the warfare has ended,” and it “is finished.” He says through death Jesus destroyed “him who had the power of death, that is the devil,” and so “he destroyed our enemy.”
How was “her warfare is ended” fulfilled? (John 19:28, Hebrews 2:14)

Now, number two: “Her warfare is ended,” completed in accomplishment. We find that in John 19:28: “Jesus, knowing that all things were now accomplished.” Here he is on the cross, he’s dying, he’s at the last few minutes of his life, he had just drunk the vinegar to fulfill prophecy, and he knew all things were accomplished. The warfare has ended. “It is finished.” It’s complete. And bowing his head, he gave up his spirit. Hebrews 2:14: “Through death Jesus might destroy him who had the power of death, that is, the devil.” You see, he destroyed our enemy. The warfare is ended. Hallelujah, Jesus on the cross.
How was “her warfare is ended” fulfilled? (John 19:28, Hebrews 2:14)

John 19:28: After this, Jesus, knowing that all things were now accomplished, that the Scripture might be fulfilled, said, “I thirst!” Hebrews 2:14: Inasmuch then as the children have partaken of flesh and blood, He Himself likewise shared in the same, that through death He might destroy him who had the power of death, that is, the devil,
How is “her iniquity is pardoned” fulfilled? Is any sin too big to be forgiven?

He says the blood of Jesus cleanses from “all sin,” including what he calls the unpardonable sin, and that Paul being saved as the “greatest sinner” is an example for everybody. He says “don’t let Satan or people get down on you because you make some mistakes,” because we have an advocate with the Father and can take it to the cross.
How is “her iniquity is pardoned” fulfilled? Is any sin too big to be forgiven?

Now, “her iniquity is pardoned.” 1 John 1:7: “The blood of Jesus Christ His Son cleanses” from how much sin? All sin. Does that include the unpardonable sin? Yes, it does. And these Christians going around like they are just too evil to be saved, or these people too evil to be saved: remember, Paul was the greatest sinner. You cannot be a worse sinner than Paul, and God saved him for an example for everybody. Now, if you think you’re too impossible, the Bible says it’s not; his blood is more powerful than anything you can do. Hallelujah. Yeah. Romans 8:2: “The law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has made me free from the law of sin and death.” Free! I’m pardoned. I deserve to die, I deserve to be punished, I deserve to be punished for eternity, but the resurrection of Christ, that Spirit that raised Christ from the dead, dwells in us, and we are pardoned. Hallelujah. That’s the third prophecy: “Her iniquity is pardoned.” You know, don’t let Satan or people get down on you because you make some mistakes. The Bible says we have an advocate with the Father. We can go to Jesus and we can still be forgiven as Christians, for 30 years, 40 years, however long it takes. All you got to do is take it to the cross. Amen. And don’t get down; stay up by the power of the blood to forgive and cleanse. And our warfare is ended; stop struggling with God. Stop struggling as a Christian; your warfare has ended. Amen. Hallelujah.
How is “her iniquity is pardoned” fulfilled? Is any sin too big to be forgiven?

1 John 1:7: But if we walk in the light as He is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus Christ His Son cleanses us from all sin. 1 Timothy 1:15-16: This is a faithful saying and worthy of all acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am chief. However, for this reason I obtained mercy, that in me first Jesus Christ might show all longsuffering, as a pattern to those who are going to believe on Him for everlasting life. Romans 8:2: For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has made me free from the law of sin and death. 1 John 2:1: My little children, these things I write to you, so that you may not sin. And if anyone sins, we have an Advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous.
What does “received double for all her sins” mean for Christians? (1 Peter 2:24)

He says natural Israel received double for her sins, but in the new covenant “God puts our punishment of sin on Jesus Christ.” He says Christ “took the double portion, the double punishment, for our sin,” which he calls “a relief,” so now we can “work on living.”
What does “received double for all her sins” mean for Christians? (1 Peter 2:24)

Number four: “She has received the Lord’s hand double for all her sins.” We saw natural Israel received double for her sins. John 1:29, John the Baptist, Jesus coming, and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God that takes away the sin of the world.” He takes away the sin of the world. We’re supposed to reap everlasting damnation and the punishment for our sin here on earth, but Jesus, the Bible says, takes away the sin of the whole world. How did he do that? How did he do that? 1 Peter 2:24: Jesus himself bore, carried, took our sins in his own body on the tree, the cross, “that we, having died to sins, might live for righteousness.” Christ took the double portion, the double punishment, for our sin. And, folks, that’s comforting words, that’s encouraging words, that’s a relief. Amen. I don’t have to worry about those things anymore; I got to pursue life. See, he’s took my punishment, he took my blame, he took my shame; now I can work on living. Amen.
What does “received double for all her sins” mean for Christians? (1 Peter 2:24)

John 1:29: The next day John saw Jesus coming toward him, and said, “Behold! The Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world! 1 Peter 2:24: who Himself bore our sins in His own body on the tree, that we, having died to sins, might live for righteousness—by whose stripes you were healed.
Does God give back double what sin and Satan took? (Job, Elisha, Exodus 22:4)

He says that a thief caught “has to pay what? Double back,” that Satan is the thief, and that when we turn to Christ “God restores what? Double.” He points to Job, who received “twice as much,” and to Elisha’s “double portion,” and says “think big” about God.
Does God give back double what sin and Satan took? (Job, Elisha, Exodus 22:4)

Unlike natural Israel, in the new covenant God puts our punishment of sin on Jesus Christ. Okay? In fact, if you read this right, another way: “shall receive double for their sins.” You can read in there the other side of the story, that you will receive double for everything sin took from you. Are you out there? See, sin and Satan robs us; the Bible says he’s a thief, he’s a robber. And you come to Christ, and God says, “Hey, I’ll give you back double what Satan and sin took from you.” Hallelujah. Yeah, powerful. And how do we know that’s true? Job. Job, after Satan was done, Job received what? Twice what he had before. See, God allowed Satan to touch Job and all that, and then the Bible says Job received double, twice as much. You remember Elisha, what kind of portion did he get from Elijah? A double portion. You see, in Exodus 22:4 the thief, when he’s caught, has to pay what? Double back. Who is the thief? Satan. When we turn to Christ, Satan’s exposed, Satan is destroyed, and he has to let us go, and we get double all the pain and all the problems that he caused in our life by us listening to him. God restores what? Double. Amen, amen, hallelujah, very powerful. Okay, and what was the blessing of the firstborn, by the way? A double portion. Folks, think big. When you think about God, think big. Stop, stop thinking so puny and whiny and wimpy. People have this thing: “Well, I’m just humble, I’m not worthy of anything.” No, you’re not worthy; you never will be worthy. But Jesus has given us things, and here he’s given us double. Hallelujah. And if you were a Christian all your life, he’s going to give you a double portion of the blessings of God anyway, like Elisha got from Elijah. So don’t think you got to go out and sin to get double; you’re going to get double anyway. Can I hear an amen? Amen. Hallelujah.
Does God give back double what sin and Satan took? (Job, Elisha, Exodus 22:4)

Exodus 22:4: If the theft is certainly found alive in his hand, whether it is an ox or donkey or sheep, he shall restore double. Job 42:10: And the LORD restored Job’s losses when he prayed for his friends. Indeed the LORD gave Job twice as much as he had before. 2 Kings 2:9: And so it was, when they had crossed over, that Elijah said to Elisha, “Ask! What may I do for you, before I am taken away from you?” Elisha said, “Please let a double portion of your spirit be upon me.”
What does “the glory of the Lord shall be revealed” mean, and what is grace? (John 1:14)

He says the Word became flesh and “we beheld, we saw his glory,” and that Jesus’ glory is “grace and truth.” He says grace is not only favor but God “exerting his influence,” “divine enablement,” turning people to Christ, keeping and strengthening them.
What does “the glory of the Lord shall be revealed” mean, and what is grace? (John 1:14)

Now, “The glory of the Lord shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together.” This number five, the glory of the Lord being revealed. John 1:1: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.” Period. John 1:14: “The Word became flesh and dwelt amongst us,” we beheld, we saw his glory. “The glory of the Lord shall be revealed, and all flesh shall see it together.” Those people saw the glory of God. Amen. “The glory as the only begotten of the Father.” Now, we know who he was. Who is the only begotten of the Father? Jesus Christ is the only one that was birthed by God. Adam was made out of the dust, Eve was made from his bone, but Jesus was birthed by God in the womb of Mary. Hallelujah. “Became flesh and dwelt amongst us.” And this is his glory: he’s full of what? “Grace and truth.” Grace and truth. And if America would just understand the power of grace, instead of this “favor,” and we’re just a bunch of whims: “Well, I’m saved by grace, I’m saved by grace, I’m saved by grace,” like, and God just favors me no matter what. Grace is much more powerful than that when you read it in the Bible. And I like this definition that Vine’s Dictionary came up with: “Grace means good will, kindness and favor.” That is true, but Vine put it all together, all the verses, and they said this: “by which God, exerting His influence, divine enablement, upon souls.” People, see, grace isn’t just “I’m in favor.” I’m in favor? No, God is exerting his influence upon me. God is coming to me, he’s enabling me, he’s convicting me, he’s drawing me, to what? To turn them to Christ, to keep them in Christ, to strengthen them in Christ and increase them in Christ. Amen.
What does “the glory of the Lord shall be revealed” mean, and what is grace? (John 1:14)

John 1:1: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. John 1:14: And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we beheld His glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth.
Is being humble the same as being a wimp? (grace and the example of Moses)

He says “we’ve been taught such a wimpy grace” and that Moses, “the meekest man,” stood up to Pharaoh and broke the golden calf. He says “being humble is standing for God’s Word no matter what the crowd does,” and that grace has a doctrine: “to live holy and righteous in this world.”
Is being humble the same as being a wimp? (grace and the example of Moses)

Amen. Are you there, church? We’ve been taught such a wimpy grace. We don’t inherit the power of God; we just think we’re a bunch of humble wimps walking around. You know, if you say you got something in God, then you’re prideful and you’re arrogant; you got to humble yourself. Doesn’t the Bible say the weak should say they are strong? Yeah. How many... you know, Moses was the meekest man, the Bible says, except Jesus, of course. Was he a wimp? No! He stood right up to Pharaoh and said, “Hey, let my people go. God said let my people go.” He didn’t go in there, “Pharaoh, I’m not worthy to be here, but would you please let my people go? God says, you know, you need to let his people go. Would you do that?” Okay, didn’t do that. He walked in there and said, “God said let my people go,” and he is the meekest man outside of Jesus, amen. Did he come down off the mountain and saw those people worshiping that golden calf, he go, “Oh, oh, you shouldn’t be doing that. I don’t want to hurt your feelings, but you know, you really, you really shouldn’t be making a golden calf”? No! He went on, “Say, what are you people doing?” He grabbed that calf, broke it up, crushed it into the dust, threw it in the water, made them drink out of it, and that’s diarrhea, folks, all the way. Are you there? See, we can be humble without being a wimp. See, Moses knew who he was; he knew God was with him. David knew God was with him. My goodness, they possess these things, and you can possess these things. Being humble is not being wimpy. Being humble is standing for God’s Word no matter what the crowd does. You just simply stick with God’s Word, and that’s what Moses did, and that’s why he was humble. Amen. The crowds wanted to kill him, the people wanted to kill him, they wanted another leader; it didn’t bother him a bit. He stood on God’s side. He didn’t get, “Oh, my God!” And American Christians just fall apart at the slightest opposition and accusation, because we don’t understand these things.
