At that time they were less than 1% of the population, and I’ll tell you why it happened: because the church stayed in their walls, happy with going to church, happy with, you know, bringing kids in from the neighborhood and teaching them Sunday school and having a choir and all that, and I’m happy with just the status quo, going home and just being Christians. And so we, by our removal, allowed the liberals and the homosexuals and the atheists and the humanists to impress our nation and change laws that favor them.
How does he say the church should respond?

He says the church has been satisfied with worshiping Jesus for decades and has let the nation go to hell, so it has to wake up, confront this, and ask God to give it the spirit of Lot. He says Satan uses our failures to put us down, but we need to stand up like Lot did and keep going back to righteousness. He says the church is afraid to speak out on Bible moral issues, and that not speaking up means not warning people so they have no chance to get saved.
How does he say the church should respond?

Lesbian, gay, bisexual, transsexuals, all the sexual deviant lifestyles: they are pushing to make legal, and have got them legal now. Some people are saying that a guy who realizes he was a girl can now go into the girl gym and the girl shower. Now, how many you know there’s— these are supposed to be the best of the nation in politics, and they make a law like that. They got their own flag. I don’t see a heterosexual flag anywhere. You see, a flag is a symbol of a united nation, a people united. See, they have an agenda, and they’ll eventually change the American flag. You’re looking at me like you never thought of this stuff. See, while we’ve been satisfied with worshiping Jesus for decades, satisfied with the status quo, we’ve let our nation go to hell. We’ve got to wake up, and we got to confront this thing. We need to ask God to give us the spirit of Lot. Yes. We got some— how many got some failures in you? Yeah. How many are working on it? And see, that is another thing that Satan uses to put us down. But we need to stand up like Lot did, with his mistakes; keep going back to righteousness and winning this battle of America before God judges it. Now, guess who they’re trying to put in the closet: Jesus and his followers. See, they want to censor the Bible, they want to censor Christians, and they’ve done it. And so they’re out of the closet, publicly declare, and who are they putting in the closet? Jesus Christ, the Bible and his followers. And the church has fell for it in America. We’re afraid to speak out on Bible moral issues, and in not speaking up you don’t warn the people, and they don’t have a chance to get saved. And God said in Ezekiel he’d hold you accountable if you didn’t— he said they’ll die in their sins, but I’m going to hold you accountable. Hallelujah.
How does he say the church should respond?

Ezekiel 33:8: When I say to the wicked, ‘O wicked man, you shall surely die!’ and you do not speak to warn the wicked from his way, that wicked man shall die in his iniquity; but his blood I will require at your hand.
What does God judge nations for, and how are righteous people delivered?

He says God judges individuals, cities, nations and the world, for homosexuality, sexual immorality, pride, prosperity, idleness, weakening the poor, abominations and forcing sin on others. He says Bible moral Christians are delivered, like those in the lion’s den, the fiery furnace and Egypt, by their righteousness, not by grace or faith, and that a visitation and a judgment message will come before the judgment. He says the judgment message has been lacking in America for thirty-some years.
What does God judge nations for, and how are righteous people delivered?

What do we learn, real quick? God judges individuals, cities, and nations, and the world. God judges. What do we learn? Crimes and sins or conditions that God judges us for: they are homosexuality, sexual immorality, pride, prosperity, idleness, weakening the poor, abominations, and forcing sin on others. Bible moral Christians are delivered. As one thing you can rest assured, you might go into the lion’s den, but you’re going to come out. You might go into the fiery furnace, but you’re going to come out. You might go into Egypt, but you’re going to come out. You got that? And it’s not your grace and it’s not your faith that’s going to get you out; it’s what? Your righteousness before the judgment. Miraculous things will take place. An angel, or some kind of spirit being, God himself, Jesus, will bring a visitation before the judgment, and he will bring the judgment message. And this is what’s lacking in America for thirty-some years: the judgment message. We’ve been preaching God is love and Christians and faith and grace and all this, and Christians in America are just a bunch of wimps, because they have no fear of God, because the judgment of God is not preached, and the judgment, the punishment, because of specific sins.
What does he say about people who call the Bible a book of myths and allegories?

He says they are wrong, and that the events in the Bible happened and occurred. He says the allegorical part is that these real occurrences happened to teach us, as illustrations, and that science can never explain supernatural things.
What does he say “strange flesh” means in Jude 7?
He says strange flesh is same-sex, unnatural, and he links it to the way Romans uses the word unnatural. He says Sodom is an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal fire.
Does he say angels can have children with humans?
No. He says angels do not have sex organs and calls the idea that angels procreate with humans nonsense and a bunch of baloney.
What does “fullness of bread” mean in his teaching on Sodom?
He says it means they did not lack food, and that is why Lot went to the prosperous area. He asks whether that sounds like America, where nobody goes hungry and we feed them all.
What does he say about helping the poor?

He says that strengthening the poor means teaching them a job skill so they can support themselves. He says that when you give somebody something they expect it and lose their ambition and drive, and he says America needs to teach the poor a career and provide jobs.
What did Abraham ask God about Sodom?

He says Abraham started with fifty righteous people and went all the way down to ten, and God said he would not destroy the city for ten righteous’ sake. He asks whether we should likewise be interceding for our nation, and answers yes.
Why does he say Lot lingered when the angels told him to flee?

He says Lot said he had to think about it and pray, which he says is a big thing with Christians who want to process before they are ready. He says God had a timetable and the Lord, being merciful to Lot, brought him out, and the angels took hold of him and literally dragged him out of the city.
Why does he say good Christians can lose children to wickedness?

He says Lot lost two daughters who married wicked men in the city, who thought he was joking when he told them to come out. He says some of it has to do with putting children in public schools where they get brainwashed or living where the pressure sways them, and that avoiding things as much as possible would help.
Do our mistakes affect later generations, according to this message?
He says some mistakes carry on to other generations, as Lot’s did, even though we can be forgiven and restored. He says it still causes problems for those that we led astray.
What does he say about preachers saying Jesus could come any minute?

He says he is shocked that no one preaches the warning before judgment and that preachers are just scaring everybody to death that the second coming could happen any time. He says God has to warn the world and back up the gospel with a miracle, so people who reject him have no excuse.
How much time does he say Americans spend on entertainment?

He says Americans spend four and a half hours a day watching TV or playing video games, plus sixteen minutes a day on Facebook, and about an hour and a half listening to music. He says we feed our minds with entertainment instead of things that improve our job, our character and us as human beings.
Why does he say Christians must speak out on Bible moral issues?

He says the church has been afraid to speak out, and that in not speaking up you do not warn the people and they do not have a chance to get saved. He says God said in Ezekiel that he would hold you accountable if you did not warn them.
What does he say has been lacking in American preaching?

He says the judgment message has been lacking for thirty-some years, because preachers have been preaching that God is love, faith and grace. He says Christians in America are a bunch of wimps because they have no fear of God, since the judgment of God and the punishment for specific sins is not preached.

items.d: In this message Pastor David G. Kincer teaches that God shows no favoritism and that the faith of Abraham works for anyone. He uses Hannah, David, Asa, Hezekiah and Daniel to show that the blessing of Abraham…
p: In this message Pastor David G. Kincer teaches that God shows no favoritism and that the faith of Abraham works for anyone. He uses Hannah, David, Asa, Hezekiah and Daniel to show that the blessing of Abraham comes with troubles, and says the early church was changed by the word and the presence of God as people were turned from their iniquities.
What does it mean that God is not partial?

He says there is “no favoritism no respect or persons with God,” so what God did with Abraham he will do with us. He says we sometimes think others are better, more gifted, or that we are too bad to be changed, but even the unpardonable sin “was forgiven by the blood of Christ,” and spiritual education is open to everyone.
What does it mean that God is not partial?

We found today, we’re going to find that there is no partiality with God. God does not favor one above another. Absolutely no favoritism, no respect or persons with God. If God did things with Abraham, he will do things with us. Abraham’s faith works. But we got to get away from the faith that America is preaching to us and get back to the faith that Abraham had. Sometimes we think that some people are just made different. That’s why they’re better than us, and, and you know, they attain more than us. Sometimes we think other people are more gifted than us, and we excuse ourselves from obtaining these things. Sometimes we think we’re just too bad to be changed. God just can’t do it, we’re just too bad, we’ve been too bad. And I’ve showed you over and over that the unpardonable sin was forgiven by the blood of Christ, and so anything can be forgiven, and any of us can be forgiven. Amen. Sometimes we think we’re uneducated. You know, some of us could have sought a better education, but it’s not secular education that gets this stuff done, it’s spiritual education, and all of us can get spiritual education. Amen. We don’t have to be a doctor, a lawyer or a PhD. And sometimes we think God just favors other people, and uh, he’s just special because God just favored him, and that’s why the other people make great Christians and I will barely make it into heaven, if at all. That’s a lot of mentality out there, and we got to drop that and remember that God is not partial. He doesn’t come to one above another. He offers us all the same thing. Could that be true? It’s what we do with the offer that makes the difference. And hopefully today we can see that this faith of Abraham is the ingredient that all of us can have to get these promises.
What is the faith of Abraham? (Romans 4:21)

He says Abraham “was fully persuaded” that God was able to perform what He promised, and it was counted to him for righteousness. He says we can be righteous by believing like Abraham that God has the power to do what He promised, even if we do not yet see the result, and that this faith gives “great confidence.”
What is the faith of Abraham? (Romans 4:21)

Remember the faith of Abraham. Romans 4:21: Abraham was fully persuaded. He had full faith that what God God promised, God was able to perform, and it was accounted to him for righteousness. Now, if you want to be righteous before you ever obtain living a life of righteousness, then the key here is you got to believe like Abraham did, that God has the power to perform what he promised us. And I may not see the result in my life yet, but I see that God has the power to do for me what he promised to do, and that makes me righteous. Hallelujah. Besides the blood of Christ making me righteous, my faith, that’s the kind of faith I have in that blood, that blood has made me righteous, and I am being shaped and formed into living and speaking rightly, correct. And so that can give us great confidence. See, so God is not partial. If it worked for Abraham, it would work for you. And I, could that be a great amen?
What is the faith of Abraham? (Romans 4:21)
Romans 4:21: and being fully convinced that what He had promised He was also able to perform.
Why does he say the faith some preachers promote is not the Bible?

He says some preachers say “if you believe, God will do this for you,” and then blame the person when it does not happen, but “in the Bible there is no excuse” and “God doesn’t have to heal everybody.” He says God does what He wants, but He will heal, and the promise depends on God’s power, not the minister.
Why does he say the faith some preachers promote is not the Bible?

Now, this is important stuff. This is your foundational stuff to grow and mature in God and never quit and never give up. This is the real deal, and it’s that simple. It’s not this faith that they’re promoting, and all these preachers, they said, “Well, if you believe, God will do this for you.” You know, God did a lot of things for people that did not believe. See, our faith has to rise above their lack of faith, or else we just give an excuse: “Well, you know, you didn’t get your healing because you didn’t believe.” Well, that’s a great excuse, but it’s not Bible. God doesn’t have to heal everybody. God does what he wants in heaven and earth, but he will heal, he will do things. Amen. And so these preachers of this kind of faith, they always have an outlet: it’s your fault because you didn’t believe. But in the Bible there is no excuse. If you have the faith of Abraham, God will give you the promise, and it’s not the minister, now, it is God who has the power to do what he said he would do. Did that make sense to you?
Should our eyes be on a mighty man of God or on Jesus? (Mark 9:24)

He says that in America “our eyes are on the mighty man and the mighty woman of God,” but in the Bible “our eyes must be on Jesus, who has the power to perform what he promised.” He uses the father who said “Lord, I believe, help my unbelief” to show that belief with some doubt is no problem to Jesus.
Should our eyes be on a mighty man of God or on Jesus? (Mark 9:24)

See, in America our eyes are on the mighty man and the mighty woman of God. Our eyes are on somebody that has this thing with God, that if they pray for us and they do something for us, then man, my life will be changed. But in the Bible our eyes must be on Jesus, who has the power to perform what he promised. Amen. Now that’s the faith of Abraham, and we are reminded of that. And like the boy’s father, the father who came to Jesus and wanted Jesus to heal his son of a demon, and Jesus said, “I can, if you believe,” and he said, “Lord, I believe, help my unbelief.” Boy, I can identify with that one. I believe that book, but there’s some doubt. Will he do it? And Jesus what overcome his unbelief and healed the son. So see, if you got belief and some doubt, that’s no problem with him. He will help if you say, “Help, Lord, my unbelief.” He will still do what he promised to do. Isn’t that beautiful? Allelujah. So, you know, don’t exempt yourself because you got some doubt. Just say, “Lord, I believe,” like this guy did, “help my unbelief.” Amen. and And Jesus is faithful.
Should our eyes be on a mighty man of God or on Jesus? (Mark 9:24)
Mark 9:24: Immediately the father of the child cried out and said with tears, “Lord, I believe; help my unbelief!”
What are the promises given to Abraham, and who gets them? (Galatians 3:9, Genesis 12:2)

He says God promises to bless those who have the faith of Abraham: a great name, a great nation, and being a blessing to others, with troubles along the way. He says God wants to birth Christ in us and multiply the church “not through men’s techniques but the Bible’s,” and “he’s not going to favor one church above another, one believer above another.”
What are the promises given to Abraham, and who gets them? (Galatians 3:9, Genesis 12:2)

Now we got to remember God promises to bless those that have the faith of Abraham. Okay, he promises to bless those, they which be of faith are blessed with faithful Abraham. A great name, a great nation, he blesses us, we are a blessing to others, we will have troubles. He wants to birth Christ in us, not Isaac but Christ in us. He wants to multiply us as the stars of heaven, as a church, and he will protect us. Those were the promises given to Abraham, and he said if you have the faith of Abraham, then you will be blessed with faithful Abraham. “I will make you a great name.” How many would like a good name? Yeah. People say, okay. How many would like to see the church become a great kingdom in the earth? Yes. See, how many would like to see the church multiply and increase, not through men’s techniques but the Bible’s? Allelujah. You see, and if we have the faith of Abraham, then we will be blessed with the same promises that Abraham had, and God is not what? Partial. Hallelujah. He’s not going to favor one church above another, one believer above another.
What are the promises given to Abraham, and who gets them? (Galatians 3:9, Genesis 12:2)
Galatians 3:9: So then those who are of faith are blessed with believing Abraham. Genesis 12:2: I will make you a great nation; I will bless you And make your name great; And you shall be a blessing.
How did Hannah handle her troubles, and are troubles part of the Christian life? (John 16:33, 1 Corinthians 10:13)

He says Hannah prayed consistently and was provoked by an adversary until she could not eat, to show that “troubles is part of the Christian life… part of the blessing of Abraham.” He cites Jesus’ words that “you’re going to have troubles in this world” and that God makes a way of escape so that we can bear it.
How did Hannah handle her troubles, and are troubles part of the Christian life? (John 16:33, 1 Corinthians 10:13)

Now, let’s look at scriptures to see if other people were blessed when they used Abraham’s faith. Okay, let’s just look at some examples. Hannah. Hannah was married to a man, and she didn’t have any children, and Hannah went to the house of God consistently and prayed consistently. She was a good believer, but she didn’t have children, just like Sarah didn’t have a child, and she had an adversary that provoked her painfully, even to the place where it made her fret because she had no child. This verbal attack, this verbal abuse, it affected her eating habits. The Bible says she couldn’t eat. It was affecting her so much. You see, she had her troubles to go through. How many are finding out that troubles is part of the Christian life? Yeah, it’s no big deal, it comes with the package. That’s part of the blessing of Abraham. “Is you’re going to have troubles.” in this world You will have what? Tribulation. “Be of good cheer, I have overcome the world.” Your troubles may come physically, uh, it may come mentally, it may come emotionally, it may come in your marriage, it may come in your family, your kids may hate you, finances may just seem to, you know, flee from you, but you just hang tight, God God will get you through those troubles. Amen. “There is no temptation come up man that is not common to man, and God will” what? Make a way of escape, that we can what? Bear up under it. We can handle this.
How did Hannah handle her troubles, and are troubles part of the Christian life? (John 16:33, 1 Corinthians 10:13)

John 16:33: These things I have spoken to you, that in Me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation; but be of good cheer, I have overcome the world.” 1 Corinthians 10:13: No temptation has overtaken you except such as is common to man; but God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted beyond what you are able, but with the temptation will also make the way of escape, that you may be able to bear it.
Why does he say the “faith in America” is not the Bible, and what happened to Hannah?

He says the faith in America says “if you believe, no problems,” which he calls “not Bible,” and points to Adam and Eve’s trouble over the one commandment. He says Hannah, who prayed silently, finally got a child “and gave her several more,” and that “she won over the troubles” by being consistent in serving God.
Why does he say the “faith in America” is not the Bible, and what happened to Hannah?

Hallelujah. And you’re going to see every one of these people with problems, and you’ll see every one of them with success. And that that’s unlike the faith in America. The faith in America says if you believe, no problems. That is not Bible. Adam and Eve still had the problem of the tree of knowledge of good and evil. That was a problem. They only [unclear] commandment, and it troubled them, it caused him trouble, and I can go on and on and on. Uh, Hannah went to the house of God this year. She she went up every you know, but this time she went up and she did the same thing she always did. She went and prayed, and for you silent prayers, Hannah is probably the only example in the Bible where she didn’t make any noise, she just moved her mouth, she just moved her lips, praying silently between her and God. But this time God heard and gave her a child, and gave her several more. Allelujah. See, she won over the troubles. She did get blessed by God, but she was consistent in her serving God. Are you with me?
What do Elizabeth and David teach about a great name and problems? (1 Samuel 18:30, Luke 1:38)

He says Elizabeth believed God had the power to perform what He spoke, and David “behaved himself wisely” and had a great name but also problems, such as running for his life from Saul for about 13 years before God made him king. He asks how many are in their seventh or tenth year of problems and says “it does come to pass.”
What do Elizabeth and David teach about a great name and problems? (1 Samuel 18:30, Luke 1:38)

So did Elizabeth. Remember in the New Testament, Elizabeth was old and she was barren, but she believed that God had the power to perform what he spoke, and when that angel said, “You’re going to have a child,” she had no problem saying, “Okay, Lord, let there let there be a performance.” 1st Samuel 18:30: “David behaved himself wisely, more wisely than all the servants of Saul, so that his name was highly esteemed.” Okay, David had a name, a great name. People, at the name of David, people just honored David. He had a good name. Hallelujah. But David had problems. His wife divorced him. He had to live in the desert in caves and so forth, running for his life as a fugitive, because Saul wanted to kill him, and this went on for years until God came and fulfilled the promise to David to make him a king and bless him. Hallelujah, hallelujah. We don’t know how many years Hannah went through her problem, but we know David went through about 13 years. How many you’re in your seventh year or 10th year or of problems? Hallelujah. Nobody’s raising their hand. It does come to pass. It does come to pass.
What do Elizabeth and David teach about a great name and problems? (1 Samuel 18:30, Luke 1:38)

Luke 1:38: Then Mary said, “Behold the maidservant of the Lord! Let it be to me according to your word.” And the angel departed from her. 1 Samuel 18:30: Then the princes of the Philistines went out to war. And so it was, whenever they went out, that David behaved more wisely than all the servants of Saul, so that his name became highly esteemed.
What does it mean that Christ is formed in us? (Galatians 4:19, Acts 11:26)

He says the child being born is “an illustration of Christ being formed in us,” citing Galatians 4:19. He says the church was first called Christians at Antioch “because people could see Christ in their life,” and that today it only means “we believe in Christ,” while in the Bible it meant they lived and imitated Christ.
What does it mean that Christ is formed in us? (Galatians 4:19, Acts 11:26)

Now remember this child being born is really an illustration of Christ being formed in us. Galatians 4:19: “I travail in birth again until Christ be formed in you,” Paul said. “We have this treasure in earthen vessels.” The church was first called Christians at Antioch. Why? Because people could see Christ in their life. This is the way Jesus lived, this is the way Jesus talked. Christians, you know, like Christ, from Christ. Hallelujah. Christian today is just a word that means we believe in Christ. In the Bible it was different. See, that word meant they lived like Christ lived, they imitated Christ. Today we call ourselves Christians and we imitate whatever. Amen.
What does it mean that Christ is formed in us? (Galatians 4:19, Acts 11:26)

Galatians 4:19: My little children, for whom I labor in birth again until Christ is formed in you, 2 Corinthians 4:7: But we have this treasure in earthen vessels, that the excellence of the power may be of God and not of us. Acts 11:26: And when he had found him, he brought him to Antioch. So it was that for a whole year they assembled with the church and taught a great many people. And the disciples were first called Christians in Antioch.
What does Asa teach about seeking God and trouble? (2 Chronicles 14:7)

He says Asa said “Let us build cities because we have sought the Lord,” and when the people began to seek God, the economy and the land prospered. He says Asa still faced an Ethiopian army of over a million, outnumbered, and “called on God,” and he says Congress should humble itself before God as the founders did.
What does Asa teach about seeking God and trouble? (2 Chronicles 14:7)

Now let’s go on, Asa, in 2 Chronicles 14:7. He said, “Let us build cities because we have sought the Lord,” so they build and prosper. Before this, the highways were empty, there was trouble in Israel, the economy was down, but when they begin to seek God, things changed. And I’ll tell you, that’s something that our Congress needs to get. They’re trying to figure out everything, but they won’t kneel down and just humble them themselves before God. He can change the economy overnight. Uh, our forefathers did that. our Our founding constitutional people that signed the Constitution prayed in every session. I mean prayed. They would pray, not for five minutes, this went on for a while, sometimes it lasted over an hour, weeping before God. You need to read those things. But our Congress, oh no, they want to get God In Trust” out now and and so forth. But Asa was different. He got the people to seek God, God came, but Asa had problems. 1 million plus Ethiopian army came against him. He was outnumbered over 2 to one, and he called on God. See, he had his troubles, and God came and got him through the trouble.
What does Asa teach about seeking God and trouble? (2 Chronicles 14:7)

2 Chronicles 14:7: Therefore he said to Judah, “Let us build these cities and make walls around them, and towers, gates, and bars, while the land is yet before us, because we have sought the LORD our God; we have sought Him, and He has given us rest on every side.” So they built and prospered.
What does Hezekiah teach about applying ourselves and being persistent? (2 Chronicles 32:30)

He says Hezekiah prospered in all his works because he applied himself, and that “we can’t just sit and pray and fast and do nothing” if you want financial prosperity; you need a job skill. He says that when Hezekiah got sick and was told he would die, he prayed and God gave him 15 more years, so “it pays to be persistent.”
What does Hezekiah teach about applying ourselves and being persistent? (2 Chronicles 32:30)

Uh, in 2 Chronicles 32:30, Hezekiah prospered in all his works. We have to apply ourself. We can’t just sit and pray and fast and do nothing. If you want financial prosperity, you got to learn a job skill, you got to go to college, you got to go to tech school, you got to do something, you got to apply yourself. Could that be an amen? You know, and that’s another problem with the faith camp: you just name it, claim it, believe it, receive it. It doesn’t work that way. If you don’t plant a field, nothing will grow. A’t that right? And so Hezekiah, and everything he applied himself to, he what? Prospered. He was successful. You see, God blessed him with success, and he had his problems. He got sick and was going to die, and the prophet come and told him, “You’re going to die.” And Hezekiah said, “Lord, I have served you, you know, I want you to heal me and give me life.” And God turned the prophet around, who hadn’t even got out of the castle yet, send him back in and said, “God’s going to give you 15 more years.” See, it pray it pays to be persistent. Don’t give up, even if a prophet comes and tells you it’s over. Man, fight to the end. Go to your God. He’s bigger.
What does Hezekiah teach about applying ourselves and being persistent? (2 Chronicles 32:30)
2 Chronicles 32:30: This same Hezekiah also stopped the water outlet of Upper Gihon, and brought the water by tunnel to the west side of the City of David. Hezekiah prospered in all his works.
What do David’s child and Daniel in captivity teach about fighting? (2 Samuel 12:22, Daniel 6:28)

He says David fasted and prayed until his child died because “who knows if he will heal,” and says we “got to fight this battle and trust our God.” He says Daniel prospered even in captivity, being punished for the sins of his fathers, but his opponents had him thrown into the lions’ den, and some of us feel thrown in by friends, relatives and opponents.
What do David’s child and Daniel in captivity teach about fighting? (2 Samuel 12:22, Daniel 6:28)

Like David said, when his child was going to die, David fasted and prayed and sought God until the child died. Why? Because David told his servants, “Who knows? God is a merciful God, and who knows if he will heal my son or not?” So I’m going to seek him. And when the child died, he got up, went on with life, and they [unclear], “Now the child’s dead.” He said, “No, it’s over. The child’s gone.” But we got to fight. Amen. We got to fight this battle and trust our God and and seek him. And then you got Daniel in 6:28: “Daniel prospered in the reign of Darius and Cyrus.” prospered. He’s in captivity. He’s being punished for the sins of his fathers. Daniel was a just man. He didn’t have sin, but he had to go into captivity because of the way the forefathers lived, and God said, “I got to correct this.” And so innocent people also got corrected along with the guilty people. And in captivity, Daniel is high in command in the heathen nation. Daniel is well looked up to, and Daniel very prospered. But he had problems. There are some people that didn’t like him, and so they connived to get the king to turn against Daniel, and they threw Daniel in the lions’ den. And some of us feel like we’re thrown in the lions’ den by our friends, our relatives and our opponents.
What do David’s child and Daniel in captivity teach about fighting? (2 Samuel 12:22, Daniel 6:28)

2 Samuel 12:22: And he said, “While the child was alive, I fasted and wept; for I said, ‘Who can tell whether the LORD will be gracious to me, that the child may live?’ Daniel 6:28: So this Daniel prospered in the reign of Darius and in the reign of Cyrus the Persian.
Why might our troubles be for someone else, and why must we preach sin? (Acts 3:26, Acts 19:19)

He says God sent an angel to shut the lions’ mouths, and “you never know why your troubles are there,” and “it might be for someone else’s.” He says Acts 3:26 says God sent Jesus to bless by turning us from our iniquities, so “if we don’t preach sin… how are they going to turn?” He says the American church flatters people, and he cites Acts 19:19, where people who practiced magic burned their expensive books publicly.
Why might our troubles be for someone else, and why must we preach sin? (Acts 3:26, Acts 19:19)

But God sent an angel to shut the mouths of the lions, and Daniel went to sleep, used the lions for a pillow, and come out the next day. And the king, see, Daniel had an effect on the king of Babylon. The king fasted and prayed for Daniel. Are you there? Hallelujah. Powerful. So you never know why your troubles are there. might not only be for your gain and development, it might be for someone else’s. Hallelujah. I want you to understand that problems are part of the package. Don’t get down because you’re going through problems. God’s bigger than these things. Let’s go to the early church. In Acts 3:26, God sent Jesus to bless you and turning all of you from his iniquities. Okay, this is the promise of Abraham, that you will be a blessing to all families of the earth. Jesus came and did that. And how did he bless the world? By coming and turning them from their iniquities. Now folks, if we don’t preach sin and we don’t preach what iniquities are, how are they going to turn? And this thing in the American church is, don’t preach hell, fire and brimstone, and sin, just, you know, flatter the people. That’s not Bible. Jesus taught sin. The apostles taught sin. From Genesis to Revelation the Bible talks about sin. Could that be an amen? And repent from it and turn to do right. And Jesus came to bless us by turning us to right, because wrong, remember, sin will correct you. Sin has a punishment in itself. It’s not even God, it’s just when you do wrong, there’s a price to pay. Correct. So he doesn’t want us hurt, he doesn’t want us to have ruined lives. Now that’s fine for Jesus, but you got to remember the apostles, the early church also took this message and turned people to Christ. In Acts 19:19, I love this: many who practice magic burn their books in the sight of everybody. They went out and preached the gospel. These people were into witchcraft, and books at that time were very expensive because they were handwritten, and they were hard to come by. It wasn’t like you can go down to the local bookstore and buy a book. They had to scribe it for you, they had to write it for you from the original copy. And when God’s word and God’s presence touched these people, they didn’t go to their home and just keep their book. They came out publicly and burn these books. Hallelujah. Could we use a little of that in America?
Why might our troubles be for someone else, and why must we preach sin? (Acts 3:26, Acts 19:19)

Acts 3:26: To you first, God, having raised up His Servant Jesus, sent Him to bless you, in turning away every one of you from your iniquities.” Acts 19:19: Also, many of those who had practiced magic brought their books together and burned them in the sight of all. And they counted up the value of them, and it totaled fifty thousand pieces of silver.
How did the word change people in the early church? (1 Corinthians 6:11)

He says that after “of such were some of you,” those who had been sexually immoral, thieves or drunkards were changed by “the power of the word and the power of the presence,” without a recovery program or a psychologist. He says the church needs the Bible open and prayer on our knees more than church growth seminars.
How did the word change people in the early church? (1 Corinthians 6:11)

Now folks, that’s the power of the word and the power of his presence. Okay, and you also remember First Corinthians 6:11, when he talks about sexual immorality and adultery and fornication and homosexuality and stealing and drunkenness and [unclear] and extortion and all this stuff. He says, “Of such were some of you.” You see, they preached the word and the word worked. They weren’t homosexuals anymore, they weren’t adulterers anymore, they weren’t thieves anymore, they weren’t drunkards anymore. Why? God changed their life. The blessing of Abraham, and everybody knew it. They never had to go to a recovery program, they never had to go to a psychologist or to a psychiatrist or anything. It was the power of the word and the power of the presence that came and changed these people’s lives. And the early church is a great example of inheriting the blessings of Abraham. And I really believe, and I’ve been preaching it for decades, that instead of going to church growth seminar, we need to get that book open, get on on our knees. That’s the formula, that’s the pattern that worked back then. That pattern has not changed. You can have people in a church, and they may not be born again at all, but when they come through God’s pattern, it’s real and it’s public, and people see the difference. Could that be an amen? These congressmen that say, “Well, you know, I don’t wear God on my sleeve,” well, where do you wear him? In the book. The public knew where you stood. You can’t hide this thing. Are you understanding me? Allelujah. The power of the early church, they were a blessing to the people.
How did the word change people in the early church? (1 Corinthians 6:11)
1 Corinthians 6:11: And such were some of you. But you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified in the name of the Lord Jesus and by the Spirit of our God.
He says “God does not favor one above another.” He says there is “no respect or persons with God.”
What does he say about the unpardonable sin?
He says he has shown “over and over that the unpardonable sin was forgiven by the blood of Christ, and so anything can be forgiven.”
Do we need a degree to be used by God?
He says it is “not secular education that gets this stuff done, it’s spiritual education,” and that we do not have to be a doctor, a lawyer or a PhD.
Does he say God has to heal everyone?
He says “God doesn’t have to heal everybody. God does what he wants in heaven and earth, but he will heal.”
What if I have some doubt?
He says “if you got belief and some doubt, that’s no problem with him,” and to “just say Lord I believe… help my unbelief.”
How does he say the church should grow?
He wants to see the church “multiply and increase, not through men’s techniques but the Bible’s.”
Are troubles part of the Christian life?
He says “troubles is part of the Christian life… it comes with the package,” and that they may come physically, mentally, emotionally, or in the marriage and family.
Why does he use Hannah as an example?
He says she prayed consistently and silently, and “this time God heard and gave her a child… but she was consistent in her serving God.”
How long does he say David went through problems?
He says “David went through about 13 years” before God fulfilled the promise to make him king.
What does he say “Christian” meant in the Bible?
He says it “meant they lived like Christ lived, they imitated Christ,” unlike today when it “is just a word that means we believe in Christ.”
What does he say about name it and claim it?
He says “you just name it, claim it, believe it, receive it. It doesn’t work that way,” because “if you don’t plant a field, nothing will grow.”
What happened to Daniel in the lions’ den?
He says God sent an angel to shut the mouths of the lions, Daniel “used the lions for a pillow,” and the king of Babylon fasted and prayed for Daniel.
Why does he say we must preach about sin?
He says “Jesus taught sin. The apostles taught sin,” and that sin “has a punishment in itself,” so flattering people is not Bible.
What does he say about recovery programs and the early church?
He says the early believers changed by “the power of the word and the power of the presence,” and “never had to go to a recovery program” or a psychologist.

items.d: In this message Pastor David G. Kincer continues the series on God not being partial, explaining how the early church grew by preaching the word and seeing changed lives, using Philip in Samaria as an example.…
p: In this message Pastor David G. Kincer continues the series on God not being partial, explaining how the early church grew by preaching the word and seeing changed lives, using Philip in Samaria as an example. He warns against a “plastic” church that is always learning but not possessing, shares points an atheist made about religion that he agrees with, and calls the church to the demonstration of the Spirit and power.
Does the church today make people feel okay in sin?

He says today’s message is that drinking, sexual immorality and stealing are okay and “God loves you anyway,” because “we don’t want to get the homosexuals mad at us… people shacking up… thieves,” so “we won’t preach anything,” and nothing changes. He says that was not the message the early church brought.
Does the church today make people feel okay in sin?

Today, alcohol, drugs, sexual immorality, stealing and all that are the same problems, but we are just making everybody feel okay in it. In fact, if you like to drink, well, then we want to promote drinking, cuz we’ll say Jesus drank. you You know, you want to have sexual immorality, well, that’s okay, you know, God loves you anyway. Come on, folks, that’s not the the message that the early church brought. Could that be an amen? You know, we don’t want to get the homosexuals mad at us, we don’t want to get people shacking up mad at us, you know, we don’t want thieves mad at us, so we won’t preach anything. Well, you’re not changing anything either.
How did people in the early church show they had changed? (Acts 6:7)

He says the early believers “publicly changed,” and “everybody knew they changed.” He says Acts 6:7 says the number of disciples multiplied greatly “including a great company of the priests,” the very ones who had Jesus killed, now serving Christ, and that their life shows it.
How did people in the early church show they had changed? (Acts 6:7)

These people publicly changed. Everybody knew they changed. Now that’s good. “Preaching the word of God increased, and the number of disciples multiplied greatly, including a great company of the priests.” Now the priests were the ones that had Jesus killed. They were the ones there enticing the people to have Jesus crucified. And after Jesus died and this message of the gospel went out, these priests who stirred the people against Christ are now what? Serving Christ. And the public knows it. Are you hearing me? They’re not hiding anything. Everybody knows this. Why? Their life show it. And God multiplied and God increased.
How did people in the early church show they had changed? (Acts 6:7)
Acts 6:7: Then the word of God spread, and the number of the disciples multiplied greatly in Jerusalem, and a great many of the priests were obedient to the faith.
Why do we want God to multiply our church?

He says the goal is “not because we want numbers, but because we want to see people saved from hell.” He says this is the difference between church growth seminars and “the Bible plan,” which is to have a heart for people who are going to hell, and that the church wants “a nice, enticing word” but not to be changed where neighbors see it.
Why do we want God to multiply our church?

Do we want God to multiply our church not because we want numbers, but because we want to see people saved from hell? Yes. See, that’s the difference between the church growth seminars and the Bible plan. Is we’ve got to have a heart for people going to hell. The biggest problem in America are people dying and going to hell every day, and there’s really no focus, concerned about it. The church just wants to hear a nice, enticing word, but we don’t want to be changed to where our neighbors see it, our family sees it, and they get ignited and come to Christ. Hallelujah.
What does Acts 16:5 say about churches established in the faith? (Acts 16:5, Romans 4:21)

He prays for the early church’s power to be fulfilled “in my generation… in my local community.” He reads Acts 16:5, that the churches were established in the faith and increased in number daily, and says the faith was “Abraham’s faith,” believing that God has the power to perform what He promised.
What does Acts 16:5 say about churches established in the faith? (Acts 16:5, Romans 4:21)

God fulfilled this in the early church, and church, we need it fulfilled in our generation. I thank God for what he did in the early church. I thank God for what he did in past revivals. But my prayer is, God, I appreciate what you did yesterday, but we need this in my generation. I need it, Lord, in my lifetime. I need it in my local community. This is what we need. Could that be a good prayer? Acts 16:5: “The churches were established in the faith and increased in number daily.” How often? Daily. But they were established in the faith. What faith? Abraham’s faith. Say it: Abraham’s faith. They had the faith to believe that God had the power to perform what he promised, and they went out and preached the word, and they lived for God, and God fulfilled his promise, and they multiplied. But look at this: they were established. The church was established. The church was strong.
What does Acts 16:5 say about churches established in the faith? (Acts 16:5, Romans 4:21)
Acts 16:5: So the churches were strengthened in the faith, and increased in number daily. Romans 4:21: and being fully convinced that what He had promised He was also able to perform.
Is the church in America strong, and what would make it “the real deal”?

He says he is not criticizing the American church but looking at the facts: “is it strong? No. Me, am I strong? No. I need to change.” He says the early church was strong, established and “accepted as true,” people called them “the real deal,” and he prays “Lord, establish us.”
Is the church in America strong, and what would make it “the real deal”?

Is the church strong in America? Now I’m not saying that to put the American church down and criticize and all that. I’m saying that that we have to look at the facts. Say, our church, is it strong? No. Me, am I strong? No. I need to change. The church needs to change. America church needs to change. Could that be true? The church was strong, established, it was solid, it was successful. And listen to this part of established: the church was accepted as true. Wow. The people said, “They’re the real deal.” Is that what Americans are saying about the church in America right now? No way. But we need to shake loose and become the real deal. Amen. We don’t need to give up and quit and go on in our apathy. We need to become the real deal, and my prayer is, Lord, establish us. Hallelujah. Establish me.
How did the early church grow without gimmicks? (Acts 8:5)

He says it multiplied “without gimmicks… without mailers… without a marketing scheme,” and without church growth seminars, recovery programs or theology debates; “they simply went out and preached the gospel, and the Spirit of God worked with them and changed lives.” He introduces Philip, one of the seven deacons, in Acts 8:5 as an example.
How did the early church grow without gimmicks? (Acts 8:5)

The early church multiplied without gimmicks, without big days, without mailers, without a marketing scheme. They had one. I’ll show you, it wasn’t a planned marketing scheme, it was God’s plan. They grew without church growth seminars, without recovery programs, without theology debates and microscoping every jot and tittle of a Bible verse like we do today, or microscoping the Greek and Hebrew meaning. They simply went out and preached the gospel, and the Spirit of God worked with them and changed lives. It was that simple. God was doing something. Now here’s how they did it. Acts 8:5. Here’s an illustration of how they did it, very clear, very direct. There’s other illustrations, but this one is very good. Philip was a deacon, one of the seven deacons. He served tables. You know, if you’re a cook and a toilet cleaner and sweeping up the floor and all this, you’re a candidate, because that’s what a deacon is. Uh, you run the sound, you know, whatever, mow the lawn, repair things, that’s what deacons do.
How did the early church grow without gimmicks? (Acts 8:5)
Acts 8:5: Then Philip went down to the city of Samaria and preached Christ to them.
What did Philip do in Samaria? (Acts 8:6-8)

He says deacons do “unimportant” jobs like running the sound and mowing the lawn, yet Philip simply went down and “started preaching” Christ in Samaria. He says the people “not only heard the word, but they saw the miracles,” unclean spirits came out and the lame and paralyzed were healed, so “there was great joy in the city.”
What did Philip do in Samaria? (Acts 8:6-8)

See, unimportant jobs, actually they are important, because without them how you going to get the big stuff done? But that’s what deacons did. Now he takes, there were two of them that were powerful. This one here, Philip, preached Christ to the city of Samaria. Okay, he just went down and started preaching. Can you see this guy just getting on a street corner and preaching Christ? Allelujah. “The people with one accord gave heed to what Philip spoke, hearing.” See, they not only heard the word, but they saw the miracles which he did. Now how many even know that’s a great marketing scheme? Is God partial? He has to do the same thing for every generation, and he wants, it’s not he has to, he wants to do it. I mean, that’s just a great marketing scheme: preach the word, and then the word backs up what the word says. “And they saw the miracles which he did. For unclean spirits, crying with loud voices, came out of many; many taken with palsies,” they were paralyzed, “and many that were lame,” something happened to them, you know, they were crippled, they were healed, “and there was great joy in the city.” Publicly, there was what? Great joy. I mean, the whole city. This affected the whole city. Are you out there?
What did Philip do in Samaria? (Acts 8:6-8)

Acts 8:6-8: And the multitudes with one accord heeded the things spoken by Philip, hearing and seeing the miracles which he did. For unclean spirits, crying with a loud voice, came out of many who were possessed; and many who were paralyzed and lame were healed. And there was great joy in that city. Acts 8:7: For unclean spirits, crying with a loud voice, came out of many who were possessed; and many who were paralyzed and lame were healed.
What two things did Philip use, and why do changed lives get attention?

He says Philip used “the spoken word” and let God heal people, and a person healed will go home and “squawk about it.” He says a changed drunkard, homosexual or thief “gets people’s attention,” and that “the miracle of salvation is still the greatest miracle.”
What two things did Philip use, and why do changed lives get attention?

So he used two things. He used the spoken word, and he let God heal people. Let me tell you, somebody gets healed, they’re going to go home and they’re going to squawk about it, and it’s free advertisement, and it’s good advertisement. But you get a life change, now, not just the healing, but a drunkard that changed. How many, you know, that gets people’s attention. A homosexual that changed, that gets people attention. A thief that changed, that gets people’s attention. See, he spoke the word, and they saw the miracles. Well, the miracle of salvation is still the greatest miracle. You know, when you were a drug addict and throwing away your money and stealing to get it and lying and everything else, and then people see a transformation, you’re not doing that anymore, and you’re living a good, consistent, good life, man, it gets people’s attention. See, that’s the best marketing skills that we can have, is not only physical healing, but change lives will bring the crowds in. The word will get out. Hallelujah. That’s how simple it was.
What does he mean by a “plastic” church or believer?

He says plastic is a “man-made thing” that is “not a real mineral,” and that Christians can become plastic by letting their surroundings change them into something that looks real but is not. He says the hippies said “don’t be plastic, man, be real,” which was true, but they were very plastic.
What does he mean by a “plastic” church or believer?

Now we must be careful not to become a plastic local church or a plastic believer. Now what did I say? We must be careful not to become a plastic local church or a plastic believer. Why do I use the word plastic? Because plastic is not real. It’s a synthetic, human hand, um, man-made thing that we use. It’s everywhere, but it’s not a real mineral. Are you there? And it’s easy for us to become plastic and not anymore. Polymerized is how plastic is made, through polymerization, and a lot of Christians have been polarized, polymerized, I should say. you We’ve let our surroundings, some some igniter, change our lives into something that looks like something, but we’re not real. Are you with me? Now the hippies were good at this. they That’s one of their statements: “Don’t be plastic, man. Be real.” And it was a true statement, but they were very plastic.
What does 2 Timothy 3:7 say about being “ever learning” but not possessing? (2 Timothy 3:7)

He reads 2 Timothy 3:7 about people “forever learning” but never arriving at knowledge of the truth, and says the plastic church knows Christ died and cleanses but does not “possess him.” He says the American church is good at “talking and going through the motions of learning and not possessing it.”
What does 2 Timothy 3:7 say about being “ever learning” but not possessing? (2 Timothy 3:7)

2 Timothy 3:7: “They are forever inquiring and getting information, they’re forever learning, but are never able to arrive at a recognition and knowledge of the truth.” They never grasp the truth. They think going to Bible studies, hallelujah, “I did my thing,” or listening to a tape or somebody on the radio or whatever, they’re ever learning, but they’re not possessing what they learn. That’s the plastic church. They know Christ died on the cross, but they don’t possess him. See, they know he cleanses and forgives and delivers from sin, but they don’t get deliverance. They know he baptizes in the Holy Ghost, but they don’t get it. They know he offers wisdom to anyone that will ask him, but they don’t get wisdom. The American church is good at talking and going through the motions of learning and not possessing It’s like a kid, you know, you teach your kid, they go, “Yeah, yeah,” and then they go and do what what they want. Huh. “Yeah, yeah.” Yeah, that’s a plastic church, and that’s a plastic believer.
What does 2 Timothy 3:7 say about being “ever learning” but not possessing? (2 Timothy 3:7)
2 Timothy 3:7: always learning and never able to come to the knowledge of the truth.
What points does he say atheists make about religion that he agrees with?

He says an atheist he debated made strong points: religion gets people to believe something untrue, such as the any-minute rapture and the deathbed ritual, and bases lives on a falsehood, such as candles, holy water and incense. He says that “still does not change the word of God.”
What points does he say atheists make about religion that he agrees with?

See, do I have Christ? That is important. I was debating with some atheist. Talking, debating. I can’t get into a talk with people without getting into a debate, it seems like. And they have some strong points. Okay, they say religion gets people to believe something untrue, and that’s true. Gosh, pre-tribulation any-minute rapture is untrue. It is a theory. This deathbed ritual, deathbed, right? You say this thing and you automatically go to heaven. That’s not true. Are you out there? We do. And I have to say, I I agree, a lot of religious people, they believe untrue things, I mean, you know, but that doesn’t make the Bible untrue. They say religion makes people base the way they run their lives on a falsehood. That’s true. I said, “You know, you got me again.” Lighting candles does nothing for anyone. Holy water, incense, a lot of this nonsense, they’re basing their life on something that has no substance. But that still does not change the word of God. The word of God is truth. Because people change things does not change the word of God. Could that be an amen?
What does he say about sectarian religion and relying on outside authority? (Hebrews 12:2)

He says he agrees many religions are sectarian and “won’t listen to anything outside their camp,” and that people lean on the pope or the pastor or a TV evangelist when “we should be looking through Jesus the author and the finisher of our faith.” He says this is people distorting the Bible, not the Bible being untrue.
What does he say about sectarian religion and relying on outside authority? (Hebrews 12:2)

They say religion stops people thinking in a rational and objective way. I go, you “You’re right.” A lot of religion are sectarian, and they they offer extreme beliefs, and they won’t listen to anything outside their camp. Man, if you say anything outside that their group or their leader, man, they won’t listen. You’re right. I mean, atheists aren’t stupid. But that doesn’t change the Bible being a book of truth, because people distort it and make up their own stuff. Could that be an amen? They said religion forces people to rely on outside authority rather than becoming self-reliant, self-controlled, self-contained people. And I go, “You got to me again.” If they Catholic, you think the pope is the authority. If you’re a Protestant, the pastor, is some TV evangelist, we lean on people, and we shouldn’t be doing that. We should be looking through Jesus, the author and the finisher of our faith. Could that be an amen? Atheists aren’t stupid, folks. They have some strong points that they make.
What does he say about sectarian religion and relying on outside authority? (Hebrews 12:2)

Hebrews 12:2: looking unto Jesus, the author and finisher of our faith, who for the joy that was set before Him endured the cross, despising the shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.
What does he say about irrational religious rules and the number of religions in America?

He agrees that some churches impose rules such as no makeup, no jewelry or no meat on Friday, and that some religions have jihads, but says “the Bible does not back up these things.” He says there are over 1,600 different religions in America, so “you better know your Bible.”
What does he say about irrational religious rules and the number of religions in America?

“Religion imposes irrational rules of good and bad behavior.” I go, “You know, you’re right again.” You know, there’s churches: no makeup, no jewelry, no pants, no meat on Friday, you know, you cannot say God’s name. There’s religions that have jihads, you know, going to go to heaven if you kill people. You’re going to go to heaven if you obey your husband. It’s true, but that doesn’t change the Bible. The Bible does not back up these things. But church, we got to get back to the, B it’s important that you know your Bible in this generation. There are over 1,600 different religions in America, and you better know your Bible. They’re all coming with these weird things along with good things, and we are at a place where we got to what? Know our Bible.
What does he say about church government, women and other races?

He agrees that church structures where the pastor is “the guru” or a denominational headquarters “owns everything” are bad government because people have no say. He also agrees that churches have not treated women and other races equally, but says “you can’t go to the Bible and get that stuff,” and calls for a solid Bible church.
What does he say about church government, women and other races?

“Religion divides people.” That is true. 1,600 religions in America, that’s division. “The hierarchy structure of most religions is anti-democratic and offends a lot of human rights.” And that is true. The way a church government is set up is very important, and so many churches are set up up where the pastor is the guru, he owns everything, or the group owns everything, or the, you know, headquarters, Springfield, owns everything, if you’re in a certain denomination. And that is true. And the people have no say. Whatever Springfield says, that’s what goes. Whatever the pastor or the pope says, that’s what goes. The people have no recourse, and that is true. That’s bad government, and most Christians don’t even think about the government of a church when they go to it. See, the atheists have some things to say that we can hear and correct. Could that be an amen? I said, “But that doesn’t change the Bible. The Bible doesn’t give that kind of government.” “Religion doesn’t give equal treatment to women.” I go, “You’re right. Even Protestant churches beat up women for decades.” But you can’t go to the Bible and get that stuff. You have to twist the scriptures to get it. And other races, and we’ve been guilty. But that doesn’t change the Bible. And church, we need to be a solid church. Could that be an am? We need to be a Bible church. Could that be an amen? And we need to let God arise with his word and with his presence and touch people’s lives. Could that be an Amen. So it’s important that I get involved in the church. It’s important that I grow in God, because God can change people’s lives through me and through a church that is involved with God. The early church had the goods. They were a genuine group.
What does 1 Corinthians 2:4-5 say about the demonstration of the Spirit and power? (1 Corinthians 2:4-5)

He says Philip and Stephen did not use “enticing words of men’s wisdom” or a joke to start the sermon, but “the demonstration of the Spirit and power.” He says our faith should be in “the power of God,” like Abraham’s faith that God has the power to perform what He promised.
What does 1 Corinthians 2:4-5 say about the demonstration of the Spirit and power? (1 Corinthians 2:4-5)

First Corinthians 24 and 5: “My speech and my preaching.” See, this is what Stephen had, Philip had, was not “with enticing words of men’s wisdom.” See, they didn’t have to give up and say a joke to start their sermon. They didn’t have to use Toastmaster’s, you know, outline and speaking, and they didn’t have to limits to making everybody feel good about themselves or whatever psychology there is. “My speech and my preaching was not with enticing words of men wisdom, but in the demonstration of the Spirit and power.” Woo woo. Isn’t that what Philip had when he went down to Samaria? “That your faith should not stand in what the wisdom of man.” See, this is what [unclear] bananas. But our faith should be in what? The power of God. Abraham’s faith, that God has the power to perform what he promised. Say it: God has the power to perform what he promised. Say it: God has the power to perform what he promised, in spite of my unbelief, if I will believe what, like Abraham believed, God will work for me.
What does 1 Corinthians 2:4-5 say about the demonstration of the Spirit and power? (1 Corinthians 2:4-5)

1 Corinthians 2:4-5: And my speech and my preaching were not with persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, that your faith should not be in the wisdom of men but in the power of God.
Do we have to go somewhere else to get revival?

He says he wants to be an early church believer and a pastor of a church that possesses these things, and says “I don’t have to go to Argentina… Africa… Australia to get in that revival. I can go to Jesus who is revival.” He says “God is not partial,” and ends by asking whether we are willing not only to learn but to “reach out and possess that truth.”
Do we have to go somewhere else to get revival?

The early church was genuine. They were solid, they were established, and I want to be an early church believer, and I want to be a pastor of a church who possesses these things. How about you? We don’t have to go looking somewhere else. We need to go looking for him, and he will not be partial. I don’t have to go to Argentina to get in that revival. I don’t have to go to Africa to get in that revival. I don’t have to go to Australia to get in that revival. I can go to Jesus, who is revival. Because [unclear] needs revival, the families of [unclear] need revival, Orange County need rev— Folks, we need Jesus and his word, and we need to focus on that. Could that be an amen? God is not partial. He can use us, but we got to get out and speak the word. We got to live the word and let God arise. Hallelujah. Now remember, they were ever learning but never coming to the knowledge of the truth, possessing the truth, embracing the truth. This morning, are we willing not only to learn but reach out and possess that truth?
What does he say about people who promote drinking because Jesus drank?
He says today “we want to promote drinking, cuz we’ll say Jesus drank,” and says that is not the message the early church brought.
Why does he say we do not preach against sin?
He says “we don’t want to get the homosexuals mad at us, we don’t want to get people shacking up mad at us… so we won’t preach anything. Well, you’re not changing anything either.”
Who were the priests who believed?
He says they were “the ones that had Jesus killed,” who stirred the people against Christ and are now serving Christ, and “the public knows it.”
Why does he want God to multiply the church?
He says “not because we want numbers but because we want to see people saved from hell,” and the biggest problem in America “are people dying and going to hell every day.”
He prays, “God, I appreciate what you did yesterday, but we need this in my generation… in my lifetime… in my local community.”
What faith does he say the early churches were established in?
He says “Abraham’s faith,” the faith to believe “that God had the power to perform what he promised.”
Does he say the American church is strong?
He says no, and includes himself: “our church, is it strong? No. Me, am I strong? No. I need to change. The church needs to change.” He says the point is not to criticize but to look at the facts.
What did the early church not need?
He says they grew “without church growth seminars, without recovery programs, without theology debates,” and without microscoping every jot and tittle of a Bible verse.
What does he say a deacon does?

He says a deacon serves tables, runs the sound, mows the lawn, repairs things and does the “unimportant jobs,” which “actually they are important, because without them how you going to get the big stuff done?”
What does he say is the best “marketing” for the church?
He says “not only physical healing but change lives will bring the crowds in.”
Why does he say atheists have strong points?

He says “atheists aren’t stupid,” and agrees religion can make people believe untrue things and rely on outside authority, but that “doesn’t change the Bible being a book of truth, because people distort it.”
What does he say about the any-minute rapture?
He calls “pre-tribulation any-minute rapture” “untrue” and “a theory,” along with the deathbed ritual, as examples of untrue religious beliefs.
Who does he say we should look to instead of a pope, pastor or TV evangelist?
He says “we should be looking through Jesus, the author and the finisher of our faith.”
Does he say church government matters?
He says “the way a church government is set up is very important,” and that it is bad when the pastor, the group or a headquarters owns everything and “the people have no recourse.”
What does he say the early church had that enticing words do not?
He cites 1 Corinthians 2:4-5, “the demonstration of the Spirit and power,” and says Philip had it in Samaria and that our faith should be in “the power of God,” not the wisdom of men.

items.d: In this message Pastor David G. Kincer answers two challenges, why a good God allows suffering and why He requires the killing of women and children, by teaching that God is Judge with the right and necessity…
p: In this message Pastor David G. Kincer answers two challenges, why a good God allows suffering and why He requires the killing of women and children, by teaching that God is Judge with the right and necessity to judge now and at the end. He gives Bible examples before the law (Cain, Enoch, Noah) and after it, and distinguishes shadow laws from civil laws.
What does the parable of the wheat and tares say about the righteous and the wicked? (Matthew 13:30)

He says Jesus said to let the tares and the wheat “grow together” until the harvest, which is the end of the age when Jesus returns. He says the wicked will get more wicked and the righteous will get more righteous until then.
What does the parable of the wheat and tares say about the righteous and the wicked? (Matthew 13:30)

In Matthew 13:30, Jesus said, in the parable of the [unclear] and the field and the enemy coming in and sowing tares, He said, “Let both the tares,” the righteous and the wicked, “grow together.” Let both the tares and the wheat grow together, the righteous and the wicked grow together until the harvest. And He tells us the time of the harvest is at the end of the age, the end of the world, when Jesus returns again. So what He’s saying is the wicked and the righteous are going to be in the earth, and the wicked are going to get more wicked and the righteous are going to get more righteous until the time of the harvest. They are to grow together. All right. Now we’re going to also answer these two questions, or these two challenges, by our enemy: “If the Bible’s God is good, why does He allow sufferings and wars in the earth?”
What does the parable of the wheat and tares say about the righteous and the wicked? (Matthew 13:30)

Matthew 13:30: Let both grow together until the harvest, and at the time of harvest I will say to the reapers, “First gather together the tares and bind them in bundles to burn them, but gather the wheat into my barn.” ’ ”
What two challenges does he answer: why does God allow suffering, and why does God require the killing of women and children?

He says two challenges are, “if the Bible’s God is good, why does He allow sufferings and wars in the earth,” and why God requires the killing of women and children. He says he will answer them by establishing that God is Judge with the right and necessity to judge, and by showing God’s judgment before and after the law was given.
What two challenges does he answer: why does God allow suffering, and why does God require the killing of women and children?

And “Why does God require the killing of women and children?” And “The Bible is just a bunch of BS,” bull, sh-, sh-. Okay, that’s the challenge for my enemies. We’re going to answer these questions while we are addressing “God is the Judge.” And what we’re going to do, we’re going to establish that God is Judge and has the right and necessity to judge. Then we’re going to establish the evidence of God’s judgment before the law was given and then after the law was given, and then we’re going to show you how the righteous and the wicked are to grow together until Christ come. God is the Judge, and He has sentenced the wicked to eternal life in the lake of fire, according to Jesus Christ and His statement. He is the Judge, and He has sentenced all the wicked to the lake of fire. All right.
Does God have the right and the necessity to judge, and does He judge now? (Psalm 75:7, Ecclesiastes 3:17)

He reads Psalm 75:7 that God is Judge and Ecclesiastes 3:17 that “God shall judge the righteous and the wicked,” both now and at the harvest. He says God “didn’t wait for the Judgment Day” with Herod Agrippa, and “if He cannot deal with things now, He is worthless.”
Does God have the right and the necessity to judge, and does He judge now? (Psalm 75:7, Ecclesiastes 3:17)

Now, establishing that He is the Judge and has the right and the necessity to judge: Psalm 75:7 plainly says God is the what? Judge. Ecclesiastes 3:17: “God shall judge the righteous and the wicked.” Okay, and he says there is a time. In this Scripture, “there is a time, there is a season for every purpose and for every work.” You see, so what does that tell us? He is the Judge of the righteous and the wicked both now and when He comes at the harvest, at the end of the time. Okay, and I can give you proof. Herod Agrippa, in Acts 22:23, they exalted him as God, he did not renounce it, and so the Bible says God smote him with worms, that he died. See, God didn’t wait for the Judgment Day, He dealt with it now. And my submission to these people that challenge my God, the God of the Bible, is He is the Judge, and He has the right to judge, and He has the necessity to judge. It is necessary that He deals with things now, and if He cannot deal with things now, He is worthless. And why would I want to serve a worthless God?
Does God have the right and the necessity to judge, and does He judge now? (Psalm 75:7, Ecclesiastes 3:17)

Psalm 75:7: But God is the Judge: He puts down one, And exalts another. Ecclesiastes 3:17: I said in my heart, “God shall judge the righteous and the wicked, For there is a time there for every purpose and for every work.” Acts 12:21-23: So on a set day Herod, arrayed in royal apparel, sat on his throne and gave an oration to them. And the people kept shouting, “The voice of a god and not of a man!” Then immediately an angel of the Lord struck him, because he did not give glory to God. And he was eaten by worms and died.
How did God judge a wicked king of Judah and his family?

He tells of a king of Judah who killed his own brothers and led Israel into sin; six years into his reign God “smote him with an incurable disease of the bowels,” he suffered two years and died at age 40. He says God also dealt with the king’s whole family, and that “God has a right to deal with wickedness right now because He’s the Judge.”
How did God judge a wicked king of Judah and his family?

In the Old Testament, [unclear] was the king of Judah. He killed his own brothers, he caused Israel to sin, commit adultery, sexual immorality, and everything else, the king. So God comes along. He was 32 years old when he began to reign, and God came just six years later and smote him with an incurable disease of the bowels. For two years he suffered in pain, and then died from that incurable disease, and the Bible says God smote him. God judged him. He also judged his whole family, his wife, who was the daughter of Ahab, an evil king of Israel that served Baal. Her children produced were all dealt with. Are you there, church? See, God has a right to deal with wickedness right now, because He’s the Judge, and don’t you go calling my God unrighteous and unfair and everything else because He’s doing His job. Can I hear an amen? As you can tell, I get upset and I get fired up when people attack the Bible and God. There are Bible answers for this stuff.
What does it mean that God is a judge? (Ezekiel 18:30)

He reads Ezekiel 18:30, “I will judge you,” according to your ways, and says a judge is “a lawgiver,” “an executioner,” “a punisher,” and “a justifier of the innocent.” He says Christianity is “an entryway into the spiritual kingdom,” not just a philosophy of principles to live by.
What does it mean that God is a judge? (Ezekiel 18:30)

So he died at the age of 40. See, there is a time for every purpose of judging, and God needs to deal with things now and in the eternities. Ezekiel 18:30: “I will judge you. I will judge all of you according to your ways,” your lifestyle, your choice of living. I’m going to judge you. And now remember, “judge” is a lawgiver, He is an executioner, He is a punisher, and He is a justifier of the innocent. That’s what a judge is. Does that sound like our God? Absolutely. And I don’t like it when the homosexuals and the humanists and the atheists and the liberals and all that attack the Bible and attack God. Church, we have answers, and we have a God that isn’t a fairy tale. It’s not just a philosophy, as Bill O’Reilly said. Christianity is more than a philosophy. It’s an entryway into the spiritual kingdom, the spiritual domain. Hallelujah. The supernatural. Don’t ever reduce Christianity down to just a mere philosophy of principles to live by. We do have principles to live by, but we have a supernatural God that empowers us to live rightly. There’s no other religion in the world that has that.
What does it mean that God is a judge? (Ezekiel 18:30)

Ezekiel 18:30: “Therefore I will judge you, O house of Israel, every one according to his ways,” says the Lord GOD. “Repent, and turn from all your transgressions, so that iniquity will not be your ruin.
Will God judge secret sins? (Romans 2:6, Romans 3:5-6)

He says “God will judge the secrets of men by Jesus Christ,” and “you ain’t hiding it from God.” He says that when people call the Bible a myth and say God is unrighteous, God answers in Romans 3, “is God unrighteous who takes vengeance?” and vengeance means “making things right because someone has done something wrong.”
Will God judge secret sins? (Romans 2:6, Romans 3:5-6)

Romans, the New Testament, 2:6: “God will judge the secrets of men by Jesus Christ.” You think you’re hiding something, huh? God sees it all. You might hide it from your mama, your daddy, or your wife or your husband, you ain’t hiding it from God, and God will judge you even though you’re doing it in secret, not publicly. He’s going to hold you accountable. Romans 3:5-6: God, here’s the statement. See, they said my God was unrighteous, that’s what they’re saying, that the Bible is just a bunch of BS, it’s a bunch of fairy tales and myth. That’s exactly what the homosexual leader said, that was his words: “Don’t believe the BS of the Bible.” That was his exact words. The atheists call it a myth, a fairy tale. And so God answers them in Romans: “Is God unrighteous who takes vengeance?” You know what vengeance is, don’t you? Yeah, making things right because someone has done something wrong, a day of reckoning, you hold them accountable.
Will God judge secret sins? (Romans 2:6, Romans 3:5-6)

Romans 2:16: in the day when God will judge the secrets of men by Jesus Christ, according to my gospel. Romans 3:5-6: But if our unrighteousness demonstrates the righteousness of God, what shall we say? Is God unjust who inflicts wrath? (I speak as a man.) Certainly not! For then how will God judge the world?
Why does God allow suffering, and what about the women and children of Canaan?

He says God allows suffering “because He deals with the wickedness and the sin in this world now,” including wars and plagues, and that He sentenced the women and children of Canaan because “they had been sinning for hundreds of years” and their sin came to maturity. He says “he has the right to do that,” and that God’s decisions are His business, and “we need to fear God.”
Why does God allow suffering, and what about the women and children of Canaan?

I told you before, when I was in Salvador, a band came into a church family’s home and killed the father and took all the livestock and the valuables that they could carry away. Well, the people in that little village went after them and slaughtered them right there where they found them, just killed them, took matters right into their own hands.
