Okay, just continue with me: “for the powers of heaven shall be shaken.” How many know we don’t fight against man, flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers and wickedness in high places? Okay, he’s going to expose the source of their thinking. See, there’s only two kinds of children in the world, the children of God and the children of Satan. Okay, when we follow God and do what’s right and preach his word, we are enemies of those who follow Satan and preach his philosophy, we’re clashing. And remember, Isaiah said there was going to be a time of peace on earth, and the lamb shall lay down with the lion, and so forth, a reverse evolution. Animals are not going to eat meat anymore. I mean, God’s going to do everything he can to get mankind’s attention and expose all their ideas, because he’s God and he can do this stuff. Amen. And does he need to? Yeah, he does need to, because mankind aren’t listening to the gospel being preached. So, “the powers of heaven,” then “they shall see the Son of Man coming in a cloud with power and glory.” So what happens before he comes? God demonstrating his power in the heavens, God dealing with the Gentiles to bring them to him, to get them out of that false science, in that humanistic religion where they are gone, and to bring them to himself, and we find in Revelation a multitude that cannot be numbered of Gentiles in heaven. Now, that’s power, folks, that’s a God. Can I hear an amen? Amen. Hallelujah. All he can do is snatch me out? Uh-uh. He’s going to do a lot more than snatch me out of this earth, he’s going to demonstrate to the world his power, his truth, for the whole purpose of bringing in a harvest of those that will listen, number one. God has ordained to deal with the Gentiles, and those who won’t repent, he will, they will die, that’s second death, in the lake of fire. But we found that many will when we preach the gospel and they hear and God demonstrates his power in the earth before he comes. And I want, boy, I’d love to be there. Wouldn’t you like to be there at that time where God’s doing his thing, and you’re like, “Moses, get him, God! Allelujah! Joshua, yeah, take that, Pharaoh! Yeah, I told you, [unclear], you should have listened.” See, we act like God never did these things before. He did do them before, in Egypt, and he, you know, he did them before, he rained rocks out of heaven to destroy armies, he demonstrated his power, he’s a supernatural God. About 10 or 15 years ago there was a woman in India. She was pregnant, her and her husband worked in India in the labor fields, they carried heavy loads, and if you didn’t show up for work, someone was there waiting in line to replace you. This woman’s pregnant, she’s working and carrying these heavy loads, building this construction project, she’s in her ninth month, and she’s carrying these heavy loads because she can’t dare, and her and her husband can’t dare quit, because they want this child to be born and they want this child to have the best chance of life they can, and so they know they need money to do that, cuz work is tough, big unemployment rate in India. So one day she’s working and the birth pains come. She works right through them, if she stops she’ll lose the job. Finally her water breaks, and then she knows that baby’s coming out of the canal, she goes off like she’s going to the bathroom, her husband goes with her, and that baby’s born, they cut the umbilical cord, wipe, wrap that baby up, put her around the mother like they do in the back there, you know, and she goes right back to working on that job. Why? Because she wants that baby to live. She puts her comfort, she puts her life on the line, cuz she wants, and her husband both want that baby to live. And I’m going to be emphasizing man and wife today instead of moms, I’m going to be emphasizing moms and dads. Folks, the humanists are winning the battle of the family. 40%, over 40% of kids are born to one-parent homes, 30% of Americans don’t even bother getting married. They’re changing the family structure, the Bible family structure. These two did whatever they could as a team, and, folks, mothers alone are not going to have the impact as a mother and a father will. Amen. Two are better than one, we need each other, and Father’s Day, I’m going to say the same thing, we need the family back to what God says it was, a man and a woman raising kids. Period. Hallelujah. And they did, they raised that baby, they were Christian people, that’s how I know the story, I got it from the missionary over there, couple in the church. Now, let’s go to the Middle East, where it’s a crime to be a Christian. Also a family pulls up, a family of five, they have a teenage daughter 17 years old, they have a 14-year-old boy and a young girl, they pull up to a roadblock trying to get to a refugee camp because they’re being persecuted where they’re at. The soldiers see the young girl, she’s mature, her breasts have grown, and she’s a young lady, and she’s a Christian, an infidel, and they tell that mother and father, “Leave your daughter here.” They plead with these three soldiers at the checkpoint, the mother even offers herself. But there’s a place where they knew if they didn’t stop they would just be shot and they’d have their daughter anyway. Now, they couldn’t do anything, but they could do this: go down the road, pull over to the side, shut the lights off, go back in the darkness around through the terrain to this shack where these soldiers lived, where they took their breaks, and sure enough they go there, they’ve got the daughter stripped naked, they’re molesting her, one of them’s in there molesting her, they go into that shed and they kill that soldier, they took his own gun and shot him cuz he was so involved in what he was doing he didn’t even notice him coming in, and then the two soldiers heard the shot and they come running in and they killed them too. Mom just laid them out. Why? Cuz she wanted her daughter to live. They put their life on the line so that their children could live, and specifically this young teenage girl went back to the car and drove away, got to the refugee camp, and, folks, that’s what God wants. The humanist, he wants them to live, and he’ll do anything, and he’s trying to move you to speak to them, to share the gospel with them, share truth with them. He wants them to live, he wants them to have eternal life, he wants them to know him.
How does he say God will win the Gentiles, and what does he say about the rapture and the tribulation?

1 Thessalonians 1:10: and to wait for His Son from heaven, whom He raised from the dead, even Jesus who delivers us from the wrath to come. Revelation 7:9: After these things I looked, and behold, a great multitude which no one could number, of all nations, tribes, peoples, and tongues, standing before the throne and before the Lamb, clothed with white robes, with palm branches in their hands, Matthew 24:29: “Immediately after the tribulation of those days the sun will be darkened, and the moon will not give its light; the stars will fall from heaven, and the powers of the heavens will be shaken. Luke 21:25-26: “And there will be signs in the sun, in the moon, and in the stars; and on the earth distress of nations, with perplexity, the sea and the waves roaring; men’s hearts failing them from fear and the expectation of those things which are coming on the earth, for the powers of the heavens will be shaken.
What are the two things God asks the Gentiles to do?
He says “hear number one and heed number two.”
Does he believe there is life on other planets?
No. He says “there is no life out there in space.”
What does he mean by “the army of the word”?
He says an army we forget about “is the word,” used “to convince people” and that “it’s not always swords and spears.”
What does he say Psalm 9:19 wants the Gentiles to know?
He says the prayer is to “put them in fear,” so that mankind knows “they’re just humans” and that God is “the supernatural God.”
What does he say the birthright is today?
He says “birthright to us today is being born again, born of the word, born of the Spirit.”
What does he say the oil and light in the ten virgins mean?
He says “the word is light, our right behavior is light,” and that the foolish virgins “had no word and they had no action to back up” it.
Who does he say Zion is?
He says “Zion is the church, Zion is the people of God.”
Does he say meteor showers fulfill the falling stars?
No. He says “don’t mistake these meteor showers we have for the fulfillment of this verse.”
Does he say he has to prove the Bible is true to skeptics?
No. He says “I don’t have to argue that the word of God is true,” and “I’m going to keep bringing you to the cross.”
How many times does he say the sun is darkened in the Bible?
He says “it says three times in Revelation that the sun’s going to be darkened,” and that Old Testament prophets spoke of it “five times.”
What does he say are the two ways to get eternal life?
He says the first is to “believe on Jesus, trust in him,” and the second is “keep the commandments,” and that preachers rarely teach it.
Where does he say Jesus is sitting now?
He says “he sits on the throne now… ever since he ascended.”
Does he say Christians should hate their enemies?
No. He says “we want to hate our enemies… no, no, God’s going to do things to get their attention so they can be delivered through Christ Jesus.”
What does he say God wants for those who reject him?
He says “he wants them to live, he wants them to have eternal life, he wants them to know him.”

items.d: In “Government Aid: Is It Successful?”, Pastor David G. Kincer looks back at political promises to end poverty and says government aid has not won the war on poverty, while marriage, education and job skills…
p: In “Government Aid: Is It Successful?”, Pastor David G. Kincer looks back at political promises to end poverty and says government aid has not won the war on poverty, while marriage, education and job skills have. He then gives the Bible’s solutions: the family takes care of family, the poor work for their aid as in the gleaning laws, every able person works, and one law and one custom apply to citizen and immigrant alike.
Is United States government aid successful?

He asks whether government aid is really the best choice and looks back at political promises, saying the New Deal “didn’t work” and that the Great Society and War on Poverty promised to annihilate poverty.
Is United States government aid successful?

We thank you for coming, taking your time to expose bad choices so we can make better choices, and hopefully the best choices. Today we’re going to ask this question: is the United States government aid successful? Is it really the best choice? So we’re going to go back and think on past political promises. Liberal Democrat Roosevelt’s New Deal, which encompass three parts: relief for the unemployed and the poor, recovery from the economy, and reform so it never happens again, 1932, and it didn’t work. Uh, the liberal Democrat Lyndon Johnson’s 1960 Great Society, War on Poverty, Medicaid, Medicare, is going to annihilate poverty [unclear].
Will poverty ever end, according to the Bible?

He says there have been 49 recessions, panics or depressions since 1776, and that Deuteronomy 15:11 says the poor will never cease out of the land. He says the parties promising to fix poverty did not prevent it and most of the time caused it.
Will poverty ever end, according to the Bible?

Republican President Hoover, conservative Republican President Hoover, in 1930 said he was going to change the unemployment rate and help the poor, and he started building the Hoover Dam, the stimulus to get the economy going, and that didn’t work. So think on these facts for a moment. There have been 49 economic recessions, panics or depressions since 1776, or one in every five years. The results, of course, were increased unemployment and increased poverty. Deuteronomy 5:11- 15:11 says the poor will never cease out of the land. Now, if God, the Bible, is true, they’re giving us promises they really can live up to. Now think on this: the government parties promising to fix poverty and unemployment are the same government parties that did not prevent it, and most of the time they caused it. And think on this: James Madison, founding father, “Charity is no part of the legislative duty of government,” a federal government. Ben Franklin: “The best way of doing good to the poor is not making them easy in poverty, but leading them out of it.”
Will poverty ever end, according to the Bible?
Deuteronomy 15:11: For the poor will never cease from the land; therefore I command you, saying, ‘You shall open your hand wide to your brother, to your poor and your needy, in your land.’
Who helped the poor before the New Deal?

He says relief for the poor and unemployed was the responsibility of families, private charities, churches and local governments, and the poor had to work for that money if they could work. He says unplanned births went from nine percent to over 40 percent today.
Who helped the poor before the New Deal?

Now, I’m going to give you some things for your consideration about government aid. Before the New Deal, before the War on Poverty, financial relief for the poor and unemployed was the responsibility of families, private charities, churches and local governments, who got the money from property taxes to help the poor. But the poor had to work to get that money, if they could work. So consider this: before the New Deal, unwed versus unplanned births were nine percent. Before the War on Poverty they had moved up to 10 percent. Today unplanned births are over 40 percent of births.
How have marriage and child poverty changed since the War on Poverty?

He says marriage dropped from 91 percent before the New Deal to less than 50 percent of Americans getting married today, while child poverty went from 20 percent to 23 percent. He says the War on Poverty has not accomplished what they said it would.
How have marriage and child poverty changed since the War on Poverty?

Now consider this: before the New Deal, 91 percent were married. Before the War on Poverty, 89 percent were married; they’ve dropped down a couple of percentages, according to the Census Bureau. Today less than 50 percent of Americans are getting married. Now consider this: before the New Deal, child poverty was 20 percent, and before the War on Poverty it was still 20 percent. According to the USA Today, this year, 2014, child poverty now is 23 percent. Obviously this War on Poverty has not accomplish what they said they would do.

He says a child raised in a single-parent home has up to a 71 percent chance of growing up in poverty, while the poverty rate in a married household is nine percent. He says children of high school dropouts face 83 percent.

Now consider this: child poverty in a single family home today, 60 to 71 percent live in poverty, dependent on the survey that you accept. So a child that is brought up in a single-parent home has a 71 percent chance of growing up in poverty. But consider this: child poverty rate in a married household today is nine percent. Even though less than 50 percent are getting married, the poverty rate in a married household is nine percent. Now consider this: child poverty of high school dropouts, whether they are married or not married, is 83 percent.
What really wins the war on poverty?

He says those with a college degree or job skill who are married have only 1.8 percent poverty, so marriage and training for a job skill are winning the poverty war without government aid, and a hand up rather than a handout brings people out of poverty.
What really wins the war on poverty?

So if you are the child of a high school dropout, you have a 83 percent chance of growing up in poverty. But those who have a college degree or a job skill, a tech degree, and they are married, poverty is only 1.8 percent of this group. Hmm. That’s the Heritage Foundation and the Bureau of Census. So the conclusion of this consideration about government aid: marriage and training for a job skill is winning the poverty war without government aid. Consider this also, that tax is saved from the government handling aid; it leaves you more money to help your family and those poor in your family. And giving most people, most poor folks, a hand up rather than a handout brings them out of poverty.
Are poor Americans really poor today?

He says the War on Poverty distracted us from marriage, education, job skill and responsibility. He lists appliances, cars and homes most poor households have and says it does not sound like poverty, but the homeless on the street, he says, is poverty the government has not solved.
Are poor Americans really poor today?

You see, evidently the War on Poverty has distracted us from marriage, education, job skill and responsibility to take care of ourselves and take care of our family and avoid poverty. So we need to give people a hand up instead of a handout and lead them out of poverty. United States government aid did raise the poverty living standard. According to the Census Bureau, over 93 percent have a TV, a recorder, a fridge, a stove, washer, dryer, microwave, Xbox, adequate food and clothing; eighty percent have air conditioning; 81 percent have cell phones; 75 percent have one car or more; 66 percent have cable and satellite TV service; 58 have more than one computer and one or more computers; and 42 percent own their own homes. It doesn’t sound like very poverty to me. But when you look at the homeless out on the street, 633,782 adults and 1.3 million youths out on the street, that is poverty. They have nowhere to live, they have no way of making money, and our government has not solved that problem with their War on Poverty.
What does the Bible say about family and poverty?

He reads 1 Timothy 5:8 and calls the family taking care of family the front-line weapon in God’s war on poverty. His second point is that in the Bible you work for your aid, as in gleaning (Leviticus 19:10) and the seventh-year harvest (Exodus 23:11).
What does the Bible say about family and poverty?

So let’s look at the Bible for some solutions to poverty, and also you’re going to find solutions to illegal immigrants, and these solutions. Number one, family. First Timothy 5:8: if anyone fails to provide for himself, especially his own family, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever. So the front-line weapon on God’s war on poverty is the family takes care of family. Number two, in the Bible you have to work for your financial aid or your food aid. Leviticus 19:10, the poor had to go into the field and glean what the harvesters dropped or left, but they had to work for it. Exodus 23:11: in the seventh year farmers could not harvest, so the orchards and the, what grew in the field, the poor could go in and harvest it themselves.
What does the Bible say about family and poverty?

1 Timothy 5:8: But if anyone does not provide for his own, and especially for those of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever. Leviticus 19:10: And you shall not glean your vineyard, nor shall you gather every grape of your vineyard; you shall leave them for the poor and the stranger: I am the LORD your God. Exodus 23:11: but the seventh year you shall let it rest and lie fallow, that the poor of your people may eat; and what they leave, the beasts of the field may eat. In like manner you shall do with your vineyard and your olive grove.
Did the poor have to work for help in the Bible?

He says God tells us to help the poor and tells the poor to work for that help (Leviticus 23:22). He adds that you could eat in any field but carry nothing out (Deuteronomy 23:24), as Jesus did in Matthew 12:1.
Did the poor have to work for help in the Bible?

Which, God is telling us we need to help the poor, and he’s telling us also that the poor need to work for that help, in Leviticus 23:22. You could go into any field and eat all you want anytime, but you couldn’t carry anything out with you; that’s in Deuteronomy 23, verses 24. And in Matthew 12:1 Jesus used this. He went into the field and grab wheat, corn kernels, that’s tough to eat, and they accused him of working on the Sabbath because he took grain and ate it, according to the Scriptures.
Did the poor have to work for help in the Bible?

Leviticus 23:22: ‘When you reap the harvest of your land, you shall not wholly reap the corners of your field when you reap, nor shall you gather any gleaning from your harvest. You shall leave them for the poor and for the stranger: I am the LORD your God.’ ” Deuteronomy 23:24-25: “When you come into your neighbor’s vineyard, you may eat your fill of grapes at your pleasure, but you shall not put any in your container. When you come into your neighbor’s standing grain, you may pluck the heads with your hand, but you shall not use a sickle on your neighbor’s standing grain. Matthew 12:1: At that time Jesus went through the grainfields on the Sabbath. And His disciples were hungry, and began to pluck heads of grain and to eat.
What causes poverty, according to the Bible?

He lists conditions of the poor: a servant fired for cheating (Luke 16:3), a man born with a handicap who begged (Luke 18:35), a working family that is simply not rich (Proverbs 13:23), and ruin through bad judgment or injustice.
What causes poverty, according to the Bible?

Uh, Luke 16:3 gives our first condition of the poor: the servant [unclear] cheated his master and he got fired, and he was ashamed to beg. In 18:35, the bl- blind man, who was created with a handicap and was poor, he went out and begged. The poverty family: much food is in the tillage of the poor. Here is a family that’s working and they have food, but they’re just not rich like some people are rich, in Proverbs 13:23. That is the third condition of poor, and probably the most popular one. And the fourth one is ruin comes through bad judgment. People make bad judgments, or injustice, where people come and steal from them, and it keeps them poor. Second Thessalonians 3:10, the New Testament backs up this work ethic.
What causes poverty, according to the Bible?

Luke 16:3: “Then the steward said within himself, ‘What shall I do? For my master is taking the stewardship away from me. I cannot dig; I am ashamed to beg. Luke 18:35: Then it happened, as He was coming near Jericho, that a certain blind man sat by the road begging. Proverbs 13:23: Much food is in the fallow ground of the poor, And for lack of justice there is waste. 2 Thessalonians 3:10: For even when we were with you, we commanded you this: If anyone will not work, neither shall he eat.
What does “if any man doesn’t work, neither should he eat” mean?
He says the third principle of God’s solution is to work diligently and hard “or you shouldn’t eat.” He names laziness and excuses as further sources of poverty, from Proverbs 10:4 and Proverbs 20:4.
What does “if any man doesn’t work, neither should he eat” mean?

So number three is work. If any man doesn’t work, neither should he eat. Work with your own hands so you may lack nothing, First Thessalonians 4:11. So the third principle of God’s solution is work, and work diligently, and work hard, or you shouldn’t eat, and your tummy will drive you to work. Here is the fifth source of poverty: he who has a slack hand, they’re just lazy, becomes poor. They’re show up late, they miss work, when they do work they’re taking a lot of water breaks and doing a lot of yakking and talking. They’re just not productive, they’re just lazy. The sluggard, the lazy person, will not plow by reason of the cold. Here’s our sixth source of poverty, is excuses. They have an excuse: well, you know, I’m born in the wrong neighborhood, the wrong family, uh, whatever, that’s my excuse. And he will beg in the harvest and have nothing. Why? Because the people in Proverbs 20, verse 4, saw what he did, and they wouldn’t give him anything if he begged, because he could have provided for his own self.
What does “if any man doesn’t work, neither should he eat” mean?

2 Thessalonians 3:10: For even when we were with you, we commanded you this: If anyone will not work, neither shall he eat. 1 Thessalonians 4:11: that you also aspire to lead a quiet life, to mind your own business, and to work with your own hands, as we commanded you, Proverbs 10:4: He who has a slack hand becomes poor, But the hand of the diligent makes rich. Proverbs 20:4: The lazy man will not plow because of winter; He will beg during harvest and have nothing.
What does the Bible say about immigrants and work for aid?

Reading Numbers 15:16, he says one law and one custom apply to the citizen and the stranger. He says aid recipients can do work such as cleaning hotels and harvesting fields, which he says would reduce illegal immigration.
What does the Bible say about immigrants and work for aid?

Numbers 15:16: one law and one custom shall be for you, the citizens of the land, and the immigrant, the stranger. You can’t bring in your own laws, you can’t bring in your own customs; you got to go with the customs and laws of the nation. So aid recipients can clean hotels, they can harvest the farmers’ field, they can mow lawns and clean swimming pools, and in doing that, while they’re getting government aid, they will reduce illegal immigrants, because there won’t be any jobs. These guys that get financial aid will be working. So the Bible advises marry, having a family, being loyal to it, taking care of it, and education, getting a job skill, and working, and you will be financially successful, and you will be 98.2 percent of Americans that will avoid poverty and will never have to have government aid.
What does the Bible say about immigrants and work for aid?
Numbers 15:16: One law and one custom shall be for you and for the stranger who dwells with you.’ ”
What is the best choice in the war on poverty?
He says the Bible declares the best choices: marry, be loyal to and take care of your family, get an education and a job skill, and work hard, and you will be successful.
What is the best choice in the war on poverty?

The Bible confirms these choices, and the Bible declares that these are the best choices. Marry, be loyal to your family, take care of your family, get an education, get a job skill, work hard, and you will be successful, and you will make the best choice on the war of poverty.
What were the three parts of the New Deal he describes?
He says it encompassed relief for the unemployed and the poor, recovery from the economy, and reform so it never happens again.
What quote about the poor does he give from Ben Franklin?
He quotes: “The best way of doing good to the poor is not making them easy in poverty, but leading them out of it.”
How often does he say recessions or depressions happen?
He says there have been 49 economic recessions, panics or depressions since 1776, or one in every five years.
What chance of poverty does he give for a child in a single-parent home?
He says 60 to 71 percent, depending on the survey you accept.
Is it better to give a hand up or a handout?
He says giving most poor folks a hand up rather than a handout brings them out of poverty.
What does he call real poverty?
He points to the homeless on the street, who have nowhere to live and no way of making money, and says the government has not solved that problem.
What is the front-line weapon in God’s war on poverty?
He says it is the family taking care of family, from 1 Timothy 5:8.
Why was Jesus accused when He picked grain?
He says Jesus went into the field and took grain and ate it, and they accused Him of working on the Sabbath.
What does he say about laziness?
He says he who has a slack hand becomes poor: showing up late, missing work, taking breaks and talking instead of being productive.
How do excuses lead to poverty?
From Proverbs 20:4 he says the sluggard who makes excuses will beg in the harvest and have nothing, because people saw he could have provided for himself.
Should immigrants follow the laws and customs of the nation?
He says from Numbers 15:16 that you can’t bring in your own laws or customs; you go with the customs and laws of the nation.
How does he say most Americans can avoid poverty?
He says marrying, being loyal to your family, getting an education and a job skill, and working will make you financially successful and keep you from needing government aid.

items.d: In this message Pastor David G. Kincer begins in 1 Corinthians 15 with the gospel and the evidence for the resurrection, then teaches that grace is not only a favor but a power, “the divine influence upon the…
p: In this message Pastor David G. Kincer begins in 1 Corinthians 15 with the gospel and the evidence for the resurrection, then teaches that grace is not only a favor but a power, “the divine influence upon the heart,” that moved Paul to work. He follows grace through John 1, Luke 2, Luke 6, Acts 11 and Colossians 3, and asks whether our grace is increasing.
What responses to the gospel does Paul describe? (1 Corinthians 15:1-2)

Reading 1 Corinthians 15:1-2, he says there are two choices: “you can reject it or you can accept it.” He says “Receive means you accept it, you take it,” to stand means “you take your stand, you continue in it, you don’t waver,” and being saved means “you’re rescued, you’re set free from sin, from hell, from the lake of fire, and from the day of wrath.”
What responses to the gospel does Paul describe? (1 Corinthians 15:1-2)

We are in chapter 15, and in chapter 15, verse 1, Paul says, “I declare to you the gospel which I preached.” Now, there are four responses here to when he preached the gospel, and this is what the gospel should do. “Which you have received.” You accept it. See, you got two choices: you can reject it or you can accept it. Receive means you accept it, you take it. All right. Number two, “in which you stand.” You see, you take your stand, you continue in it, you don’t waver. Number three, “by which also you are saved.” You’re rescued, you’re set free from sin, from hell, from the lake of fire, and from the day of wrath. For instance, if God judged America in His anger to correct them, you would be rescued from that wrath of God, and then there’s a day of wrath coming at the end.
What responses to the gospel does Paul describe? (1 Corinthians 15:1-2)

1 Corinthians 15:1-2: Moreover, brethren, I declare to you the gospel which I preached to you, which also you received and in which you stand, by which also you are saved, if you hold fast that word which I preached to you—unless you believed in vain.
What is the gospel, and what does it mean to hold fast? (1 Corinthians 15:2-3)

He says to hold fast means “we hang on, we don’t give up, we don’t quit,” because “if you let it go, it doesn’t do you any good.” He says the gospel is that “Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures,” which means the Old and New Testaments are both Scripture, and he says “the Old Testament is still for today.”
What is the gospel, and what does it mean to hold fast? (1 Corinthians 15:2-3)

Then He says, “if you hold fast.” See, we also hold fast, we hang on, we don’t give up, we don’t quit, to what was preached, this gospel that was preached, “unless you believed in vain,” or your belief was worthless. If you let it go, it doesn’t do you any good. And then he is going to tell us what the gospel is. He said, “For I delivered unto you first of all that which also I received: how that, number one, Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures.” Now, that means the Old Testament is considered Scriptures, and the New Testament is considered Scriptures, because the Gospels and the epistles talk about the death and burial and resurrection of Christ. So here is evidence that the canon, New Testament, is recognized as Scripture. Got it? You need to know that, because some churches say the new, the Old Testament is not for today. Uh, it is, the Old Testament is still for today.
What is the gospel, and what does it mean to hold fast? (1 Corinthians 15:2-3)
1 Corinthians 15:3: For I delivered to you first of all that which I also received: that Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures,
What does he say about the burial and the third day? (1 Corinthians 15:4, Luke 24)

He says the gospel includes that Jesus “was buried” and “rose again the third day.” From the two disciples in Luke 24 who said it was “the third day since all these things happened,” he counts Friday, Saturday and Sunday and says, “These people are trying to keep Jesus in the grave for three 24-hour periods. It is ridiculous.” He says “Never diminish the death, burial, and resurrection of Jesus Christ. It’s still the foundation of everything the Bible’s built on.”
What does he say about the burial and the third day? (1 Corinthians 15:4, Luke 24)

Now, number two, “he was buried.” He was put in the grave. “And that he rose again the third day according to the” what? Scriptures. Old Testament tells, Scriptures tell us that, and New Testament Scriptures tell us that. Now, he rose what day? Third day. Luke 24, on the road to Damascus, there they were, two, two disciples that were talking with Jesus, didn’t know it was Jesus, and they were telling Jesus that this is the third day since all these things happened, that he was died, he was killed, he was in the grave, and then he rose the third day before sunup. Okay, if Sunday was the third day, then what would Saturday be? Second day. And what would Friday be? Third day, the first day, I’m sorry, first, second, third. These people are trying to keep Jesus in the grave for three 24-hour periods. It is ridiculous. This Scripture plainly tells us that he died on what day? Friday. He was in the grave on what day? Saturday. He arose on what day? Yeah. When he went into the grave, he went down into, uh, where the dead souls were and preached to them before the flood and, uh, gave them the gospel. And so that is the gospel. It’s all about Jesus’ death, burial, and resurrection, and that’s the power of the gospel. That’s the, that’s the power that sets us free. Never diminish the death, burial, and resurrection of Jesus Christ. It’s still the foundation of everything the Bible’s built on. Okay.
What does he say about the burial and the third day? (1 Corinthians 15:4, Luke 24)

1 Corinthians 15:4: and that He was buried, and that He rose again the third day according to the Scriptures, Luke 24:13-21: Now behold, two of them were traveling that same day to a village called Emmaus, which was seven miles from Jerusalem. And they talked together of all these things which had happened. So it was, while they conversed and reasoned, that Jesus Himself drew near and went with them. But their eyes were restrained, so that they did not know Him. And He said to them, “What kind of conversation is this that you have with one another as you walk and are sad?” Then the one whose name was Cleopas answered and said to Him, “Are You the only stranger in Jerusalem, and have You not known the things which happened there in these days?” And He said to them, “What things?” So they said to Him, “The things concerning Jesus of Nazareth, who was a Prophet mighty in deed and word before God and all the people, and how the chief priests and our rulers delivered Him to be condemned to death, and crucified Him. But we were hoping that it was He who was going to redeem Israel. Indeed, besides all this, today is the third day since these things happened.
What evidence does Paul give that Jesus rose? (1 Corinthians 15:5-8)

He says Paul lists those who saw Jesus after the resurrection, including “500 brethren at one time,” and last Paul himself. He says “there’s over 500 people that witnessed Jesus alive and well on planet Earth after he died,” and “these people that want to challenge the Bible and all this, they have to ignore these facts.”
What evidence does Paul give that Jesus rose? (1 Corinthians 15:5-8)

Now he gives us some proof that Jesus rose, some evidence, some proof. In verse 5, “he was seen by [unclear], or Peter, then by the 12.” Now, you know there’s not 12 now, don’t you? How many are there? 11. So how did Judas see Jesus when Jesus went down to preach to those that were in the holding pen of the earth? That, yeah, yeah, he saw him a little too late, huh? Anyway. “And then by 500 brethren at one time, and then by James, and then by all the apostles. Then the last of all he was seen by me as one born out of due time.” And so he’s saying these people saw Jesus after the resurrection. There’s over 500 people that witnessed Jesus alive and well on planet Earth after he died. Now, how many you know that’s a good evidence? Hallelujah. These people that want to challenge the Bible and all this, they have to ignore these facts. You see?
What evidence does Paul give that Jesus rose? (1 Corinthians 15:5-8)

1 Corinthians 15:5-8: and that He was seen by Cephas, then by the twelve. After that He was seen by over five hundred brethren at once, of whom the greater part remain to the present, but some have fallen asleep. After that He was seen by James, then by all the apostles. Then last of all He was seen by me also, as by one born out of due time.
What does Paul say about the grace that made him who he was? (1 Corinthians 15:9-11)

Reading Paul, he says “I’m the least of all the apostles” and “not worthy to be called an apostle because I persecuted the church of God,” yet “by the grace of God I am what I am.” He points out that “labored” means work, and reads “I labored more abundantly than all the rest, yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.”
What does Paul say about the grace that made him who he was? (1 Corinthians 15:9-11)

Now he’s going to say something that’s going to be very powerful here. “I’m the least of all the apostles, who I’m not worthy to be called an apostle because I persecuted the church of God.” Now I’m going to jump down to verse 11. “Whether it were I or they,” these 500 and some people, “so we preached, and so you” what? Believed. You trusted in that gospel, you accepted it, you received it. Now he says, “I’m not worthy to be called an apostle, but by the grace,” say the word, grace, “by the grace of God I am what I am.” So he was an apostle by what? The grace of God. “And his grace toward me was not profitless,” in vain, “but I labored.” Say the word, labored. What’s another word for labor? Work. Yeah, you got intelligent people out there. I tell you, “I labored.” Watch this, watch this closely, because Paul knows what he’s talking about. “I labored more abundantly than all the rest, yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” So this grace is what moving him to work.
What does Paul say about the grace that made him who he was? (1 Corinthians 15:9-11)

1 Corinthians 15:9-11: For I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am, and His grace toward me was not in vain; but I labored more abundantly than they all, yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me. Therefore, whether it was I or they, so we preach and so you believed.
Does he say grace moves us to work? (Ephesians 2:8-9)

He says that although we are saved by grace through faith and not by works, “grace here moves us to what? Work.” He says “grace isn’t just something, you know, bestowed upon us, it also is a power that moves us,” and that “this grace was a power that worked in their life to be an example and a light for Jesus Christ.”
Does he say grace moves us to work? (Ephesians 2:8-9)

And you, you need to hear that, because this Scripture that everybody quotes, “We’re saved by grace through faith, and that not of itself, it is the gift of God, not by works, lest any man should boast.” But grace here moves us to what? Work. Are you there? Was, did Paul have to work to preach the gospel to the Corinthians? Yeah, he had to put forth some effort. And see, grace gave him a desire, I, I, to, to help people, to change people, to get the message out to people. See, grace isn’t just something, you know, bestowed upon us, it also is a power that moves us. Do you see that? See, so Paul had the grace of God that moved him to work for Christ, to preach the gospel, and to live for Christ. You never hear of the apostles running off with a church secretary, taking the church’s money, having a nervous breakdown, you never hear that stuff, getting drunk. Why? Because this grace was a power that worked in their life to be an example and a light for Jesus Christ. Hallelujah. Ain’t that powerful?
Does he say grace moves us to work? (Ephesians 2:8-9)
Ephesians 2:8-9: For by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, lest anyone should boast.

He gives the lexicon definition as “graciousness of manner, behavior, or act” and “especially the divine influence or power upon the heart,” and says the heart is “The mind, the emotions, and the will.” He says “grace shows itself by how you live,” like a reflection in a mirror. He says the King James translates the same word as acceptable, benefit, favor, gift, joy, liberality, pleasure and thank.

Now let’s take a look at grace. The definition of grace in the lexicons is “graciousness of manner, behavior, or act, whether literal, figuratively, or spiritual.” Okay, then the definition says “especially the divine influence or power upon the heart,” the divine enablement upon the heart. Now, what is the heart? The mind, the emotions, and the will. Yeah, so grace has a what? An influence, an impact on our mind, on our emotions, and our will, our desire to do things, and its reflection in life. Now, we all want know, know what a reflection is. You’re looking in the mirror, you’re seeing a what? Reflection of yourself. And what does grace do? Grace shows by how you live. See, grace shows itself by how you live. Ain’t that powerful? Now it’s used in King James as “acceptable,” a benefit, “the benefit of God was upon him,” “the acceptable of God was on him,” “the favor of God was on him,” “the gift of God was on him,” “the graciousness of God was on him,” the joy of God, the liberality, the pleasure, and the thank. It’s all translated in these different words, but it’s the same word for what? Grace. That divine influence in our life, and it shows by how we behave, how we live. Now, folks, that’s a powerful God. Hallelujah. Grace is a powerful thing. If grace is that powerful, then it would behoove us to get it. All right.
What does “full of grace and truth” mean, and what did grace do for Peter? (John 1:14, 1:17)

He reads that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” and was full of grace and truth, so receiving Christ means “receiving what? Grace and truth.” He says the disciples went back to fishing, and “Grace came after them.” Although the Bible says “If you deny me, I will deny you before my Father,” he says “grace moved God to reach out to Peter and bring him back.”
What does “full of grace and truth” mean, and what did grace do for Peter? (John 1:14, 1:17)

Now, you know more about the Bible definition when you see its use in the Scripture. All right, now watch this. “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” which is Jesus. We all know that, right? Jesus was the Word, Jesus was God, He became flesh, dwelt among us, and He was full of what? Grace and truth. So when I receive Christ in my life, I’m receiving what? Grace and truth. Hallelujah. And we can, we can back that up. When Jesus told them, “I got to go away, I will come again,” so he died and he what? Rose and came back to them. See, that’s truth. He told him the truth. Right? But you know, Peter denied Him, Peter cursed first. Uh, Peter challenged Him, and then Peter got all the disciples to go back to work. They went back to fishing after He rose from the grave. And what did grace do? Grace came after them. See, Jesus came after them. See, Jesus is filled with grace. See, He’s going to do everything He can to get you to reach the maturity and the completeness of His goals and His promises. Ain’t that beautiful? See, He kept His word, He spoke the truth, and then what He didn’t, He put aside the fact that Peter denied Him, and the Bible says, “If you deny me, I will deny you before my Father,” yet grace moved God to reach out to Peter and bring him back. And, folks, if, if Peter can do something that cannot be forgiven, how much more will God reach out to us in our failures and in our, uh, amen. So grace is important. Truth’s also important. Hallelujah. Now, “the law was given through Moses,” in John 1:17, “but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.” All right, that divine influence came through Jesus Christ.
What does “full of grace and truth” mean, and what did grace do for Peter? (John 1:14, 1:17)

John 1:14: And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we beheld His glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father, full of grace and truth. Matthew 10:33: But whoever denies Me before men, him I will also deny before My Father who is in heaven. John 1:17: For the law was given through Moses, but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.
How did Jesus increase in grace? (Luke 2:40, 52)

He says Luke 2:40 shows “the grace of God was” upon Jesus, and in verse 52 “Jesus increased in wisdom,” and “He increased in grace” with God and men. He says “grace moved Him to please the Father,” and also to “touch people.” He says “it’s grace that should drive us to church so we can grow and so we can what? Help others grow.”
How did Jesus increase in grace? (Luke 2:40, 52)

Now Luke 2:40, speaking of Jesus when he’s like 12 years old, the grace of God was what? Upon Him. Now, He was what? Filled with grace, but in His human form He was. See, the grace of God was upon Him, and look at verse 52. “Jesus increased in wisdom,” He increased in favor. What’s that word, favor? Grace. He increased in grace, look at this, “with God and men.” You see, grace moved Him to please the Father. Jesus said, “I do nothing except what I see and hear of the Father,” but grace also moved Him to what? Touch people. See, it’s grace that should drive us to church so we can grow and so we can what? Help others grow. Grace will give you a concern for other people. Amen. See, we don’t come to church just for ourself, we come for others too.
How did Jesus increase in grace? (Luke 2:40, 52)
Luke 2:40: And the Child grew and became strong in spirit, filled with wisdom; and the grace of God was upon Him. Luke 2:52: And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men.
How does he say grace is different from a favor? (Luke 6:32)

He says doing a neighbor favors or giving him money “doesn’t change him,” but “if I influence him to change to a better man, that is what grace is about.” He says “God’s just not out to do us favors, folks. He’s out to make us in His likeness and His image.” From Luke 6:32 he says “the word thank is the what word? Grace,” and that grace is a “power by God to treat people better than they’re treating you.”
How does he say grace is different from a favor? (Luke 6:32)

And so grace is that power that moves us. Now, we’re not talking about the baptism of the Holy Ghost, we’re talking about grace. Grace isn’t some, you know, “the favor of God was upon him.” You know, I can do Mr. [unclear] here a favor. He lives close to me. I lend him a lawn mower. Not a lawnmower, he’s got a better one than I do. I lend him my weed eater, and I lend him this, and I lend him that. That doesn’t change him, that doesn’t make his character any better than it was before I’m doing. I could give him $1,000 dollars, and it’s not going to change his character. I did him a favor. Are you there? But if I influence him to change to a better man, that is what grace is about. Hallelujah. See, God’s just not out to do us favors, folks. He’s out to make us in His likeness and His image, make, make us a light to the world where people can see God in us. How many could use a little increase in grace? Yeah. You know, if Jesus increased in grace, who was full of grace, how many know we should strive to increase in grace, this grace that moves us to please God and to help people? Now let’s continue the use of the word. Luke 6:32, “If you love those that love you, what thank have you?” And the word thank is the what word? Grace. “What grace have you if you just love people that love you?” See, “if you lend to people that lend to you, what grace have you?” See, “if you do good to people that do good to you, what grace have you?” See, grace is a, a power by God to treat people better than they’re treating you, to give someone that needs something, not even expecting it back. See, that’s grace in action, the reflection in life. “You’re opposing me, I’m going to love you.” And He says, “but love your enemies and do good.”
How does he say grace is different from a favor? (Luke 6:32)
Luke 6:32: “But if you love those who love you, what credit is that to you? For even sinners love those who love them.
What did Barnabas see at Antioch? (Acts 11:23)

He says grace is not something to “just take it as this favor word”: “He more than favors you, He is empowering you to please Him and to help others in this life.” In Acts 11:23 he says Barnabas “had seen the grace of God” because the Greeks were “now serving God and repenting from their sins and turning to what’s right.” He says grace “is a free gift, but you got to accept it and use it,” and that “He’s going to keep after you.”
What did Barnabas see at Antioch? (Acts 11:23)

I submit to you this morning, grace is a very powerful thing, and we shouldn’t just take it lightly, and we shouldn’t just take it as this favor word. “No matter what, or do God favors me.” No, He more than favors you, He is empowering you to please Him and to help others in this life. Now, Acts 11:23, Barnabas went down to Antioch. They had preached Christ to the [unclear], the Greeks, the Greek cultured people, and many of these Greeks believed it. It said before that they had only been preaching to Jews only, but here it says at Antioch they preached to the Greeks, see, the non-Jews, the Greek-speaking people, culture. And so when Barnabas came and had seen, see that word, he had seen the grace of God. Remember, the definition was reflection in life. See, he saw the grace of God. Why? Because he saw these Greeks now serving God and repenting from their sins and turning to what’s right. He saw the grace of God in evidence in the Greeks. Isn’t that powerful? The grace is a very powerful thing, and too many people just got this favor thing, and they don’t understand the power that’s in the grace of God, and it’s a free gift that He gives us. Grace, the Bible says, is a free gift, but you got to accept it and use it. See, Mr. Barnes could lend me his lawnmower, but if I never used it to mow my lawn, it what? Doesn’t do any good. Hallelujah. Now, “and he was glad, and encouraged them all with purpose of heart to continue with the Lord.” See, they had turned to the Lord. Isn’t that powerful? Should grace be seen in our life? Yes, church. Not only will Jesus go to the extreme to influence you to live for Him, I don’t care if you’re committing adultery, drunkenness, He’s going to keep after you. Why? ‘Cause He’s full of grace, and He wants to win you back, He wants to improve your life. But grace also is a power that works in me, that works in you, to help people and live a life that’s pleasing to God. Now, that changes everything.
What did Barnabas see at Antioch? (Acts 11:23)
Acts 11:23: When he came and had seen the grace of God, he was glad, and encouraged them all that with purpose of heart they should continue with the Lord.
How does grace relate to worship and the word? (Colossians 3:16, Acts 20:32)

Reading Colossians 3:16, he says singing “with grace in your hearts” means singing with “the divine influence of God.” He says “Grace wants you to worship God. Why? Because it’s a principle of God that brings His presence. When His presence comes, you start taking on His nature.” Reading Acts 20:32, he says the Scriptures are “grace, that divine influence upon your mind, your emotions, and your will.”
How does grace relate to worship and the word? (Colossians 3:16, Acts 20:32)

Colossians 3:16, “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom, teaching and admonishing one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.” Singing with favor, singing with benefits, or singing with the divine influence of God upon you. Amen. See, and it agrees with the Holy Spirit. See, the Holy Spirit came upon them, the Holy Spirit was with them, and they did things by the Spirit. Here, grace comes upon, grace is with us, grace is working in us, and it’s the same result. We want to worship God. People that don’t want to worship God, they need an increase of grace. Yeah. Grace wants you to worship God. Why? Because it’s a principle of God that brings His presence. When His presence comes, you start taking on His nature. Hallelujah. Powerful, very powerful. Now, Acts 20:32, “I commend you to God, and I commend you to the word of grace.” Oh, see, the Scriptures are what? Grace, that divine influence upon your mind, your emotions, and your will to make you into someone who can act different than the people of the world. Isn’t that beautiful? And again, we’re not talking about the baptism of the Holy Ghost, we’re talking about grace. So even if you reject the infilling of the Holy Ghost, there’s still power in what? Grace. Power. Now, what does this grace do? Grace is able to what? Build you up. Build you up to what? His likeness and His image. He’s out to make you a light to the world, that people can see your good works and bring glory and honor to Jesus Christ. Isn’t that beautiful? Hallelujah. See, grace not only worked in Paul, drove him to work, but grace built Paul up to be the apostle that God had intended him to be.
How does grace relate to worship and the word? (Colossians 3:16, Acts 20:32)

Colossians 3:16: Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom, teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord. Acts 20:32: “So now, brethren, I commend you to God and to the word of His grace, which is able to build you up and give you an inheritance among all those who are sanctified.
Can everyone be a light to the world, and what inheritance does grace give?

He says “you may not be an apostle, but you can still be a light to the world. You can be a disciple of Christ.” He says someone who stays a drunkard after being saved would show no “reflection” of grace, but at Antioch “he saw the change in their life.” He says grace “will give you an inheritance among all them which are sanctified,” and that Jesus “has activated the will” through His death and resurrection.
Can everyone be a light to the world, and what inheritance does grace give?

Now, you may not be an apostle, but you can still be a light to the world. You can be a disciple of Christ. Can’t we all be disciples? Can we all come to maturity? Yes. We may not be a prophet, we may not be an apostle, we may not be a pastor, but we can be a light to the world. We can be a disciple of Christ that people can see the results of grace in. See, if I’m a drunkard and I get saved and I stay a drunkard, when Barnabas come, he would not have what? Seen the grace of God. Why? ‘Cause there’s no reflection. See, but there was a reflection when he went down there to Antioch. He saw the change in their life. And, folks, that’s what grace will do to all of us. And this grace will give you an inheritance among all them which are sanctified. Now, we have an inheritance: Jesus Christ, the gifts of the Spirit, the fruit of the Spirit, the wisdom and knowledge, understanding and counsel and strength, and all these things are part of our inheritance. And he says grace is able to give you, to obtain this inheritance that God has promised, because Jesus, Jesus died on the cross. There cannot be an inheritance without the death of the one who wrote the will, and he’s dead, folks. And he come back to alive, and so we, he has activated the will, and we can have our inheritance if we will embrace grace and let grace work in our life.
Can everyone be a light to the world, and what inheritance does grace give?
Acts 20:32: “So now, brethren, I commend you to God and to the word of His grace, which is able to build you up and give you an inheritance among all those who are sanctified.
Are you increasing in grace, or is your grace limited?

He says some Christians “just take favor, go to heaven, wait for the rapture,” while others “grow in grace” and so have more influence in “changing people’s lives and bringing them to Christ.” He asks, “are you increasing in grace, or is your grace limited?” and says grace “will change that and put a focus on Jesus and his focus on others.”
Are you increasing in grace, or is your grace limited?

See, why is it that some Christians are concerned about others, are concerned about, about going to church, and are concerned about growing? They’ve entered into a dimension of grace. See, that’s influencing them. Others, they just take favor, go to heaven, wait for the rapture, that’s it. They do what they want, they stay home, they don’t pray, they don’t, you know, they can’t win souls to Christ because they don’t know the word or anything else. But others, they respond to that grace, and they grow in grace, and the more they grow, the more influence they have in helping people and changing people’s lives and bringing them to Christ. My question, or the, I should say the Holy Spirit’s question to us this morning is: are you increasing in grace, or is your grace limited? If you don’t like things or you, you don’t want to do things, you just don’t do them. You got no influence of God to overcome your personal desires and wishes and laziness and attitude and beliefs. Everything’s got to be for you and focused on you. Grace will change that and put a focus on Jesus and his focus on others to come to him and grow in him.
He says “Receive means you accept it, you take it.”
What does he say it means to hold fast to the gospel?
He says “we hang on, we don’t give up, we don’t quit,” and that if you let it go, “it doesn’t do you any good.”
Does he say the Old Testament is still for today?
Yes. He says some churches say it is not, but “the Old Testament is still for today.”
Which days does he count for the burial and resurrection?
He says Jesus died on Friday, was in the grave on Saturday, and arose on Sunday, and he calls trying “to keep Jesus in the grave for three 24-hour periods” ridiculous.
How many people does he say saw Jesus after the resurrection?
He says “there’s over 500 people that witnessed Jesus alive and well on planet Earth after he died.”
He asks “What’s another word for labor? Work.” and says the grace of God was with Paul as he labored.
Does he say grace is only something given to us?
No. He says “it also is a power that moves us.”
How does he describe grace as a divine influence?
He says it is “the divine influence or power upon the heart,” and the heart is “The mind, the emotions, and the will.”
What does he say grace did for Peter?
He says “grace moved God to reach out to Peter and bring him back,” even though Peter had denied Him.
What does he say about Jesus increasing in grace?
He says “He increased in grace” with God and men, and that grace moved Him to please the Father and to touch people.
How does he say grace differs from a favor?
He says a favor “doesn’t change him,” but “if I influence him to change to a better man, that is what grace is about.”
Does he say grace is a free gift?
Yes. He says grace “is a free gift, but you got to accept it and use it.”
What does he say grace does for worship?
He says “Grace wants you to worship God,” and that when His presence comes, “you start taking on His nature.”
Does he say everyone can be a disciple?
Yes. He says “you may not be an apostle, but you can still be a light to the world. You can be a disciple of Christ.”

p: In this message a speaker at Vine Cluster Church teaches Proverbs 4:23, “above all else guard your heart,” and says what we take in is what comes out. He compares Israel’s request for a king, Saul’s disobedience, David’s heart after God and Solomon’s turned heart. He closes with Romans 8 and Philippians 4:8 and the choice of which side, the flesh or the spirit, we feed.
What does Proverbs 4:23 mean when it says to “guard your heart”?

He says “guard your heart for everything you do flows from it,” and that in the chapter Solomon passes on what his father taught him: get wisdom, hold on to instruction and stay off “the path of the wicked.” He says “the path of the righteous is straight and full of light,” while evildoers “stumble in the darkness.”
What does Proverbs 4:23 mean when it says to “guard your heart”?

Proverbs 4:23 says above all else in other words above everything else guard your heart for everything you do flows from it when you go to the beginning of this proverb here in chapter 4 it starts out by saying and it’s Solomon talking he says listen to a father’s instruction pay attention and gain. Understanding then you go down to verse 4 it. No. He says “I don’t care if you’ve served God for five minutes or five years it still happens even if you served him for decades,” because the fleshly side “still rises up within you once in a while.”

He says “we have this king but nobody can see him but we can feel his presence,” and that other nations asked “where’s your king” and Israel’s answer was that “our king’s God.”

He says “that country was almost destroyed” because of Pharaoh’s “hardness of heart” and that “it cost him economically.”
