He says, “Are not they which eat of the sacrifices partakers of the altar? When they went to the temple to offer the burnt offering, the atoning offering, did they partake of that sacrifice and the results of that sacrifice? Atonement for sin.” And the people had to say, “What?” Yes, they were partakers. He’s got them in the communion table now. He’s got him in the Israel of old. What am I saying then? That the idol is anything? No, we know the idol is nothing. Or the food sacrificed to idols or their music or whatever is anything? No. No. We’ve got knowledge that that’s nothing. But we also have knowledge that when we partake of the communion table, we’re partaking of the body and blood of Jesus Christ. When Israel of old partook of the sacrifices and the and the shadow laws that God had them to partake of to illustrate spiritual things to come, they were partakers. Now he’s going to hit them when the iron is hot. [Unclear]. But I say the things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to devils, not to God. And I would not that you should have what? Fellowship participators with devils. He’s got them and he’s got you.
What does communion teach about partaking with idols? (1 Corinthians 10:16-21)

Proverbs 9:10: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom, And the knowledge of the Holy One is understanding. 1 Corinthians 10:16-17: The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ? For we, though many, are one bread and one body; for we all partake of that one bread. 1 Corinthians 10:18: Observe Israel after the flesh: Are not those who eat of the sacrifices partakers of the altar? 1 Corinthians 10:19-20: What am I saying then? That an idol is anything, or what is offered to idols is anything? Rather, that the things which the Gentiles sacrifice they sacrifice to demons and not to God, and I do not want you to have fellowship with demons.
What does he say American Idol shows about idolatry?

He says the show tries to “make someone into a musical idol where the teenagers especially will adore them.” He says “the focus is on sex, pleasure, partying, drinking, just a loose life. See, it’s idolatry.”
What does he say shapes the minds of young people the most?
He says music is first and TV, “the media,” is second, and “that’s why kids dress like they dress, wear their hair like they do.”
What did the Romans and Greeks believe about the afterlife?
He says for the Romans, if you were good, “you went to the Milky Way,” and for the Greeks, “you went to Hades.”
He says it was “where you could go and any God you wanted to worship was there,” so you did not have to go to a specific temple.
Why does Paul begin by talking about knowledge?
He says some in the Corinthian church “had it all figured out through human knowledge just like today,” so Paul tackles that first, and notes that “knowledge puffs up. It makes us proud.”
How does Paul deal with human thinking about spiritual problems?

He says Paul “knows his Bible,” and “he’s going to neutralize this human thinking factor in trying to find solutions to spiritual problems,” citing what the Bible already says about not being wise in your own eyes.
What does he say godliness is?
He says godliness is pleasing God, not pleasing your friend or your spouse. He says “living to please God is the final measuring stick of anything you believe.”
Does he say there is more than one way to God?
No. He says “there is no other gods” and “there isn’t any other way to God but God’s way.”
Does what you eat make you more spiritual?
He says food “has nothing to do with spirituality,” including diet and healthy eating, and that if you honor your parents and obey God’s word, he says the Bible promises long life and health.
What does Romans 14 say about eating?

He reads that one believes he may eat all things while another who is weak eats herbs, and that the one who eats should not despise the one who does not, and “let not him which eats not judge him that eats.”
What is a stumbling block in 1 Corinthians 8?

He says Paul is appealing not to their mental understanding but to their conscience, “that what you do can hurt other people,” and that your liberty can become a stumbling block to those who are weak.
Why does Paul call some believers weak?
He asks, “why do you think he’s calling them weak?” and answers that it is to make them “feel more important. We love it. We like to be the one that’s better. But wait till he gets done with it.”
What does he say most Christians do when they read the Bible?
He says “they read passages in the Bible and they come up with human thinking instead of the mind of the spirit.”
What does he conclude about people being offended?
He says he finally decided “I’m just going to do what I know is right. And if they get offended, that’s their problem. And that was a big freedom.”
Does he say Christians should never judge?

He says Paul tells them to judge what he is saying: “Here he is telling us to judge what he’s saying.” He contrasts that with “Judge not, let you be not judged,” and says the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom.

p: In this message Pastor David G. Kincer continues 1 Corinthians 10, teaching that the cup of the Lord and the cup of devils cannot be shared and that churches cannot be built on human opinions. He gives Paul’s practical advice about meat sold in the market and offered to idols, then turns to Acts 15:29, greed as idolatry, and the works of the flesh. He closes by arguing from James 2 and Revelation 2 that believers should not say “my faith” but follow the faith of Jesus.
What does it mean to sacrifice to devils and create your own religion? (Leviticus 17:7)

He says it is “Old Testament stuff”: they sacrificed “to devils, not to God, to gods whom they knew not.” He says “they created their own religion. And when you create your own religion, you’re going the way of Satan,” and he cites Leviticus 17:7, “They shall no more offer their sacrifices unto” devils.
What does it mean to sacrifice to devils and create your own religion? (Leviticus 17:7)

Well, what do you mean, to sacrifice to the devils? Well, it’s Old Testament stuff, basic. People know this that read their Bible. They sacrificed to devils, not to God, to gods whom they knew not. To knew God, they created their own religion. And when you create your own religion, you’re going the way of Satan. See, he loves for you to alter the one true God and the Bible that tells us how to get there. He’s just quoting Old Testament Scripture, Leviticus 17:7: “They shall no more offer their sacrifices unto” what? Devils. To idols, their own.
What does it mean to sacrifice to devils and create your own religion? (Leviticus 17:7)
Leviticus 17:7: They shall no more offer their sacrifices to demons, after whom they have played the harlot. This shall be a statute forever for them throughout their generations.” ’
Can you drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of devils? (1 Corinthians 10:21-22)

He says Paul’s point is “they’re not compatible.” Using your human understanding that an idol is nothing to “violate the direct commandments of God and provoke God to jealousy” is, he says, saying “we are God”: “You don’t come out and say it, you just do it with your beliefs, from your human thinking.”
Can you drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of devils? (1 Corinthians 10:21-22)

Religion isn’t that good. Hallelujah. Verse 21, still in 1 Corinthians chapter 10:21: “You can’t drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of devils, nor be partakers of the Lord’s table and of the table of devils.” They’re not compatible. “Do we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than He?” Because you got some human understanding that an idol is nothing and the meat sacrificed to the idol is nothing, do you use that understanding to violate the direct commandments of God and provoke God to jealousy? Are you stronger than God? Have you become a God? And when we do our own religious ways, come up with our own way of serving God--
Can you drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of devils? (1 Corinthians 10:21-22)

1 Corinthians 10:21-22: You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons; you cannot partake of the Lord’s table and of the table of demons. Or do we provoke the Lord to jealousy? Are we stronger than He?
What does “all things are lawful for me, but not all things are profitable” mean? (1 Corinthians 10:23)

He says you can do something “because of your human understanding of it,” but it is unprofitable because you start “taking on the nature, as we read earlier, of the religion that you’re embracing.” He asks how going into a pagan temple builds up the church, and says “that’s what we’re doing in America: we’re making our own religions, we’re coming up with our own way, and we just throw Jesus into it.”
What does “all things are lawful for me, but not all things are profitable” mean? (1 Corinthians 10:23)

We are saying we are God. You don’t come out and say it, you just do it with your beliefs, from your human thinking. Do you get it? He approached the human thinking way of justifying doing something against Scripture, and then he comes in with the spiritual allegory, the spiritual illustration, very powerful. “All things are lawful for me.” Yeah, you can eat the food, yeah, you can do it because of your human understanding of it, “but all things are not profitable.” What’s the profit in you doing it? There’s no profit there at all. In fact, you keep doing it, it’s going to be unprofitable, because you’re going to start what? Taking on the nature, as we read earlier, of the religion that you’re embracing. You’re going to take on the nature. You’re going to have eyes that see not, ears that hear not, a mouth that can’t speak-- Anymore. Isn’t that right? “All things are lawful for me, but all things” what? “Edify not.” It doesn’t build up. How? What does me, my liberty going into a pagan temple, how does that build me up, and how does that build the church up, when I’m directly violating the Ten Commandments and other commandments? How does that edify the church? It just what? Doesn’t. Isn’t this argument good? And folks, that’s what we’re doing in America: we’re making our own religions, we’re coming up with our own way, and we just throw Jesus into it, and it’s not profitable and it’s not edifying. Can I hear an--
What does “all things are lawful for me, but not all things are profitable” mean? (1 Corinthians 10:23)
1 Corinthians 10:23: All things are lawful for me, but not all things are helpful; all things are lawful for me, but not all things edify.
Can you build a healthy church on human opinions or denominations?

He says “you can’t build a healthy church and violate God’s Word,” and “it must be Jesus, His truth, His words, and the apostles’ doctrine.” He says “being a Baptist has nothing to do with anything. Being a Catholic has nothing to do with anything,” and that Paul gives a practical solution next “because Christians get weird.”
Can you build a healthy church on human opinions or denominations?

Amen. Conclusion of this approach, the spiritual approach, the spiritual illustration: do not partake of idols nor food sacrificed to idols. His conclusion was the same in both approaches. I like this guy, Paul. You can’t build a healthy church and violate God’s Word. You can’t build a healthy church, you’ve been using human understanding. You must have the mind of the Spirit. You cannot build a healthy church using your own opinions and your own beliefs. It must be Jesus, His truth, His words, and the apostles’ doctrine, who got their doctrine straight from Jesus. So Calvin, Wesley, and all the rest down through, or Roberts, Billy Graham, have nothing to do with anything. I must build my Christianity on Jesus Christ, His words, His truths. Amen. Being a Baptist has nothing to do with anything. Being a Catholic has nothing to do with anything. Verse 25 of chapter 10, 1 Corinthians 10:25: now here’s the practical solution. And why is he bringing out the practical? Because Christians get weird. You know, we read in the Bible, uh, to be modest. Well, then we decide, well, I can’t wear short-sleeve shirts, I can’t wear shorts, I can’t wear jewelry, or, and the Bible says don’t, women, don’t decorate yourself with your hair, don’t fix your hair up, and, and, and outward adorning of makeup and jewelry and all this stuff. So we don’t wear jew-- it doesn’t say jewelry there, but then we don’t wear jewelry, and we look like death warmed over, and we want to get a handsome man.
What extremes do Christians fall into?

He says “we go to extremes,” and recalls growing up in Pentecost churches where people wrote “spirit writing” that “made no sense.” Of people who say they have a word from God for you, he asks, “why do I need to keep getting words of God from people when I have the Bible, which the Bible says is a more sure word of prophecy?”
What extremes do Christians fall into?

And see, we go to extremes. You know, Pentecostalism, I grew up in Pentecost churches, and they had spirit writing, “Holy Ghost, come home,” and they’d write something and it made no sense, and all kinds of goony stuff. Today it’s a prophecy: “I got a prophecy, I got a word from God for you.” Well, why do I need to keep getting words of God from people when I have the Bible, which the Bible says is a more sure word of prophecy? I mean, what’s the problem here? Is it so you can--we--you can feed your ego by feeling like you know you’re in touch with God and I’m not? And I can go on and on. The Catholics and their holy water and their images, come on.
What extremes do Christians fall into?
2 Peter 1:19: And so we have the prophetic word confirmed, which you do well to heed as a light that shines in a dark place, until the day dawns and the morning star rises in your hearts;
Should Christians ask questions about food sold in the market or served at a feast? (1 Corinthians 10:25-27)

He says “don’t get weird in this stuff whatsoever.” About meat sold in the market, “ask no questions for conscience’ sake. Just buy the meat, because you already know it means nothing,” and at an unbeliever’s feast eat what is set before you, since over-investigating makes “a miserable life for ourselves.”
Should Christians ask questions about food sold in the market or served at a feast? (1 Corinthians 10:25-27)

Church, we got to approach God His way, and so we can’t get extreme. And so he’s going to give a practical thing: don’t get weird in this stuff whatsoever. “Sold in the marketplace,” the meat market, “ask no questions for conscience’ sake.” Just buy the meat, because you already know it means nothing. You know, don’t be one of these weird Christians: “Is it got the stamp? Is it culture? Is it got the Christian approval on it?” Don’t get--don’t investigate, just buy the stuff and go eat it. Doesn’t that make sense? But oh no, us-than-thou people, us witch hunters, we got to--we got to dissect and [unclear] everything, we don’t want any, and we--we create a miserable life for ourselves. “Ask no questions for the conscience’ sake. If any believer bid you to a feast, and you go, whatsoever is set before you”--any unbeliever, now they’re going to an unbeliever’s house, they’re throwing a festival, and it’s probably around their idol, because that’s what they did--“just what is set before you, eat, asking no questions for conscience’ sake.”
Should Christians ask questions about food sold in the market or served at a feast? (1 Corinthians 10:25-27)

1 Corinthians 10:25: Eat whatever is sold in the meat market, asking no questions for conscience’ sake; 1 Corinthians 10:27: If any of those who do not believe invites you to dinner, and you desire to go, eat whatever is set before you, asking no question for conscience’ sake.
When should you not eat meat that was offered to idols? (1 Corinthians 10:28-29)

He says if someone tells you it was offered in sacrifice to idols, “don’t eat it, for whose conscience’ sake? His, the one who told you,” so you don’t “offend the conscience of the other one, even the idolater.” He then says that in his youth things like pool were called sin, and “now we’re going to the other thing: everything’s okay, now there is no restraints.”
When should you not eat meat that was offered to idols? (1 Corinthians 10:28-29)

“Whose conscience? If any say it’s offered in sacrifice to idols, don’t eat it, for whose conscience’ sake?” His, the one who told you. See, now the cat’s out of the bag, you know, to obey the Scriptures. So you go, you know, “I’ll--I’ll just eat the potatoes and beans today.” Why? Because you don’t want to offend the conscience of the other one, even the idolater who knows you shouldn’t be eating meat sacrificed to his god. That’s why he brought it up. Then you can say, “Well, I didn’t know. I--I won’t have any of that, thank you. Just give me the mashed potatoes and the gravy and the beans, and everything will be fine.” Are you there? Is this good or what? Oh, this is--see, back in my day you couldn’t even have a deck of cards in your house. Back in my day, my teenage, you could not play billiards, pool. That was sin. Why? Because all the pool tables were in the bars or a pool hall where all the hoods and everybody hung out. So instead of saying the atmosphere was wrong, we--they just said playing pool, “that’s the devil’s game, man, that’s a sin.” And how many, you know, there’s nothing wrong with playing pool. How many, you know, I got a pool table in my garage. See, we got extreme, but now we’re going to the other thing: everything’s okay, now there is no restraints.
When should you not eat meat that was offered to idols? (1 Corinthians 10:28-29)

1 Corinthians 10:28-29: But if anyone says to you, “This was offered to idols,” do not eat it for the sake of the one who told you, and for conscience’ sake; for “the earth is the LORD’s, and all its fullness.” “Conscience,” I say, not your own, but that of the other. For why is my liberty judged by another man’s conscience?
What did the Jerusalem church decide about meat offered to idols, blood and things strangled? (Acts 15:29)

He says the apostles, elders and members “unanimously made it clear” in Acts 15:29 to “abstain from meats offered to idols,” and “100% unanimously voted yes.” On blood and things strangled, he says it relates to Christ’s blood sacrifice: “we only eat of His blood in the communion table,” because “the shedding of blood was imperative for the forgiveness of sins in the Bible from the beginning.”
What did the Jerusalem church decide about meat offered to idols, blood and things strangled? (Acts 15:29)

But isn’t this good? Isn’t this practical? You know, the Bible says in Ecclesiastes, “do not be extreme in anything.” Okay, and so we need to watch out with being extreme. We need to be practical. Now, the apostles, the elders, and the members of the church in Jerusalem unanimously made it clear--unanimously means they were not divided, which was the first topic that he talked about for four chapters, went to division--this church is in unity, and they make it very clear, Acts 15:29: “Abstain, abstain from meats offered to idols.” Is that clear? The apostles, the elders of the church, and the members, 100% unanimously voted yes, this is what we’re to follow. And these people, with their human thinking, were violating what they had already come up with. Can I hear an amen? Are you there? Through their human thinking. And he says, “from blood and things strangled.” Now, why do you think they said, don’t partake of blood and don’t eat of meat strangled? Because it’s related to Christ’s blood sacrifice for us. The blood had to be shed. You know, you can drink blood and you won’t die from it. You know, blood is a food, and unless it has germs and bacteria and disease in it, you’re not going to catch anything. Okay, a lot of nations and cultures eat blood, blood of cows and so forth. They will cut the vein in the neck of a cow-- Let the blood come out, just shoots out, fill up their cup, then they put pressure on the wound, and in just a few seconds the blood stops flowing. They drink their blood. See, it’s a food, but we don’t do it because of what Christ shed His blood, and so we only eat of His blood in the communion table, and we only partake of the thing that was shedding blood, not strangled, because the shedding of blood was imperative for the forgiveness of sins in the Bible from the beginning. Are you with me? It had nothing to do with being bad. Yes, the shedding of blood in Genesis--
What did the Jerusalem church decide about meat offered to idols, blood and things strangled? (Acts 15:29)
Acts 15:29: that you abstain from things offered to idols, from blood, from things strangled, and from sexual immorality. If you keep yourselves from these, you will do well. Farewell.
What does he say about Catholic idols and believers who still keep rituals? (Acts 21:20)

He says that “according to Paul, they’re wrong,” but “before you condemn them to hell” he points to Acts 21:20, where thousands of Jews who believed were still “doing the shadow laws that Christ fulfilled.” He says “people can actually be a believer in Christ and be doing things in an erroneous way and still be a believer,” and “you better start looking at yourself and at the Bible.”
What does he say about Catholic idols and believers who still keep rituals? (Acts 21:20)

Three, God sacrificed the first animal. Okay. And “from fornication”: sexual immorality. What was the second topic? Sexual immorality. Just thought I’d pass that on. Now, what about the Catholic idols? Well, obviously, according to Paul, they’re wrong. According to the Scriptures, they’re wrong. Can I hear an amen? They’re using human knowledge to clear their conscience of having something and having people partake in something that they should not be doing. Now, whether you like it or not, and whether your family’s Catholic or not, I’m sorry, when you’re wrong, you’re just what? Wrong. But using Paul’s wisdom, before you condemn them to hell, let’s take a little further look. Acts 21:20: Paul had come down to Jerusalem to, uh, sacrifice at the temple and preach the gospel down there in Jerusalem, and the apostles come to him and the leaders, and they say, “You see, Paul, how many thousands of Jews there are which believe.” See, there were thousands of Jews that came to the temple for the same feast of Israel, and this guy, these people, say, the leaders say, there are thousands of Jews which what? Believe. Are they believers? Are they believers? Yeah, it plainly says what they’re-- Believers, “but they are all zealous of the law.” They’re still offering animal sacrifices, they’re still burning incense, they’re still wearing certain clothes, they’re still doing the shadow laws that Christ fulfilled and have nothing to do now with anything in the shadow. We are now participators of the truth of those laws. Hello, church. I see, I had to work through this, because in the circles I was in, the Catholics were the [unclear] on the hill. In Revelation. They were the beast. You know, they were the church of, you know, man, man, you know, you’re a Catholic, boom, you’re dead, you’re gone, you’re, you’re hopeless. And it took God opening my understanding to things, that people can actually be a believer in Christ and be doing things in an erroneous way and still be a believer, because they haven’t learned or come to the place yet where they can let go of the rituals and just embrace the truth. Now, folks, that is good stuff. So before you condemn them, you better start looking at yourself and at the Bible. Okay. Now, what about Protestant idols? Oh, Protestants don’t have idols. Oh, they don’t? You didn’t know Protestants had idols?
What does he say about Catholic idols and believers who still keep rituals? (Acts 21:20)
Acts 21:20: And when they heard it, they glorified the Lord. And they said to him, “You see, brother, how many myriads of Jews there are who have believed, and they are all zealous for the law;
Are there Protestant idols, and is greed idolatry? (Colossians 3:5)

He says America is not into images: “they worship things that they should not worship.” Reading Colossians 3:5, he says greed is idolatry, and he criticizes the prosperity message, saying he watched ministers “talk senior citizens into giving their whole Social Security check.” But being rich does not make a person greedy: “the Bible doesn’t back up that at all.”
Are there Protestant idols, and is greed idolatry? (Colossians 3:5)

Well, they wouldn’t have an image. No Protestant church would have an image. I told you at the beginning that America wasn’t into images, they’re into things. They worship things that they should not worship. Well, show me a Protestant idol. Okay, glad you asked. First Colossians, that shouldn’t be First Colossians, I put that one in there to--never mind. Colossians 3:5: “Mortify, put to death, therefore, your members which are upon the earth”: sexual immorality, that’s one of the topics he talked about, “impurity, lust, evil desires.” That was the source of division. “I want it my way, I want it my way, and if you don’t go my way, I can’t go anywhere with you.” Division, and “greed, which is” what? “Idolatry.” Oh, greed is idolatry. Ew. Kenyon, Oral Roberts, A. A. Allen, T. L. Osborn, Kenneth Hagin, Jimmy Swaggart, Jim Bakker, Robert Tilton, Benny Hinn, Kenneth Copeland, Creflo Dollar, Eddie Long, Joyce Meyer, Paula White are just the few in the Protestant-- Arena that promote prosperity is what God wants for everyone. The prosperity message is promoted by all of these big men, and who? It’s a Ponzi scheme. You give to Kenneth Copeland, God will bless you; you give the dollar, God will bless you. The Ponzi scheme is: the ones on the top get what? The money, they get the benefit, and the ones down here get nothing. And I watched this as a young Christian in the church world. I watched these ministers talk senior citizens into giving their whole Social Security check, and I knew these senior citizens, I knew they just barely survived and barely lived. I even went up to them and I says, “You know, that old lady over there sitting beside me dropped in her whole paycheck, her whole Social Security. You know, you--aren’t you going to give that back?” “No way, man.” They had their Rolls-Royce Silver Shadow sitting out there, they had $500 suits. “Nothing is too good for the man of God.” I had to work through this stuff. See, you’re lucky, I’m telling you the truth. You don’t have to figure this stuff out. Greed is what? Idolatry. Now, does it mean because a person is rich that they’re greedy? No, the Bible doesn’t back up that at all. If a person goes to college, learns a good job skill, and they make good money of being a lawyer or doctor or whatever, that’s just the good old capitalistic system, and the system that the Bible--
Are there Protestant idols, and is greed idolatry? (Colossians 3:5)
Colossians 3:5: Therefore put to death your members which are on the earth: fornication, uncleanness, passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry.
What are “individual idols,” and what are the works of the flesh? (Galatians 5:19-21)

He says individual idols, neither Protestant nor Catholic, are “wrong” according to Paul. In Galatians 5:19 “the works of the flesh are evident. They’re very clear, they’re very plain,” and he says the list, including idolatry, division and quarreling, belongs to “the topic of division that Paul covered”; “you’re carnal, you’re babies when you do this.”
What are “individual idols,” and what are the works of the flesh? (Galatians 5:19-21)

Promotes. And the sad thing is, these ministers just keep finding new suckers to support them, because they promise some miracles and they promise them, you know, “God’s going to, it’s going to be amazing, people just come, come along and give you money that you wouldn’t even know about,” and it doesn’t happen. Are you there? Now, the Catholic church, I can’t find any of this taught in the Catholic church. It’s Protestant. Hallelujah. Okay, what about individual idols? Individual idols, not Protestant, not Catholic. Well, according to Paul, they’re wrong, although they use human knowledge to clear their conscience. Galatians 5:19: “The works of the flesh are evident.” They’re very clear, they’re very plain. Okay, the bottom line: the works of the flesh will not inherit what? The kingdom of God. So what are the works of the flesh? Well, “adultery, fornication,” what Paul-- Addressed in his seminar on church growth, “uncleanness, envy, lewdness, idolatry,” what Paul is addressing now. Idolatry is a what? Work of the flesh. So if idolatry is in there, then any work of the flesh is what? Idolatry. “Spiritual adultery, sorcery, witchcraft, hatred”: you don’t like a certain race, you don’t like women because they’re women, or men because they’re men, or rich because they’re rich. “Hatred, wrath, contention, selfish ambitions, and dissensions”: quarreling, selfish ambition--do you want it your way?--and division are all in the topic of division that Paul covered. Are you there? It’s a work of what? The flesh. In fact, that’s what Paul said, it’s a work of the flesh. You’re carnal, you’re babies when you do this. “Jealousies, heresies, murders, drunkenness”--
What are “individual idols,” and what are the works of the flesh? (Galatians 5:19-21)

Galatians 5:19-21: Now the works of the flesh are evident, which are: adultery, fornication, uncleanness, lewdness, idolatry, sorcery, hatred, contentions, jealousies, outbursts of wrath, selfish ambitions, dissensions, heresies, envy, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and the like; of which I tell you beforehand, just as I also told you in time past, that those who practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.
Does the church adopt what culture pressures it to accept, and how do I examine myself?

He says “in every generation the church warms up to it in America and accepts it, and everybody’s okay, when it’s really idolatry.” Turning to the listener, he asks about drunkenness, hatred, jealousy, adultery and horoscopes and says “before we start straightening everybody else out, we need to” straighten ourselves out.
Does the church adopt what culture pressures it to accept, and how do I examine myself?

Intoxication. A big thing now is Christians getting drunk. We can get tattoos, no problem, our body is a, uh, what do they call the artist [unclear]? Yeah, and so I’m putting “Jesus saves” on my arm, hallelujah. Man, when the Bible prohibits it. Works “is dead.” Don’t say “my faith.” I will know your faith by how you act, how you speak, what you speak, what you do. That’s the first place that’s used.

James 2:18: But someone will say, “You have faith, and I have works.” Show me your faith without your works, and I will show you my faith by my works. Whose faith is “My faith” in Revelation 2, and why use the name of Jesus?

He says in Revelation 2 Jesus says “You have not denied My faith,” and asks “whose faith? Who’s speaking there? Jesus Christ.” Jesus “was persuaded that He was God, that He was the Son of God, that He was the Savior of the world, that no man could get eternal life but through Him.” He says to use the name of Jesus because “God” is “a general word that can fit into anywhere.”
Whose faith is “My faith” in Revelation 2, and why use the name of Jesus?

Second place, before you condemn them to hell, my little thing: in Revelation 2:12, to the church of Pergamos, “I know your works.” Faith without works is dead. “You have not denied My faith.” Whose faith? Who’s speaking there? Jesus Christ. Only used two times. The first one is, my faith must be accompanied with works that Jesus said for me to do, or it’s dead. Here Jesus plainly says it is “My faith” that you should-- Have. What was Jesus persuaded in? Jesus was persuaded that He was God, that He was the Son of God, that He was the Savior of the world, that no man could get eternal life but through Him. Jesus was persuaded in the Bible faith, God’s faith. He was persuaded that He would do nothing without the will of the Father. Are you there, church? That’s the faith of Jesus Christ. Did Jesus sin? No. He said, “Yeah, well, He’s God.” Yes, but we should be pursuing the goal, shouldn’t we? Hallelujah. Even to martyrdom they would keep the faith of Christ, even if it cost them their life. If they were in a bad marriage, they wouldn’t give in to the bad spouse; they would keep the faith of Christ even if that spouse left them. If they had a rebellious son or daughter that wanted to do something else, they would keep the faith of Christ no matter what that child-- Did. So the real statement should not be “my faith,” but “the Bible.” If we believe the Bible, it says, yes, we should say, “Yes, I’m a Christian and I follow Jesus and His Word.” Why is it important to use the name of Jesus? Because today “God” is a general word that can fit into anywhere, but they hate Jesus. Even though He’s God, they don’t want Jesus, because of what Jesus stood for. They want the freedom to go to heaven and have eternal life without a lifestyle that represents Jesus Christ.
Whose faith is “My faith” in Revelation 2, and why use the name of Jesus?

Revelation 2:12-13: “And to the angel of the church in Pergamos write, ‘These things says He who has the sharp two-edged sword: “I know your works, and where you dwell, where Satan’s throne is. Can faith alone save a person, and what is “faith in your faith”? (James 2:14)

You get his argument. “Can faith save him?” And Paul is asking this question, and why? Because in America faith is all you need. The Baptist faith is all you need, you can live any way you want, but if you believe in Jesus, you’re going to heaven. That’s the truth. Can faith without works save anyone? That’s what James is saying. Am I talking to the right people? And these preachers in Protestant arenas that preach prosperity back it up with faith. Faith and prosperity is their message. And when you have faith in your faith, or faith in a church, or faith in a minister-- You don’t have the right faith. Now, I think this is liberating stuff. You’re looking at me like, “Man, this is deep.” Do you know how many people I know that have faith in their faith, and the Bible never says to have faith in your faith? We’re to have the faith that Jesus had, faith in God, faith in God’s Word, and be living and believing what He says. I may not be there yet, but I’m working on it. See, there’s a difference. One says, “I don’t see nothing wrong with this,” the other one says, “You know, I’m working on this. I’m working on--I haven’t got through this one yet, but I’m working on it, and God promised me that I will get through it, and I’ll get to another arena, and there’ll be another one.”
Can faith alone save a person, and what is “faith in your faith”? (James 2:14)
James 2:14: What does it profit, my brethren, if someone says he has faith but does not have works? Can faith save him?
Is atheism a kind of faith?

He says those who hold beliefs such as atheism “have faith in what they believe.” He says the Supreme Court declared atheism a religion “because they have a belief system. They believe there’s no God, and they have no evidence there is--that there isn’t one. That is faith, that is belief.”
Is atheism a kind of faith?

Amen. Atheists, evolutionists, humanists, homosexuals, the freethinkers, pro-choice, the liberals, Democrats, the Socialist Party, all have faith in what they believe. It’s totally faith. The evolutionists have no evidence; it’s totally faith. The socialists have evidence that socialism has not worked, and they still believe socialism will work. That’s a fact, and it’s never-- Worked. That’s their faith. See, it doesn’t edify, it doesn’t profit anybody else. And all of these are 501(c)(3), just like our religious exemption. They say they’re nonprofit corporations, they’re religions, they’re a belief system. The Supreme Court declared atheism a religion because they have a belief system. They believe there’s no God, and they have no evidence there is--that there isn’t one. That is faith, that is belief.

He says it asks whether you use human understanding to “violate the direct commandments of God and provoke God to jealousy.” He asks, “Are you stronger than God? Have you become a God?”

He says “all things are lawful for me, but all things” do not edify. He asks how his liberty in going into a pagan temple builds him up or the church “when I’m directly violating the Ten Commandments and other commandments.”

He says you cannot build a healthy church “using your own opinions and your own beliefs. It must be Jesus, His truth, His words, and the apostles’ doctrine, who got their doctrine straight from Jesus.”
Why does he point to the Bible when people say they have a word from God?
He asks, “why do I need to keep getting words of God from people when I have the Bible, which the Bible says is a more sure word of prophecy?”
Does he say playing pool is a sin?

No. He says “there’s nothing wrong with playing pool,” and that he has a pool table in his garage. He says in his youth it was called sin because the tables were in bars, “so instead of saying the atmosphere was wrong,” people called the game itself sin.

He says “the Bible says in Ecclesiastes, ‘do not be extreme in anything.’” He says “we need to watch out with being extreme. We need to be practical.”
Why did the apostles say to abstain from blood and things strangled?
He says it is “because it’s related to Christ’s blood sacrifice for us. The blood had to be shed.”
Does he say a person in a church with rituals cannot be a believer?

No. He says it took God opening his understanding that “people can actually be a believer in Christ and be doing things in an erroneous way and still be a believer because they haven’t learned or come to the place yet where they can let go of the rituals and just embrace the truth.”
Does he say rich people are greedy?
No. He asks, “does it mean because a person is rich that they’re greedy? No, the Bible doesn’t back up that at all.”
Is hatred listed among the works of the flesh?

He reads it in the list and says hatred is when “you don’t like a certain race,” or women because they are women, or men because they are men, or rich because they are rich. He says it is a work of the flesh.
What does he say about reading the horoscope?
He asks, “do you read the horoscope every day?” and says “that’s an idol.” He says “before we start straightening everybody else out,” we need to straighten ourselves out.
How many times is “my faith” used in the Bible?
He says it is “only mentioned twice in the Bible”: the first place is James, where a person says “show me your faith without your works,” and the second is Jesus speaking to the church of Pergamos.
What does he say Jesus was persuaded of?

He says Jesus “was persuaded that He was God, that He was the Son of God, that He was the Savior of the world, that no man could get eternal life but through Him,” and that He “would do nothing without the will of the Father.”
Why does he say it matters to use the name of Jesus?
He says “God” is “a general word that can fit into anywhere, but they hate Jesus,” and they want “the freedom to go to heaven and have eternal life without a lifestyle that represents Jesus Christ.”

p: In the second part of Intro to Bible Economics, Pastor David G. Kincer describes the wise worker from Proverbs and Ecclesiastes: honest, diligent, educated, skilled and keeping up with technology. He teaches that two are better than one in marriage and work, that Paul commanded “if anyone will not work, neither shall he eat,” and that a believer who will not provide for his family is worse than an unbeliever.
What is a wise worker, according to Proverbs? (Proverbs 13:11; 14:23)

He says a wise worker does not gain dishonest wealth; the employee should give an honest day’s work and the employer an honest day’s pay. He says if employers paid employees as they would like to be paid “we’d have this thing cured and that’s Christian character,” and in all labor there is profit, but idle chatter leads only to poverty.

Amen.
